log: Rolls-Royce commits to the Joint Venture

public_statements.boeing:
Five years ago I said I thought we'd turned the ship. I'm comfortable now saying it's turned. The 737 line has run steady at the rate we set. We keep adding 787 capacity in Charleston, and the balance sheet is where it belongs and has stayed there. That isn't luck. It's a lot of people doing it the right way, every day.

Over the next several years more customers will want 737s than we're going to build. I know that's frustrating for some of them, and I don't take it lightly. But I'd much rather have a customer waiting than a production system that goes unstable again. The KPIs tell us when we can do more, not the calendar.

On a new airplane, how we decide hasn't changed. We will do a new airplane when the market and the technology and we're ready, and all three have to be there. We're in good shape financially and the technology is coming along, but the business case isn't there yet. I'm not going to launch an airplane to meet a date. We're keeping the work going on the airplane and on how we'd build it, so we're prepared when the case is there. When we do launch, the airplane will be planned around a stable supply of parts, engines first, with more than one engine source and durability ahead of everything else. I won't give you a date before we're ready to launch. When we launch, there'll be headroom in the schedule, and we won't take on development at a fixed price.

We'll keep working with the rest of the industry for a tariff-free environment in aerospace. That's good for everybody in this business.

It is so much more important that we do this right than fast.
public_statements.airbus: Our core principles of safety, quality, integrity, compliance and security will remain at the heart of all we do. Our next-generation single-aisle aircraft is in development, and it is the centre of our work to prepare the Airbus of the 2030s. We continue to plan for it to enter service in the second half of this decade, once its technologies, its production system and its engines are mature. Safety and quality come before the calendar. Its engine selection stays open to all three narrowbody engine makers, and we plan for a dual-source engine supply, with each engine entering service only once its durability is proven. How the engine makers organise themselves is their decision. A stable, diversified supply of parts, engines first, is a condition of a disciplined and controlled production ramp-up. The A320neo family, with its two engine options, stays in production through the transition: its lines keep running longer while the new aircraft ramps up, so customers are served without a break. We are giving our suppliers long-range signals for that ramp, and we continue to secure our own materials and work packages. We take on one major development at a time and fund it from our own cash flow, preserving our financial flexibility and a strong balance sheet. With our partners across the industry, on both sides of the Atlantic, we keep working for a tariff-free, zero-for-zero trade regime in civil aerospace. And we keep recruiting and training, in Europe and across our global footprint, the people who will design and build the Airbus of the 2030s.
public_statements.cfm:
Safety, quality, delivery and cost, always in that order. That's how we run this business, and it's how we made this call.

Here's what we know. CFM, with our partners at Safran, is on Airbus's next single-aisle, and we appreciate the confidence. We'll support that airplane with the LEAP family, and we'll earn our place on it every day, on time on wing. LEAP-1A durability hardware is in every new -1A engine and is going into the fleet through the shops. On the -1B, we'll tell you the results when the fleet data is in. The GEnx upgrade is ready for our 787 customers.

Here's what we don't know: when the next new narrowbodies will be launched, by whom, and on which engines. That's really not for us to say; it's the airframers' call. We don't have a birthright on that next order. We intend to earn it. A LEAP derivative is on offer to every airframer, and CFM will commit a new engine with a committed airframer.

RISE stays all in as technology, together with Safran. When that architecture enters service is really not for us to say. We'll tell you about dates when the testing tells us.

We get paid in dollars, not in percentages. It's that simple, ain't that hard.
public_statements.pratt_whitney: I'll start with what we still owe our customers. For years the GTF fleet was not where it needed to be, and we own that. The next engine will be judged on time on wing, and that is how we will judge it ourselves. So we control what we can control. GTF2, launched in 2030, is in its last year of development and is due to be ready in 2036, six years from launch. It is not proven yet, and it will be proven before it enters service. Airbus has named Pratt & Whitney alongside CFM and Rolls-Royce for its next-generation single-aisle, and we intend to earn that place. GTF2 will not enter service until its durability is proven: endurance testing in severe environments, life-limited parts at full life at entry into service, and time on wing before fuel burn. We will not compress testing to make a date. Any feature that is not proven in time waits for a later block. We will sign Airbus's rate-gated supply agreements on standard terms. We are planning our castings and forgings ahead of the ramp, and the fleet flying today keeps first call on material. For any airframer that selects Pratt & Whitney, GTF2 comes on standard terms. We're not in the early entry phase. The GTF Hot Section kit remains available at shop visit, and we will report its time on wing once the fleet has proven it. We have no Joint Venture to announce: we share risk and investment with partners, not our core technology. We speak for our engines, not for any airframer's dates or rates. We have learned our lesson from the prior iterations of the GTF. These are responsible bets with responsible paybacks.
public_statements.rolls_royce: So. Rolls-Royce commits to a Joint Venture with Pratt & Whitney for the next narrowbody. Our preference has always been partnership, and there is no change of strategy. The commitment stands, for an airframe that has chosen both of us, on terms that credit the technology we bring. No solo narrowbody programme. The engine enters service only when it is ready and its durability is proven. Maturity sets the date, and we compress nothing. Support through partner shops will be in place before entry into service. Widebody is our core, and we will protect it. We are not after market share. We won't do anything not profitable. I will say that categorically.
public_statements.embraer:
Safety first and quality always: that is the foundation of our culture. We believe we are still in our harvest season, right? We keep delivering our plan with the products we have: the E2 family, our executive jets, defence and services. And we keep a healthy balance sheet to support a potential next move.

On a new airplane I will give the same answer I always give. We are investing in new technologies so that we are prepared to make that decision when the time comes. A launch needs a strong product with a strong value proposition and a robust, I mean, funding strategy, because we don't want to put in risk the financial health of the company. We have done the work, and the numbers today do not prove the return. So today we have no decision to announce, and we will not discuss a segment or a date. We continue to talk to our partners, including in Korea, and to all the engine makers. Any large investment will be made with partners, with the funding defined at the time of approval. I will not say conservative, but I would say, realistic.

On the decisions of other manufacturers: those are their decisions. We have our own strategy, and I can only speak for Embraer.

On trade, Embraer is about engineering. We focus on data and things that are under our control. More than 40% of our aircraft is US content, so tariffs mean fewer US parts bought and fewer US jobs. We continue to work with both governments for zero tariffs in aerospace, and we are cautiously optimistic.

We compete hard in every campaign, but we don't sell our aircraft below cost. As we proudly say in Embraer, We Live for the Challenge.

boeing.detail: Production capacity for 787 rates in the teens, not a development program [BX-1317, B-2336]. Funded inside the debt lines. Not priced on the board. Pope finds that the added 787 demand fits inside it.

boeing.move: Next-narrowbody engine requirement: a stable, multi-source engine supply (restated)
boeing.detail: We tell CFM, P&W and Rolls-Royce again that Boeing's next narrowbody will be planned around a stable supply of parts, engines first, with more than one engine source and durability first [BX-1298]. No launch, no date and no engine selection this round. It serves Control's engine enabler at no grid cost (Board recommendation 5).

boeing.move: Zero-for-zero tariffs in civil aerospace, with the industry
boeing.detail: We keep working with industry associations for a tariff-free regime for aircraft and parts. A tariff-free environment is good for every company in the industry [B-2290]. No grid effect.

airbus.move: NGSA engine selection stays open to all three makers (code 7, final)
airbus.detail: We restate that NGSA's selection names CFM, Pratt & Whitney and Rolls-Royce. CFM is the floor and P&W GTF2 is the planned second source. Each engine enters service only once its durability is proven. How the engine makers organise themselves is their decision, and we neither invite nor discourage any partnership. We offer no payment, advance or take-or-pay to induce any engine launch (anything above EUR 300m would be a separate Board item, and none is proposed). We exchange no confidential information [A-0243, A-0360, AX-0054].

airbus.move: Long-range, rate-gated supply signals for the 2037-45 ramp
airbus.detail: We give CFM and P&W signals early, as for the A320neo ramp, covering the LEAP-1A and GTF tail on the A320 Alt plan and the NGSA engine sets. They are sized to our own needs only: on two sources our CFM call stays at or below today's 51 sets a month (Wagner). We announce them in general terms only, with no volumes and no internal plan targets [A-0159, AX-0005].

airbus.move: Secure our own materials and work packages
airbus.detail: Titanium through Aubert & Duval, additive manufacturing, the raw-materials watchlist, and the Spirit work packages fully integrated. All of it serves our own ramp only [AX-0060, AX-0061, AX-0062, AX-0063].

airbus.move: Recruiting and training for the 2039-44 ramp and the Airbus of the 2030s
airbus.detail: Our own hiring, apprenticeships and training, in Europe and across our global footprint. It targets no rival's staff [A-0485, A-0366].

airbus.move: Zero-for-zero trade advocacy in an industry coalition
airbus.detail: With industry associations on both sides of the Atlantic, Boeing included as an ally on trade. It stays strictly to public trade policy, with no exchange of pricing, capacity, programme or engine-selection information [AX-0088, AX-0046].

cfm.move: RISE kept whole as technology with Safran
cfm.detail: RISE stays fully funded as a joint CFM technology programme, with no product launch and no 'program dividend' [CX-0174, CX-0214]. It is never cancelled for cost [CX-0398]. Testing continues with our partners, and RISE technology keeps flowing into LEAP upgrades [CX-0162]. No entry date and no ground-test or flight-test date [CX-0205, CX-0009]. This fits joint practice, and Safran is a full partner in RISE.

LEAP-1A durability hardware is in every new -1A engine and goes into the fleet at shop visits [CX-0209, CX-0225]. We report the -1B when the fleet data is in, and we make no claim before then [CX-0210]. Spares never crowd out OE engines [CX-0529]; this is joint practice with Safran. Facts only, no new promise dates [CX-0436].

pratt_whitney.move: Answer Airbus's rate-gated supply agreements on standard terms
pratt_whitney.detail: P&W will sign the rate-gated agreements for the A320neo GTF tail on the Alt plan and the NGSA framework agreement on standard terms. Volumes stay inside our castings and forgings plan, with no discount, concession or free upgrade. We announce no volumes, no NGSA share and no Airbus date or rate [PX-0055, PX-0062, PX-0099]. No grid effect.

pratt_whitney.move: GTF2 available to any new narrowbody that selects P&W, on standard terms
pratt_whitney.detail: This answers Boeing's call for a stable supply from more than one engine source, durability first, and Embraer's talks with all engine makers. GTF2 is ready six years from launch (2036), on standard terms, for any fps or new narrowbody that selects P&W, sole or shared. We claim no selection and say nothing on any airframer's dates [PX-0109, P-0746, PX-0062]. No grid effect.

We have no Joint Venture to announce, and we are not opening terms this round. We share risk and investment with partners, never our core technology [P-1233]. The answer is respectful and leaves the door neither shut nor open. No grid effect.

pratt_whitney.move: GTF Hot Section kit continues at shop visit, standard terms
pratt_whitney.detail: Upgrades are sold, not given [PX-0100]. No time-on-wing figure until the fleet proves it, per Mitchill's ground-4 advice [PX-0088, PX-0106]. No grid effect.

rolls_royce.move: Standing Joint Venture commitment with Pratt & Whitney, on standard terms
rolls_royce.detail: The `jv_with_pw: commit` is public at once and stands until withdrawn. It is for an airframe that has chosen both makers. The terms credit the technology Rolls-Royce brings, which asks for value; it is not a concession. There is no payment to P&W or to any airframer, no launch-style pricing and no free upgrades. No dates.

rolls_royce.move: Continue UltraFan technology maturation inside the existing R&D envelope
rolls_royce.detail: Demonstrator and geared-architecture work carries on inside base R&D and feeds Trent time on wing. No new programme, no new bill, no dates.

embraer.move: Deliver the plan and keep building cash to support a potential next move
embraer.detail: We keep delivering the E2 family, the business jets, defence and services to plan in the harvest season. Productivity comes before new capacity. Commercial output rises toward about 120 jets a year only where the return justifies it, keeping supply-chain headroom [EX-0053, EX-0080, EX-0077, EX-0078, EX-0087]. The cash and the low net debt ($0.7B) are kept to support a potential next move. The board does not price this.

embraer.move: Keep technology readiness funded for the next product cycle
embraer.detail: Studies continue for a new cycle of products, naming no segment and no date. We keep talking to all the engine makers and select none, because engine selection comes before any business case [EX-0112, EX-0141, EX-0133, EX-0044]. Meijer's readiness advice is logged for any later case: supplier headroom for a second line beside the E2 ramp, P&W's durability-before-entry-into-service stance, and a four-year clean-sheet certification against the E2's roughly five years.

embraer.move: Trade: argue on data, not politics
embraer.detail: We keep working with both governments for zero-for-zero in aerospace. Our case is more than 40% US content and US jobs: tariffs mean fewer US parts bought and a limited ability to invest in the future [EX-0098, EX-0100, EX-0101, EX-0124]. The 10% share cut is already in the brief. It is not a reason for this decision, and on this grid it is worth $0.00-0.05B.

boeing.move: Long-range, rate-gated CFM LEAP-1B supply and durability support
boeing.detail: Pope's list, at no grid cost: rate-gated LEAP-1B OE and spares cover through the MAX phase-out (2044-60); joint capacity planning with CFM so it can support our rate and our competitor's [BX-1264, BX-1325]; embedded staff on durability [B-0073, B-2097]; LEAP durability hardware in new engines and at shop visits. We are 46-53% of CFM's narrowbody OE output (Pope). None of this adds a second MAX source, so the enabler stays unmet.

boeing.move: Keep fragile suppliers funded and hot, with buffers
boeing.detail: Cash for readiness [BX-1243, B-2330], plus supplier buffers [B-2043]. Any future step needs demonstrated supplier output first [B-2308].

boeing.move: fps definition and production-system maturation (no launch, no date)
boeing.detail: Board recommendation 3. The baseline for the launch round is the 10-year Solo with code 7, at Renton only under Pope's wind-down condition: take down each Renton MAX line only after the fps is certified and has shown rate on its replacement line [BX-1263]. No fixed-price development terms [BX-1262, BX-1304]. Keep the Korean-supplier watch item (Pope).

boeing.move: Trained workforce through the MAX phase-out
boeing.detail: Pope's finding: on a second hold our narrowbody output is down 50% (2052) or 69% (2055) from 2044 by the earliest fps EIS. Plan retention, transfers and hiring so that the experienced workforce and the supply base are there for a successor line, as Boeing did in 2022 when it hired 10,000 engineers [B-1941]. The board does not price it. This is advice, not a premium.

boeing.move: Keep the 787 Re-engine file current (no commitment)
boeing.detail: Pope's readiness finding goes on the record for any later re-test: the GEnx upgrade (ready since 2033) meets her engine-path condition, strain is $0, Charleston fits and we can hold to no production-certification concurrency. Watch item: a re-engined 787 would start on GE alone. We re-test on each brief and stand aside for good once an A350 Re-engine is on the record (H3).

airbus.move: Contingent CFM framework for the single-source case
airbus.detail: If GTF2 slips past 2037 or P&W stops it, CFM carries NGSA alone, up to about 99 Airbus sets a month by 2044 (Wagner). This is a contingent, rate-gated framework, sized only to our own needs and triggered only by a P&W slip. It reserves nothing against other customers and claims no capacity Boeing uses. NGSA's date does not move for it.

airbus.move: GTF2 readiness watch at the Board's product-safety review
airbus.detail: Wagner reports at each twice-yearly review: GTF2's one-year readiness margin (ready 2036 for EIS 2037), P&W's durability testing as P&W makes it public, and the CFM fallback.

airbus.move: NGSA gate reports to the full Board
airbus.detail: The run-at-rate wing and production-system gates go to the twice-yearly product-safety review. A failed gate or an engine maturity slip re-times EIS later, never earlier, and never leads to a cancellation. The honest exposure is a one-year slip to 2038 [AX-0015, A-0225, A-0409].

airbus.move: CFO's 2035 annual cash report to the Audit Committee
airbus.detail: Covers net cash, the $0.13B headroom in 2035 and 2036, and the rating. On the static FY2025 base the payout recommendation sits near the 30% floor, unless reported FCF has grown as the brief's profit path implies; the Board sets the payout. No new buyback before 2037 without a Board re-test, and no equity raise. Launch aid is priced as our own money. The report is repeated for 2036 [AG-0058, AG-0059, AX-0102, AX-0022].

No spend is committed. The CFO brings the 2045 grid and cash arithmetic ($1.0B a year over 2045-49, no overlap, no strain), and Wagner re-tests capacity and supply. The re-test is closed if Boeing has launched a 787 Re-engine (rule 3). No programme is timed to reopen any other lever.

cfm.move: Support NGSA with the LEAP family, jointly with Safran
cfm.detail: CFM is fitted on NGSA on the record. We work with Airbus on the LEAP derivative for its entry into service and ramp. We make no claim that a new CFM engine is ready at entry into service, offer no launch-era pricing or concession, and quote no volumes Airbus has not stated. Narrowbody price and capacity are a joint decision with Safran [CX-0184, CX-0166]. Platform talks stay private [CX-0586].

cfm.move: Engine talks with Boeing and Embraer, jointly with Safran
cfm.detail: We refuse no one and lock no one out (H1) [CX-0587, CX-0185]. A LEAP derivative is on offer to both. A new CFM engine follows only with a committed airframer. Talks stay private, terms are standard, and narrowbody pricing is joint with Safran [CX-0184]. No comment on US-Brazil trade.

cfm.move: Measure supplier output before any stack (lean before capital)
cfm.detail: Ali measures actual output at the 9 suppliers and 15 sites behind 80% of past shortages [CX-0613]. The load is 2,392 LEAP engines in 2035 rising to 2,467 in 2041, plus the -1B shop-visit retrofits. We fix flow before we add capital [CX-0540, CX-0633]. No capital commitment and no board effect.

cfm.move: Hot-and-harsh core testing inside the RISE envelope
cfm.detail: Compact-core HPT durability testing in dust continues inside the existing joint RISE budget, and its results feed LEAP upgrades [CX-0222, CX-0216]. It builds the turn-on, turn-off test basis Ali says we lack for any future derivative [CX-0009]. No Ducted launch, no date, no new bill.

pratt_whitney.move: Castings and forgings plan for four loads (internal, Eddy owns it)
pratt_whitney.detail: Approved this year. The four loads: the NGSA ramp, the A320neo GTF tail to about 2045, a possible Embraer line (S5, up to about 192 engines a year gross by 2045) and the shops. On the hold row, NB engines go from 752 (2036) to 1,054 (2041) and 1,361 (2044). With 2 to 2.5 years of forging lead time [P-0079], the 2041 step must be ordered by 2038-39 and the 2044 level by 2041-42, so the plan and its gates are set now. Capital goes in tranches against Airbus's rate signals, through Mitchill. Embraer: pre-qualify suppliers, with no capital until a launch is on the record. Use the 2038-40 trough for fleet lift, GTF2 spares and shop tooling, not to shed suppliers. The fleet keeps first call on constrained material, with daily allocation, a weekly ExCo report, and the ramp balanced jointly with Airbus [PX-0123, PX-0099, PX-0110].

pratt_whitney.move: GTF2 durability gate report (internal, to the Governance and Public Policy Committee)
pratt_whitney.detail: Due at the 2036 ready year and before any entry into service. Contents: severe-environment endurance at no less than the GTF Advantage multiple; all life-limited parts at full life at entry into service; the composite fan, CMCs and gear each instrumented; GTF Advantage and Hot Section fleet removal data alongside. No compressed testing to hold any date. CMC hot-section parts are the named watch item: if they are not proven, GTF2 enters with the Advantage-derived hot section and the CMCs wait for a later block. Eddy's standing ground-1 condition is accepted as binding on any future order or statement [PX-0073, PX-0128, P-1360, P-0847].

pratt_whitney.move: Annual whole-programme GTF2 NPV review with the Board (internal), starting 2035
pratt_whitney.detail: Baseline from Mitchill: +6.10 net on the hold row, of which +6.08 comes from 2041-50. Without that decade the programme nets about -0.04. The 2039-40 trough is read as timing. Management's own 2035 cash and debt figures go to the Finance Committee at the first review as a dated follow-up; we do not invent a number today [P-1191, PG-0016].

If Airbus moves NGSA off P&W, there is no chasing on price. GTF2 completes anyway: this is the last cancel round, and a cancel trails hold by 3.89 even in S2, because a ready GTF2 still carries about $4.2B of engine value. We win our place back on durability, supply and standard terms, for NGSA in later rounds and for any fps or Embraer airframe [PX-0055, PX-0064].

pratt_whitney.move: Embraer engine standard (internal planning, Eddy's inference)
pratt_whitney.detail: If Embraer launches (EIS 2039), offer the GTF family at the Advantage standard, and GTF2 if Embraer selects it, both on standard terms. The choice is Embraer's. Eddy wants NGSA first-year data before a second GTF2 installation. Planning only, no capital and no grid effect.

Revisit only on a grid where the commit's weighted value against hold is at least 0 and no plausible column is worse than -$2B. Rolls-Royce's commitment must be on the record, or a live airframe not yet in service must carry code 1, 4, 5 or 7. The Joint Venture engine must be ready by that EIS. Terms must keep P&W's gear and core out: P&W designs and builds the gear and core modules, holds the type certificate and integration, and licenses IP for the Joint Venture product only (Eddy's terms) [P-1233].

rolls_royce.move: Name the narrowbody support plan at formation (Watson)
rolls_royce.detail:
If the Joint Venture forms this round, the plan is named at formation and in place before entry into service. It has six parts:
(1) P&W's narrowbody network, the GTF shops already supporting the A320neo fleet, as the Joint Venture's base.
(2) Partner shops on the Singapore Joint Venture model, named at formation.
(3) A spares pool, repair technology and field service, funded inside our $4B share.
(4) An EIS support team with Airbus, in place before entry into service.
(5) Narrowbody castings and forgings placed with high-performing suppliers, off the Trent lines.
(6) Our V2500 relationships with A320 operators.
The milestones stay private, because they would imply a date.

rolls_royce.move: UltraFan content in the Joint Venture engine: nothing that reopens the test programme
rolls_royce.detail: Our technology goes into the Joint Venture engine only where it does not reopen the folded engine's test programme. Anything that changes the core definition goes in as a later insertion after entry into service. The engine's ready year stays a mature date, and nothing is compressed (Watson's condition).

If the Joint Venture has not formed by 2045, the 2045 order is `jv_with_pw: withdraw`, unless a live airframe not yet in service can use the engine by its EIS. A hold would leave the commitment standing. This stops a late P&W commitment from putting $4B into an orphan programme and from locking the widebody slot (McCabe's condition, the Board's recommendation 5).

rolls_royce.move: Pricing discipline on every engine campaign
rolls_royce.detail: No concessions to buy a narrowbody selection. Every new contract goes through the Investment Committee, with win-win terms and value paid for [RX-0081, RX-0055, RX-0097]. Any aggressive term needs joint CEO-CFO sign-off, and none is proposed.

The Joint Venture share is funded from free cash flow and redeployed inside a broadly flat R&D envelope, with the UltraFan maturation work in base R&D as the natural source. No equity, no new borrowing, no levering up for buybacks. The order stays: balance sheet first, then the dividend, then investment.

embraer.move: Continue the Team Korea / KAI talks on a funding solution
embraer.detail: I follow the talks personally every two weeks [EX-0028]. The aim is a funding solution defined before any business-case approval [EX-0046, EX-0034]. On this brief's terms a launch reaches zero in S1 only with our own share near 36% (partners near 64%, about $1.9B more than the $4.5B the brief shows). It stays within -5 yp in S3 only near 45%, and clears the Board's -2 yp near 34%. No credit until a brief shows the money. No segment, no date, no commitment. Embraer keeps control and no military technology moves, so the state's consent is not needed (golden share; Board recommendation 7).

embraer.move: Carry the 2035 numbers into the 2045 package

boeing.public_statement:
Five years ago I said I thought we'd turned the ship. I'm comfortable now saying it's turned. The 737 line has run steady at the rate we set. We keep adding 787 capacity in Charleston, and the balance sheet is where it belongs and has stayed there. That isn't luck. It's a lot of people doing it the right way, every day.

Over the next several years more customers will want 737s than we're going to build. I know that's frustrating for some of them, and I don't take it lightly. But I'd much rather have a customer waiting than a production system that goes unstable again. The KPIs tell us when we can do more, not the calendar.

On a new airplane, how we decide hasn't changed. We will do a new airplane when the market and the technology and we're ready, and all three have to be there. We're in good shape financially and the technology is coming along, but the business case isn't there yet. I'm not going to launch an airplane to meet a date. We're keeping the work going on the airplane and on how we'd build it, so we're prepared when the case is there. When we do launch, the airplane will be planned around a stable supply of parts, engines first, with more than one engine source and durability ahead of everything else. I won't give you a date before we're ready to launch. When we launch, there'll be headroom in the schedule, and we won't take on development at a fixed price.

We'll keep working with the rest of the industry for a tariff-free environment in aerospace. That's good for everybody in this business.

It is so much more important that we do this right than fast.
boeing.rationale:
DECISION. Do Nothing on every field:
- fps hold (engine code null, fps_site new_site);
- rate_737 hold, the only value on offer;
- re787 hold.
No order differs from the default, so no item goes to the Board. The Board has said it approves this plan.

TEAM RULE
- Malave's buffer veto binds on every fps form. S4 runs from -3.80 (the best fps row, 10-year at Renton with the Re-engine) to -16.14, against a limit of -2.29. I accept it and claim no override. I would have reached the same answer anyway: S1 minus S4 on the fps rows is only $0.08-0.20B (his correction, accepted), so the fps fails on its base case, not on the slip.
- Pope's KPI veto has nothing to act on, since no rate order is open.
- The 787 Re-engine is my call.

MY FOUR TESTS
(1) KPIs [BX-1271]. Pope confirms no live quality, FAA or supply-chain problem, and the board has no injects. Her confirmation is that no problem is reported, not a measured KPI result. The gate is open.
(2) Market, technology, balance sheet [BX-1296, BX-1305].
- Balance sheet: ready. Net debt has been $0 since 2029 (2030 in the stress case), and Malave's 'Fundable when the 777X turns' test passes.
- Technology: ready. GTF2 is due in 2036, the GEnx upgrade has been ready since 2033, and CFM is always available.
- Market: fails for the fps. The best fps item value is -4.77 (10-year at Renton, S1). Malave puts about $2.8-2.9B of that down to the discounted debt penalty; without the penalty the fps would still trail Do Nothing by about $1.9B.
(3) Certification slip [BX-1319]. Every fps fails the buffer. The Re-engine passes at +1.72 in S4. S4 does not test the Re-engine, though; its real risk column is S3, at -1.63 against Do Nothing. That is inside Malave's $2B buffer and $0.63B outside the Board's $1B limit.
(4) Doing less, better [BX-1239]. Only the Re-engine beats Do Nothing by more than ε, and not in S3.

fps: HOLD
- It fails the business case and Malave's binding veto.
- Via Embraer runs $8.82-10.62B behind the 10-year Solo and breaks the stress-case debt line.
- The 7-year runs $1.88-2.27B behind the 10-year in every column. At new sites it breaks the stress line, and with the Re-engine it breaks H4.
- Company doctrine's reaction row 1 points to a launch this round, the round after NGSA went into development. This round that launch costs at least $4.77B, more than twice the H8 cap. So here doctrine is set aside and the grid governs, and Airbus's timeline does not set our date [B-2313].

LONG-CYCLE COST OF A SECOND fps HOLD (on the record, Board recommendation 3)
- The next decision round is 2045, so the earliest EIS is 2052 (7-year ramp) or 2055 (10-year).
- The MAX phases out from 2044: 641 a year (2045), 428 (2050), 342 (2052), 214 (2055), 0 (2060).
- Preference share is 31% (2045), 26% (2050) and 21% (2055). Delivered share is 22.2% (2050) and 12.7% (2055).
- On Malave's reading of the lead rule (inference), the long-run split falls from 42/58 (10-year now) or 45/55 (7-year now) to about 35/65 or 32/68.
- By the earliest EIS our narrowbody output is down 50% or 69% from 2044 (Pope's workforce finding). The board does not price this.
- The -0.12 political cost is already in the grid.
- Waiting has not improved the fps case: its best item value was -4.41 in 2030 and is -4.77 now.
I put this trade on the record plainly. The Board grants no extra downside for it, and at $4.77B or more it is not payable under H8.

787 RE-ENGINE: HOLD, UNDER THE BOARD'S RISK LIMIT
For it:
- +2.01 against Do Nothing in S1, S2 and S4, and +2.00 in S5; the grid's best plan in S1;
- every debt line met, stress peak $0.0B, $0.6B of undiscounted penalty;
- no overlap with any fps;
- Malave would carry it as a plan we can meet and potentially beat [BX-0548];
- Pope finds it ready for operations, with the GEnx engine path on the record seven years before EIS.
On my own tests I would carry it: my read of a same-round A350 Re-engine is below the 28% ε breakeven, with Low confidence.
Against it:
- -1.63 in S3. The Board counts S3 as plausible ('a statement does not rule a column out') and has said it would veto.
- Its recommendation 2 asks for a hold.
- I have no override against the Board, and it holds me to the case I bring [BG-0022]. A case that fails the Board's own stated test, with no new evidence on S3, is not a well-founded Board item.
- Both colleagues made their launch recommendation conditional on the Board: each concurs with a hold if the Board holds to its limit, and the Board's guidance says it does. So all three of us land on hold.
Logged: the $2.01B given up in S1 is the Board's risk limit, not a management premium. As a management premium it would break the H8 cap by $0.01B.
This hold is probably for good. A 2045 Re-engine (EIS 2050) is worth about $0.74B (2.01 x 0.368) before rival moves, below ε. By 2045 Airbus is past NGSA's EIS and free to re-engine the A350, and H3 would then bar ours.

GRID ROWS FOR THE BOARD (S1/S2/S3/S4/S5)
- Submitted row, Do Nothing: -0.29 / -0.07 / -1.75 / -0.29 / -1.67. S4 is 0.00 against Do Nothing, a pass.
- Reference, Re-engine row: +1.72 / +1.94 / -3.38 / +1.72 / +0.33. Item value +2.01 / +2.01 / -1.63 / +2.01 / +2.00.
- Reference, best fps rows:
  - 10-year at Renton with the Re-engine: -3.71 / -3.58 / -8.81 / -3.80 / -5.45;
  - 10-year at Renton alone: -5.06 / -4.93 / -6.52 / -5.15 / -6.79.
- H3, second half: in force, not engaged (no A350 Re-engine on the record). H4: no development, so no overlap.
- H1 and H3's first half were Round-1 rules and do not reach this round. H2 cannot bind; H7 has no trigger; my FAA-process gate [BX-1309] passes.

OBJECTIVE METRICS (chosen row)
- Net debt reaches the historical level in 2029 and is held at $0.0B at end-2035, 2040, 2045 and 2050.
- Stress case: back to $0 in 2030 and held, peak $0.0B.
- Engine sources: CFM alone on the 737 MAX in 2040-2050 (still 1 if P&W and Rolls-Royce launch). Two makers in the market.
- Share objectives missed (worst year 26.0%, 2050).

DOCTRINE VERSUS RECORD
- My record drove the fps hold and the debt-first reading.
- Doctrine and the Board's ask drove the standing launch-round plan: the 10-year ramp, code 7, Pope's Renton condition.
- Doctrine's row 1 was set aside under H8.

Advice not taken: launch the Re-engine. I agree with his numbers (breakevens 55% and 28%, the $0.74B long-cycle value). frame.question:
It is 2035. NGSA is in development for a 2037 EIS and is open to all three engine makers. We have no programme in development. Net debt has been at the historical level since 2029, and the 737 Rate Increase is no longer on offer. After this round the next decision is 2045, and the 737 MAX starts to phase out from 2044. So the question is whether anything clears the bar this round: an fps (and in which form), or the 787 Re-engine as our one well-founded case. If nothing does, we hold again, and the long-cycle cost of a second hold goes plainly on the record.

My four questions:
(1) Are the KPIs stable? Is any quality, FAA or supply-chain problem live in the brief? [BX-1271]
(2) Are the market, the technology and our balance sheet all ready? [BX-1296, BX-1305]
(3) What if certification takes longer than we think? I want Malave's risk-case column, S4. [BX-1319]
(4) Is each plan doing less, better, against Do Nothing in the same column? [BX-1239]

- Scores by column: -0.29 (S1, rivals hold), -0.07 (S2, A320 base plan), -1.75 (S3, A350 Re-engine), -0.29 (S4, risk case: Delay Tactics), -1.67 (S5, Embraer narrowbody).

ITEM VALUE AGAINST DO NOTHING (S1/S2/S3/S4/S5)
The grid's ΔPV already nets each plan's discounted debt penalty, so I do not subtract it again.
- 787 Re-engine alone: +2.01 / +2.01 / -1.63 / +2.01 / +2.00. It is the best plan in S1, S2, S4 and S5 and meets every debt line (stress peak $0.0B). MY FOUR QUESTIONS, AS I READ THE BRIEF

(2) Readiness: the balance sheet is ready. The technology is ready: GTF2 is due in 2036, the GEnx upgrade is on the record and CFM is always available. The market fails for the fps: every launch is at least $4.77B below Do Nothing in every column.

tests.name: Full cost of a slip or cancel
tests.threshold: Cancel write-off = bill x years elapsed ÷ development years; the debt penalty stays. Cost any slip once, in full: concessions, rework, learning curve, carrying cost. H5: never cancel a launched fps or Re-engine.
tests.numbers:
Nothing is launched, so no cancel is available.
- Any launch this round is a firm commitment. A 2035 Re-engine enters service in 2040, before the next round (2045), so no round falls inside its development. A 7-year fps is the same (EIS 2042).
- A 10-year fps could at most come up in 2045, at a full 60.32 x 10/10 write-off. H5 bars it anyway.
- The board does not price a slip of our own on the Re-engine (concessions, rework, learning curve, carrying cost). Pope's engine-path finding on the GEnx upgrade (ready since 2033) and on production-certification concurrency is the condition on it (inference).

tests.name: Rate step
tests.threshold: Only after stability, jointly agreed with the FAA. The Rate Increase was a 2030-only order on the board.
tests.numbers: No rate order is on offer this round: 'hold' is the only value. The line stays at 57 a month (684 a year) to 2044 under the KPI gate, which is Pope's seat. The brief reports no live quality, FAA or supply-chain problem and no injects.

tests.name: Premium in dollars (H8)
tests.threshold: Every doctrine or objective premium is stated in $B against the grid's best plan in the expected column (S1). The total stays within $2B, and the condition that would break the number is named.
tests.numbers:
Ask (6).
- On my recommended row (fps hold + 787 Re-engine), the management premium is $0: it is the grid's best in S1 at +1.72.
- If the ExCo or the Board holds the Re-engine: confirmed, log $2.01B in S1 as the Board's risk limit, not a management premium. As a management premium it would exceed the $2B cap by $0.01B, so it can stand only as the Board's limit.
- Engine enabler: at least $4.77B against Do Nothing (10-year at Renton, S1). Against the grid's best it is $5.43B (10-year at Renton with the Re-engine, -3.71 against +1.72). Not payable. Even paid, it cannot meet the 2040 leg: no fps is in service by 2040, so the MAX flies CFM alone. The third maker also needs Rolls-Royce to launch when selected.
- Holding the fps costs $0: every fps row is below Do Nothing.
- What would break my number: a same-round A350 Re-engine turns the Re-engine's +2.01 into -1.63. A slip of our own would deepen any fps row.
- Ask (7), long cycle of a second fps hold: the next launch round is 2045, so the earliest EIS is 2052 (7-year) or 2055 (10-year and via Embraer). The MAX builds full rate to 2044, then falls: 641 in 2045, 428 in 2050, 214 in 2055, none in 2060. Preference share is 31% in 2045, 26% in 2050 and 21% in 2055; delivered share is 22.2% in 2050 and 12.7% in 2055. On my reading of the lead rule (inference), NGSA's lead would be 15 or 18 years, so the long-run split falls from 42/58 (10-year now) or 45/55 (7-year now) to 35/65 or 32/68. The -0.12 political cost (20% x $0.44B a year x 20 years from 2045) is already in the grid, and waiting has not helped: -4.41 in 2030, -4.77 now.
- Confirmed: any return of cash to owners is reserved to the Board, outside this package.

vetoes.plan: fps: launch_10yr (new_site or renton, with or without the 787 Re-engine)
vetoes.ground: Buffer test, slip leg. In S4 the 10-year rows run from -3.80 (Renton with the Re-engine, the best fps row) to -5.52 (new sites alone), against Do Nothing's -0.29 and a limit of -2.29. That is $3.51-5.23B below Do Nothing, $1.51-3.23B beyond the limit. Binding under the team rule (teams.md §9). Advice, not binding: it also fails the business case by at least $4.77B in every column.

vetoes.plan: fps: launch_7yr (any site, any combination)
vetoes.ground: Buffer test, slip leg. In S4 the 7-year rows run from -6.44 to -7.55, against Do Nothing's -0.29: $6.15-7.26B below, beyond the $2B limit. Binding under the team rule. Advice, not binding: at new sites it breaks the stress-case debt line ($0.5-0.7B), and with the Re-engine it overlaps 5 years, which H4 bars.

vetoes.plan: fps: launch_via_embraer (any site, any combination)
vetoes.ground: Buffer test, slip leg. In S4 the via-Embraer rows run from -14.90 to -16.14, against Do Nothing's -0.29: $14.61-15.85B below, beyond the $2B limit. Binding under the team rule. Advice, not binding: it adds $52.5B of undiscounted debt penalty, runs $8.82-10.62B behind the 10-year Solo, and breaks the stress-case debt line in nearly every column.

vetoes.plan: re787: launch (with fps hold)
vetoes.ground: Not a veto: it passes my buffer test (S4 +1.72, +2.01 against Do Nothing). Advice only: I would carry it. Its real risk column, S3, is -1.63 against Do Nothing, inside my $2B buffer. It meets every debt line with a $0.0B stress peak and is fundable. It is a Board item, and it fails the Board's $1B per-item limit in S3 by $0.63B. That limit is the Board's to apply. If it holds to it, I concur with hold, and the $2.01B in S1 is logged as the Board's risk limit. Readiness conditions sit with Pope: the GEnx engine path, engineering capacity alongside Charleston, and no production-certification concurrency.

cfo.would_change_mind_if:
787 Re-engine:
- I would move to hold on readiness grounds if Pope finds that the GEnx upgrade does not meet her engine-path (durability-first) condition, that engineering capacity alongside the Charleston 787 expansion is short, that the plan needs production-certification concurrency, or that suppliers are not ready.
- I would move to hold if the Board applies its $1B per-item limit. Its call binds on Board items, and the $2.01B is then logged as its risk limit.
- Once an A350 Re-engine is on the record, never (H3).
fps:
- I would lift my veto on a later brief whose risk-case column puts an fps row (most likely the 10-year at Renton, code 7) no more than $2B below Do Nothing in the same column, with every debt line met and a $0.0B stress peak. I would then favour the 10-year ramp.
Cash:
- I would revisit any launch if the tracker showed a debt line at risk on the chosen row, the stress case included.
cfo.memo:
Kelly, my test on the grid's own numbers, risk case as the baseline.

The buffer test, the slip leg: S4 no lower than -2.29. Every fps fails. The best fps row, the 10-year at Renton with the Re-engine, is -3.80, $1.51B outside. The 10-year at Renton alone is -5.15, the 7-year -6.44 to -7.55, via Embraer -14.90 to -16.14. Delay Tactics move these rows only $0.08-0.20B, so the fps fails on its base case. About $2.9B of the 10-year's -4.77 is the discounted debt penalty; without it the fps would still trail Do Nothing by about $1.9B. My veto on every fps form binds under the team rule.

The 787 Re-engine passes every test I run. S4 is +1.72. Its real risk column is S3: $1.63B below Do Nothing, inside my $2B buffer, where last round's $2.48B was not. It is +2.00 to +2.01 elsewhere, $5B booked in 2040, $0.6B of undiscounted penalty, and every debt line holds with a stress peak of $0.0B. Your breakevens, 55% and 28%, are right.

So I would carry it: a plan we can meet and potentially beat, barring a same-round A350 Re-engine. It fails only the Board's $1B limit, by $0.63B, and that call is the Board's. If the Board holds to it, I concur with hold and we log $2.01B as its risk limit, knowing a 2045 Re-engine is worth about $0.74B.

It's maintaining the focus on fully restoring the health of our balance sheet, and we're bullish on our outlook.

tests.name: On-time, predictable delivery (record: BX-1331, applied to airplanes by inference)
tests.threshold: Can each plan's EIS be delivered as stated? Read the risk-case column S4 (Delay Tactics) against S1 and say how much of each plan's value depends on the nominal date. Where S4 does not test a plan's own date, read its worst column.
tests.numbers: S4 minus S1, by plan: Do Nothing 0.00; 787 Re-engine 0.00 (+1.72 in both); fps 10-year -0.20 at new sites, -0.09 at Renton; 7-year -0.12 / -0.10; via Embraer -0.20 / -0.08 to -0.09. Under Delay Tactics, at most 4% of any fps row (0.20 of -5.32) depends on the fps date: every fps fails on its bill, not on its date. S4 does not test the Re-engine's own date. Its worst column is S3 (-3.38, item -1.63), which is a rival-timing risk, not a delivery risk. The grid does not price our own slip. The doctrine prior for a major derivative is +2 years central (range +1 to +4). My sensitivity: about $0.19B of item value per year of slip (2.01 x (1 - 1/1.105)), $0.36B for 2 years, within epsilon (inference). Clean-sheet prior +3 years (range +2 to +5): a 10-year fps EIS of 2045 becomes 2048 central. 737 MAX: 57 a month since 2030, 684 a year to 2044, no step planned. Basis: my record for the delivery-first rule; doctrine for the slip priors.

tests.name: KPI gate and line stability: my binding veto's test (doctrine; CEO ask 1)
tests.threshold: No Rate Increase while a quality, FAA or supply-chain problem is live. Steps of 5, at least 6 months apart, KPI-gated. Never a reply to Airbus (H6).
tests.numbers: The brief reports no live quality, FAA or supply-chain problem, and the board has no injects, so the gate is open. No Rate Increase is on offer (a 2030-only order, held then), so my veto has no object this round. The brief carries no measured KPI data, only the absence of a problem. I confirm that, not a six-KPI result [B-2283, B-2274]. The MAX has run at 57 a month (684 a year) since 2030 and holds that to 2044. Then it phases out: 641 (2045), 556 (2047), 428 (2050), 214 (2055), 0 (2060). Idle slots before capacity binds: 56 (2035), 58 (2036), 79 (2037), 214 (2038). Capacity binds 2039-44. Waiting customers: 225 (2040), 438 (2041), 489 (2042), 523 (2043), 374 (2044), 97 (2045); a tenth drop out each year and the flexible 49% take Airbus slots. Confirmed: we accept unhappy customers rather than an unstable line [BX-1274]. H6: moot.

tests.name: Supplier readiness, a hard gate, and the engine enabler at no grid cost (doctrine; CEO ask 5)
tests.threshold: No move without demonstrated supplier output [B-2308]. An engine is real when its launch is in the event log [B-0524]. Beyond 47 a month the supply chain binds [B-2340].

tests.name: Two-front strain and engineering capacity (doctrine; H4; CEO ask 3)
tests.threshold: A Solo fps and the 787 Re-engine overlap at most 2 years. Strain = $3B x overlap / 5, with the fps counted from EIS-7 to EIS and the Re-engine from EIS-5 to EIS. One major development at a time [B-0341].
tests.numbers:
Re-engine alone (2035-40): overlap 0, strain $0. The 777X has delivered since 2027 and the MAX 7/10 was certified in 2026, so the Re-engine is the one major development. Charleston is production capacity for rates in the teens, not development [BX-1317, B-2336].
- Same-round 10-year fps (2038-45) with the Re-engine: overlap 2038-40, 2 years, $1.2B undiscounted, legal. On top of the 10-year fps the Re-engine adds +1.34 / +1.35 / -2.29 / +1.34 / +1.35.
- Same-round 7-year fps (2035-42): 5 years, $3.0B, an H4 breach. The Re-engine adds only +0.79 there, and -2.85 in S3.
- A Re-engine held now next comes up in 2045 (2045-50). Against a 2045 10-year fps (2048-55) it overlaps 2 years; against a 2045 7-year fps (2045-52), 5 years, barred.

tests.name: 787 Re-engine readiness for a 2035 launch and a 2040 EIS (doctrine; CEO ask 2; the Board's ask)
tests.threshold: An engine path on the record and ready by EIS, durability first [BX-1298]; engineering capacity free; no production-certification concurrency [BX-1263]; suppliers ready; Charleston capacity for the added demand.
tests.numbers:
Engine path: met. The GEnx upgrade (launched 2030, ready since 2033) is in the event log, 7 years ahead of EIS. CFM/GE frames it around time on wing, and it enters service before our EIS, so it builds fleet time first (inference). This answers my Round-1 condition (no engine on the record then).
- Engineering: one development, strain $0.
- Concurrency: we can hold to it. No re-engined 787 is built at rate before certification; Charleston keeps building today's 787 until then [BX-1263, B-2228].
- Capacity: +1 pp a year of a 170-aircraft market from 2040 is about 1.7 more 787s a year, to about 117 a year (9.75 a month) by 2050. That fits inside Charleston's rates in the teens (inference).
- Suppliers: no live problem.
- Watch item: the re-engined 787 would start on GE alone. Rolls-Royce has no widebody upgrade on the record, and the 787 flies both makers today [B-0940].
- Slip: about $0.19B a year. Under H5, re-baseline once, never cancel.
For any later re-test: if held, the next chance is 2045 (EIS 2050), worth about $0.74B (2.01 / 1.105^10) before rival moves, below epsilon (inference). H3: no A350 Re-engine is on the record, so the rule is in force but not engaged.

tests.name: Ramp choice, 7- or 10-year, with engine readiness by EIS (inference, BX-1331; CEO ask 3)
tests.threshold: Which ramp can operations deliver predictably with the engines, workforce and suppliers in the brief? State each ramp's strain, EIS and engine margin; each named engine ready by EIS with durability margin [BX-1298, B-2304].
tests.numbers:
10-year: EIS 2045. Strain $0 alone, $1.2B with the Re-engine. Worst column -6.79 (Renton) / -7.12 (new sites).
7-year: EIS 2042. Strain $3.0B with the Re-engine (barred). Worst column -9.02 / -9.39. At new sites it breaks the stress line ($0.5-0.7B).
The 10-year beats the 7-year by $1.88-2.27B in every column.
Engine margin under code 7:
- P&W GTF2, ready 2036: 9 years to a 2045 EIS (6 to 2042). Fitted on NGSA from 2037, it gets about 8 years of fleet time first (5 for 2042), and P&W will not enter service until durability is proven.
- UltraFan NB selected now: ready 2042, so 3 years to 2045 and 0 to 2042. It has no fleet time before our EIS (Rolls-Royce is not fitted on NGSA), so it is the least mature named engine.
- CFM: always available, either a LEAP derivative with the durability upgrades now in the fleet or a new engine CFM commits with a committed airframer.
A P&W-RR Joint Venture formed in 2035 would be ready in 2041; none is committed. Code 7 gives 2 sources at a 2045 EIS (3 if Rolls-Royce launches) and is in no barred pair with NGSA's code 7. A +3-year clean-sheet slip fits inside the 10-year engine margins; the 7-year leaves Rolls-Royce none. Operations can deliver the 10-year ramp predictably. The fps is held on value, so this result is for the launch round.

tests.name: Invest or partner on IP: fps via Embraer (record: BX-1330, BX-1333, applied by inference; CEO ask 4)
tests.threshold: fps Solo where Boeing owns the airframe IP. Via Embraer only if the partner adds what Boeing lacks.
tests.numbers: Boeing's bill is $100B against $60.32B for the 10-year Solo (+$39.68B), with the same EIS (launch + 10) and no strain or capacity relief on the board. Gap to the 10-year Solo: $10.61-10.62B in S1-S4 and $8.82-8.88B in S5 on its own; $11.10-11.11B and $9.31-9.37B with the Re-engine. The S5 narrowing (about $1.8B) is the one thing the partner brings: it blocks Embraer's own narrowbody. Unpriced: Embraer's engineering talent, which Boeing sought in 2018 [B-1420], set against the 2020 exit and the arbitration [B-2131]. Korean-supplier watch item, kept: Korean industry builds structures for Boeing today, so an Embraer-Korea narrowbody would compete for the same suppliers (inference). None of this comes near $8.8B. It breaks the stress-case debt line ($1.8-3.1B alone; $0.8-5.2B with the Re-engine, and the line is met only in S2). The Solo fps and the 787 Re-engine build on our own IP: invest.

tests.name: Capacity follows demand: Rate Increase (one remark, BX-1329; inference)
tests.threshold: Back the Rate Increase only where it adds value against the same plan without it in the expected column, and only where demand is visible.
tests.numbers: The Rate Increase was a 2030-only order and is not on offer; rate_737 hold is the only value. For the record: demand is visible from 2039 (523 customers waiting at the 2043 peak), but no board lever adds MAX capacity now. On the widebody, the Charleston expansion is capacity that follows visible 787 demand [BX-1317, B-2336]. The board does not price it.

tests.name: Working capital and cash conversion (record: BX-1327, BX-1332, BX-1326, applied by inference)
tests.threshold: For each option, when the bill lands and what it does to cash, as a number. Every debt line met, the stress case included.
tests.numbers:
- Do Nothing: no bill. Free cash flow $13.79B a year ($9.19B in the stress case). Net debt $0 from 2029 (stress case 2030), peak $0.0B.
- 787 Re-engine: $5B over 2035-40, about $1.0B a year: 7% of base and 11% of stress free cash flow. Booked at EIS in 2040. Every line met, stress peak $0.0B. Undiscounted debt penalty $0.6B.
- fps 10-year: $60.32B over 2035-44 (governments carry 2%). About $3.0B in year 1 and $8.4B at the year-7 peak, which is 61% of base and 92% of stress free cash flow. Every line met, peak $0.0B, at Renton or new sites, with or without the Re-engine. Penalty $19.1B.
- fps 7-year: $65.00B over 2035-41, about $9.3B a year, above stress free cash flow. At new sites it breaks the stress line ($0.5-0.7B). With the Re-engine: $2.2-2.7B at new sites. At Renton the lines are met at the checkpoints in S1, S2 and S4 (peak $1.5-1.7B) and broken in S3 ($1.7B) and S5 ($1.9B). Penalty $22.0B.
- Via Embraer: $100B, about $10B a year with a $14B peak, above base free cash flow. Breaks the stress line in nearly every row. Penalty $52.5B.
Recommended package (the Re-engine only): pass.

tests.name: Renton MAX wind-down (doctrine; CEO ask 3)
tests.threshold: No production-certification concurrency. Predictable delivery through the transition.
tests.numbers: The fps is held, so Renton has no effect this round; keep new_site (the Board's ask). At launch, Renton adds +0.21 to +0.37 on the 10-year ramp (+0.21 to +0.38 with the Re-engine) and +0.30 to +0.37 on the 7-year. It also avoids about $3.0B of new-site capex, in full if chosen at least 3 years before EIS. Renton's three lines carry 47 of our 57 a month (564 of 684 a year). My condition: take down each Renton MAX line only after the fps is certified and has shown rate on its replacement line, so that a +3-year clean-sheet slip leaves no delivery gap. A 10-year EIS of 2045 lands one year after the MAX phase-out starts (2044), the cleanest handover the game offers (inference).

tests.name: Share objectives an fps could buy (rules arithmetic, inference; CEO ask 6)
tests.threshold: Incumbency: preference share at least 40% in 2045 and 2050. The 50/50 split: at least 50% in 2040, 2045 and 2050.
tests.numbers:
Your reading is confirmed.
- Do Nothing: Boeing loses 1 pp a year from NGSA's 2037 EIS, to 31% in 2045 and 26% in 2050. The 52.6% in 2040 is Airbus's transition slack only.
- 10-year fps (EIS 2045): 8 years behind NGSA, so the long-run split is 42/58. From 31% Boeing gains 1 pp a year: about 31% in 2045, 36% in 2050, and 42% from about 2056.
- 7-year fps (EIS 2042): long-run split 45/55. About 34% in 2042, 37% in 2045 and 42% in 2050.
Delay Tactics take 5 pp for 5 years from EIS. No fps launched this round reaches 40% in 2045 or 50% in any scored year; only the 7-year meets 40%, in 2050 alone. The share objectives cannot be bought this round at any premium.

tests.name: Trained workforce through the MAX phase-out (the operating seat's judgement, dashboard_game.md §3; inference)
tests.threshold: A successor line ready as the MAX phases out from 2044, so that the trained workforce and suppliers keep their work; state the gap in aircraft a year.
tests.numbers: The board does not price this. MAX capacity, the same in every plan: 684 (2044), 641 (2045), 556 (2047), 428 (2050), 342 (2052), 214 (2055), 0 (2060). On a second hold the earliest fps EIS is 2052 (7-year ramp from 2045) or 2055 (10-year). By then our narrowbody output is down 50% or 69% from 2044, with no successor line. Doctrine answers lost experience with hiring, transfers and retention; in 2022 Boeing answered experienced-staff attrition by hiring 10,000 engineers [B-1941]. A 10-year fps launched now would enter service in 2045, one year into the phase-out. This finding goes on the record as advice, not as a ground for a premium: the cheapest fps is $4.77B below Do Nothing, above the $2B cap in H8, and the Board grants no extra downside for it.

vetoes.plan: rate_737: increase
vetoes.ground: KPI doctrine veto not invoked. No Rate Increase is on offer this round (it was a 2030-only order), the brief reports no live quality, FAA or supply-chain problem, and the board has no injects. My veto has no object.

vetoes.plan: fps: launch_7yr together with re787: launch (same round)
vetoes.ground: Hard-rule flag H4, not my veto. The overlap is 5 years (fps 2035-42 against Re-engine 2035-40), with $3.0B of undiscounted strain, beyond the 2-year cap. On top of the 7-year fps the Re-engine adds only +0.79, and -2.85 in S3. The stress-case debt line breaks at new sites ($2.2-2.7B) and at Renton in S3 and S5 ($1.7-1.9B). The rule binds the CEO.

vetoes.plan: fps: launch_7yr (any site)
vetoes.ground: Advice: operations cannot deliver it predictably. UltraFan NB has 0 years of margin to a 2042 EIS. The 7-year runs $1.88-2.27B behind the 10-year ramp in every column, and at new sites it breaks the stress-case debt line ($0.5-0.7B).

vetoes.plan: fps: launch_via_embraer
vetoes.ground: Advice: it fails invest-or-partner on IP. The bill is $100B against $60.32B, with the same EIS and no strain or capacity relief. It runs $10.61-10.62B behind the 10-year Solo in S1-S4 and $8.82-8.88B in S5. It breaks the stress-case debt line ($1.8-3.1B on its own).

vetoes.plan: re787: launch
vetoes.ground: Advice: launch conditions, not a veto. (1) No re-engined 787 built at rate before certification. (2) A conservative public EIS, with the slip range published at launch (about $0.19B of value a year). (3) Under H5, re-baseline once and never cancel, even if Airbus re-engines the A350 in the same round. The Board's $1B downside limit (-1.63 in S3) is the Board's test, not an operations test. If the CEO holds the Re-engine for that limit, the readiness finding stands on the record.

ops.would_change_mind_if: Any of the following would change my orders. (1) A brief that reports a live quality, FAA or supply-chain problem: I would hold the Re-engine until it clears, and my KPI veto would bind against any rate step (none is on offer). (2) A durability problem on the GEnx upgrade, or a withdrawn engine path: I would hold the Re-engine. (3) An A350 Re-engine on the record: no 787 Re-engine, ever (H3). (4) A reading from Ortberg or the Board that puts the chance of a same-round A350 Re-engine above about 28% (the epsilon breakeven; 55% for any gain): the Re-engine would no longer clear epsilon and I would recommend hold. I defer to the CEO on rival moves. (5) An fps row that beats Do Nothing by more than epsilon and passes Malave's buffer: then the 10-year Solo with code 7, Renton only under my wind-down condition, and no date before launch. (6) A partner that brings capital, capacity or IP Boeing lacks, so that via Embraer beats the Solo by more than epsilon in every column.
ops.memo:
My record is thin: my KPI, supplier and strain results are Boeing's operations doctrine; delivery, IP and cash are my 2022 BGS rules, applied by inference.

First and foremost, on-time predictable delivery. The brief reports no live quality, FAA or supply-chain problem. The MAX holds 57 a month, 684 a year, to 2044. Capacity binds in 2039-44, up to 523 customers waiting; we accept that rather than an unstable line. No rate order is on offer, so my veto is idle.

Second, the 787 Re-engine is operations-ready. My Round-1 condition is met: the GEnx upgrade has been ready since 2033, seven years before a 2040 EIS. It is our one development, strain $0, on our own IP; Charleston is production capacity, not engineering. The $5B is about $1.0B a year, 7% of base free cash flow; stress peak $0.0B. Each year of slip costs about $0.19B. Build nothing at rate before certification. I recommend it; the S3 downside is the Board's test, not an operations one.

Third, hold the fps. A 10-year Solo is deliverable: nine years of engine margin on GTF2, three on UltraFan, $1.2B of strain with the Re-engine. But it is $4.77B below Do Nothing. The 7-year leaves UltraFan no margin; via Embraer adds $39.7B of bill, no time.

And finally, the long cycle. On a second hold, our narrowbody output halves, from 684 in 2044 to 342 in 2052, the earliest fps EIS. The board does not price that workforce gap. Record it.

other_moves.move: Continue the Charleston 787 capacity expansion
other_moves.detail: Production capacity for 787 rates in the teens, not a development program [BX-1317, B-2336]. Funded inside the debt lines. Not priced on the board. Pope finds that the added 787 demand fits inside it.

other_moves.move: Next-narrowbody engine requirement: a stable, multi-source engine supply (restated)
other_moves.detail: We tell CFM, P&W and Rolls-Royce again that Boeing's next narrowbody will be planned around a stable supply of parts, engines first, with more than one engine source and durability first [BX-1298]. No launch, no date and no engine selection this round. It serves Control's engine enabler at no grid cost (Board recommendation 5).

other_moves.move: Zero-for-zero tariffs in civil aerospace, with the industry
other_moves.detail: We keep working with industry associations for a tariff-free regime for aircraft and parts. A tariff-free environment is good for every company in the industry [B-2290]. No grid effect.

other_moves.move: Long-range, rate-gated CFM LEAP-1B supply and durability support
other_moves.detail: Pope's list, at no grid cost: rate-gated LEAP-1B OE and spares cover through the MAX phase-out (2044-60); joint capacity planning with CFM so it can support our rate and our competitor's [BX-1264, BX-1325]; embedded staff on durability [B-0073, B-2097]; LEAP durability hardware in new engines and at shop visits. We are 46-53% of CFM's narrowbody OE output (Pope). None of this adds a second MAX source, so the enabler stays unmet.

other_moves.move: Keep fragile suppliers funded and hot, with buffers

decision.public_statement:
Five years ago I said I thought we'd turned the ship. I'm comfortable now saying it's turned. The 737 line has run steady at the rate we set. We keep adding 787 capacity in Charleston, and the balance sheet is where it belongs and has stayed there. That isn't luck. It's a lot of people doing it the right way, every day.

Over the next several years more customers will want 737s than we're going to build. I know that's frustrating for some of them, and I don't take it lightly. But I'd much rather have a customer waiting than a production system that goes unstable again. The KPIs tell us when we can do more, not the calendar.

On a new airplane, how we decide hasn't changed. We will do a new airplane when the market and the technology and we're ready, and all three have to be there. We're in good shape financially and the technology is coming along, but the business case isn't there yet. I'm not going to launch an airplane to meet a date. We're keeping the work going on the airplane and on how we'd build it, so we're prepared when the case is there. When we do launch, the airplane will be planned around a stable supply of parts, engines first, with more than one engine source and durability ahead of everything else. I won't give you a date before we're ready to launch. When we launch, there'll be headroom in the schedule, and we won't take on development at a fixed price.

We'll keep working with the rest of the industry for a tariff-free environment in aerospace. That's good for everybody in this business.

It is so much more important that we do this right than fast.
decision.rationale:
DECISION. Do Nothing on every field:
- fps hold (engine code null, fps_site new_site);
- rate_737 hold, the only value on offer;
- re787 hold.
No order differs from the default, so no item goes to the Board. The Board has said it approves this plan.

TEAM RULE
- Malave's buffer veto binds on every fps form. S4 runs from -3.80 (the best fps row, 10-year at Renton with the Re-engine) to -16.14, against a limit of -2.29. I accept it and claim no override. I would have reached the same answer anyway: S1 minus S4 on the fps rows is only $0.08-0.20B (his correction, accepted), so the fps fails on its base case, not on the slip.
- Pope's KPI veto has nothing to act on, since no rate order is open.
- The 787 Re-engine is my call.

MY FOUR TESTS
(1) KPIs [BX-1271]. Pope confirms no live quality, FAA or supply-chain problem, and the board has no injects. Her confirmation is that no problem is reported, not a measured KPI result. The gate is open.
(2) Market, technology, balance sheet [BX-1296, BX-1305].
- Balance sheet: ready. Net debt has been $0 since 2029 (2030 in the stress case), and Malave's 'Fundable when the 777X turns' test passes.
- Technology: ready. GTF2 is due in 2036, the GEnx upgrade has been ready since 2033, and CFM is always available.
- Market: fails for the fps. The best fps item value is -4.77 (10-year at Renton, S1). Malave puts about $2.8-2.9B of that down to the discounted debt penalty; without the penalty the fps would still trail Do Nothing by about $1.9B.
(3) Certification slip [BX-1319]. Every fps fails the buffer. The Re-engine passes at +1.72 in S4. S4 does not test the Re-engine, though; its real risk column is S3, at -1.63 against Do Nothing. That is inside Malave's $2B buffer and $0.63B outside the Board's $1B limit.
(4) Doing less, better [BX-1239]. Only the Re-engine beats Do Nothing by more than ε, and not in S3.

fps: HOLD
- It fails the business case and Malave's binding veto.
- Via Embraer runs $8.82-10.62B behind the 10-year Solo and breaks the stress-case debt line.
- The 7-year runs $1.88-2.27B behind the 10-year in every column. At new sites it breaks the stress line, and with the Re-engine it breaks H4.
- Company doctrine's reaction row 1 points to a launch this round, the round after NGSA went into development. This round that launch costs at least $4.77B, more than twice the H8 cap. So here doctrine is set aside and the grid governs, and Airbus's timeline does not set our date [B-2313].

LONG-CYCLE COST OF A SECOND fps HOLD (on the record, Board recommendation 3)
- The next decision round is 2045, so the earliest EIS is 2052 (7-year ramp) or 2055 (10-year).
- The MAX phases out from 2044: 641 a year (2045), 428 (2050), 342 (2052), 214 (2055), 0 (2060).
- Preference share is 31% (2045), 26% (2050) and 21% (2055). Delivered share is 22.2% (2050) and 12.7% (2055).
- On Malave's reading of the lead rule (inference), the long-run split falls from 42/58 (10-year now) or 45/55 (7-year now) to about 35/65 or 32/68.
- By the earliest EIS our narrowbody output is down 50% or 69% from 2044 (Pope's workforce finding). The board does not price this.
- The -0.12 political cost is already in the grid.
- Waiting has not improved the fps case: its best item value was -4.41 in 2030 and is -4.77 now.
I put this trade on the record plainly. The Board grants no extra downside for it, and at $4.77B or more it is not payable under H8.

787 RE-ENGINE: HOLD, UNDER THE BOARD'S RISK LIMIT
For it:
- +2.01 against Do Nothing in S1, S2 and S4, and +2.00 in S5; the grid's best plan in S1;
- every debt line met, stress peak $0.0B, $0.6B of undiscounted penalty;
- no overlap with any fps;
- Malave would carry it as a plan we can meet and potentially beat [BX-0548];
- Pope finds it ready for operations, with the GEnx engine path on the record seven years before EIS.
On my own tests I would carry it: my read of a same-round A350 Re-engine is below the 28% ε breakeven, with Low confidence.
Against it:
- -1.63 in S3. The Board counts S3 as plausible ('a statement does not rule a column out') and has said it would veto.
- Its recommendation 2 asks for a hold.
- I have no override against the Board, and it holds me to the case I bring [BG-0022]. A case that fails the Board's own stated test, with no new evidence on S3, is not a well-founded Board item.
- Both colleagues made their launch recommendation conditional on the Board: each concurs with a hold if the Board holds to its limit, and the Board's guidance says it does. So all three of us land on hold.
Logged: the $2.01B given up in S1 is the Board's risk limit, not a management premium. As a management premium it would break the H8 cap by $0.01B.
This hold is probably for good. A 2045 Re-engine (EIS 2050) is worth about $0.74B (2.01 x 0.368) before rival moves, below ε. By 2045 Airbus is past NGSA's EIS and free to re-engine the A350, and H3 would then bar ours.

GRID ROWS FOR THE BOARD (S1/S2/S3/S4/S5)
- Submitted row, Do Nothing: -0.29 / -0.07 / -1.75 / -0.29 / -1.67. S4 is 0.00 against Do Nothing, a pass.
- Reference, Re-engine row: +1.72 / +1.94 / -3.38 / +1.72 / +0.33. Item value +2.01 / +2.01 / -1.63 / +2.01 / +2.00.
- Reference, best fps rows:
  - 10-year at Renton with the Re-engine: -3.71 / -3.58 / -8.81 / -3.80 / -5.45;
  - 10-year at Renton alone: -5.06 / -4.93 / -6.52 / -5.15 / -6.79.
- H3, second half: in force, not engaged (no A350 Re-engine on the record). H4: no development, so no overlap.
- H1 and H3's first half were Round-1 rules and do not reach this round. H2 cannot bind; H7 has no trigger; my FAA-process gate [BX-1309] passes.

OBJECTIVE METRICS (chosen row)
- Net debt reaches the historical level in 2029 and is held at $0.0B at end-2035, 2040, 2045 and 2050.
- Stress case: back to $0 in 2030 and held, peak $0.0B.
- Engine sources: CFM alone on the 737 MAX in 2040-2050 (still 1 if P&W and Rolls-Royce launch). Two makers in the market.
- Share objectives missed (worst year 26.0%, 2050).

DOCTRINE VERSUS RECORD
- My record drove the fps hold and the debt-first reading.
- Doctrine and the Board's ask drove the standing launch-round plan: the 10-year ramp, code 7, Pope's Renton condition.
- Doctrine's row 1 was set aside under H8.

Advice not taken: launch the Re-engine. I agree with his numbers (breakevens 55% and 28%, the $0.74B long-cycle value). But he left the S3 limit to the Board and concurs with hold if the Board holds to it, and the Board's guidance says it does. decision.expected_scenario: S1: rivals hold. Airbus says it takes one major development at a time and has NGSA in development to a 2037 EIS, so in my reading a same-round A350 Re-engine (S3) is less likely, though still plausible. Delay Tactics (S4) cannot act while our fps is unlaunched, so S4 equals S1 on every fps-hold row. Embraer says it is still in its harvest season (S5 is possible). My confidence on Airbus is Low.

It fails the Board's $1B per-item downside limit in S3 (-1.63), the Board has said it would veto it, and I have no override. Chosen plan: Do Nothing, -0.29 in S1.
decision.premium_reason:
Management doctrine plus objective premium: $0.
- The Re-engine: the $2.01B gap in S1 between the grid's best plan (fps hold + 787 Re-engine, +1.72) and Do Nothing (-0.29) is logged as the Board's risk limit, not a management premium. The Board asked for it to be recorded this way. As a management premium it would exceed the H8 cap by $0.01B, so it can stand only as the Board's limit.
- Holding the fps costs $0: every fps row is below Do Nothing.
- The rate order costs $0: hold is the only value.
- The engine enabler is not paid for. It needs at least $4.77B against Do Nothing (10-year at Renton, S1), or $5.43B against the grid's best, above the $2B cap. Even if paid, it misses the 2040 leg, since no fps is in service by 2040.
- What would break the number: a same-round A350 Re-engine turns the Re-engine's +2.01 into -1.63. A slip of our own would deepen any fps row.
decision.objective_note:

- Keep it repaired: met. $0.0B at end-2035, 2040, 2045 and 2050.
- Stress case: met. Back to $0 in 2030 and held, peak $0.0B.
- Defend incumbency: not met (worst year 26.0%, 2050).
- Hold the 50/50 split: not met (52.6% in 2040 only through Airbus's transition slack; 31.0% in 2045, 26.0% in 2050).

On Pope's arithmetic, no fps launched this round reaches 40% in 2045 or 50% in any scored year, so the share objectives cannot be bought this round at any premium. The enabler would need at least $4.77B, above the H8 cap. The restated public multi-source requirement and the CFM capacity and durability work serve the enabler at no grid cost. At launch I will request code 7 (CFM plus GTF2, and three sources if Rolls-Royce launches when selected).

I concur. My record is thin, so this check runs on Boeing's operations doctrine. The KPI gate is doctrine [B-2221, B-2351, B-2308]; the delivery-first reading is my 2022 BGS rule [BX-1331], applied to airplanes by inference.
