airbus.public_statement: Our core principles of safety, quality, integrity, compliance and security will remain at the heart of all we do. Our next-generation single-aisle aircraft is in development, and it is the centre of our work to prepare the Airbus of the 2030s. We continue to plan for it to enter service in the second half of this decade, once its technologies, its production system and its engines are mature. Safety and quality come before the calendar. Its engine selection stays open to all three narrowbody engine makers, and we plan for a dual-source engine supply, with each engine entering service only once its durability is proven. How the engine makers organise themselves is their decision. A stable, diversified supply of parts, engines first, is a condition of a disciplined and controlled production ramp-up. The A320neo family, with its two engine options, stays in production through the transition: its lines keep running longer while the new aircraft ramps up, so customers are served without a break. We are giving our suppliers long-range signals for that ramp, and we continue to secure our own materials and work packages. We take on one major development at a time and fund it from our own cash flow, preserving our financial flexibility and a strong balance sheet. With our partners across the industry, on both sides of the Atlantic, we keep working for a tariff-free, zero-for-zero trade regime in civil aerospace. And we keep recruiting and training, in Europe and across our global footprint, the people who will design and build the Airbus of the 2030s.
airbus.rationale:
DECISION, ROUND 2 (2035): HOLD COURSE
- Every field stays at its default, and code 7 is submitted explicitly.
- There are no Board items and no override.

MY ORDER OF QUESTIONS
1. The five pillars: no covert move, and no order or statement a regulator could read as misconduct.
2. The ramp: a disciplined and controlled transition, with the A320neo lines kept longer.
3. The 2030s: NGSA stays on its technology clock to EIS 2037.
4. Can I take it to the Board? Yes. There is nothing to take, and nothing the Board said it would veto.

TEAM RULE, STEP BY STEP

1. Deletions. These are company red lines and the pillars, never traded for PV.
- Every Delay Tactics row is deleted.
  - No fps is on the public record, so any move is naked and draws the $48.32B fine (rule 4).
  - Against A, one move scores -15.69 in S1 and -15.68 in S6 and S8, and at most +0.84 elsewhere.
  - Bottleneck and both also fail the pillars, and both counts as two moves.
  - The team's stricter condition (the move must change who enters service first) also keeps it off. I do not set that condition aside.
- Every cancel row is deleted (rule 7). There is no failed case. A cancellation writes off $25.37B ($35.52B x 5/7) and loses $19.95B (S4) to $23.84B (S1, S6).
- The base-plan Re-engine row is deleted because row B dominates it.

2. Tests on the remaining rows.
- Row A (the default) is a survivor.
  - Toepfer passes it on peak cash: $5.07B in 2035 and in 2036, $0.13B of headroom, nothing from 2037. The Alt plan's $0.75B is post-EIS cost, about $0.09B a year.
  - He also passes it on robustness (positive in all nine columns; worst S9 +0.48, then S4 +2.69), on liquidity and on Board items (none).
  - Wagner passes it on the gates (nothing is reported against them), supply crunch and code 7, on the Alt plan for safety, quality, the ramp shield and supply crunch, and on the five pillars.
- Row B (A plus an A350 Re-engine launched in 2035, EIS 2040) is not a survivor.
  - Wagner passes it, at the limit: 2 years of overlap, $1.2B of strain, no slip margin.
  - Toepfer fails it on peak cash. $5.07B + $1.0B + $0.6B = $6.67B in each of 2035 and 2036. That is $1.47B over the line each year, $2.95B in all.
  - On his static base, net cash would end 2036 at about -$1.1B even at the 30% payout floor.
  - This is a binding soft veto.
- Row C (the base plan) is not a survivor.
  - Toepfer fails it on robustness: -0.16 to -1.08 against A, and S9 raw is -0.10.
  - Row C was only the fallback if Wagner failed the Alt plan. He passed it, so the fallback does not apply.

3. Choice. Row A is the only survivor and the company default.
- It is also the highest-scoring survivor in every column.
- S2: +5.36. On my rough weights it is +7.12; at equal weights, +5.65.

4. Override check.
Row B leads row A by +1.54 in S2. That clears the team rule's $1B bar, so the ExCo rule would allow an override recorded as a Board item. I decline it, for four reasons:
- (a) The Board vetoes it on its own liquidity test, and an ExCo override cannot answer a Board test. On its Qualified Majority review the Board also reads the item as trailing hold by $1.21B in S6 and $1.20B in S7.
- (b) My balance-sheet risk appetite is Low. On the static base, the breach would take net cash negative in NGSA's last cash year.
- (c) The Board approves at most one override per game. Spending it on a known veto would be poor governance.
- (d) In 2030 we said in public that we take on one major development at a time and fund it from our own cash flow. The Board recorded that as a capital-markets commitment.
Wagner's flags point the same way:
- There is no slip margin: a one-year NGSA slip would mean 3 years of overlap and $1.8B of strain.
- No widebody engine is on record for a 2040 EIS.
- Industrialisation would fall in the 2038-40 trough.

5. What holding costs, recorded honestly.
- The costs:
  - We forgo +1.54 in S2 and in six other columns.
  - The company's 2033-35 window closes this round.
  - The brief does not price a 2045 Re-engine, so no one can say whether waiting gains or loses (Toepfer).
- What holding buys:
  - No strain and no cash breach.
  - The 787 Re-engine question resolves before we commit, which avoids the -1.21 and -1.20 in S6 and S7.
- The forgone value is the cost of the cash line, not a doctrine premium.

6. Engine code: 7, submitted explicitly, on Wagner's recommendation.
- It gives CFM + P&W GTF2: 2 sources and 2 makers.
- It is in no forbidden pair and adds no cash.
- It is final, because the 2045 round falls after EIS.
- If GTF2 slips past 2037 or P&W stops it, NGSA flies CFM alone and keeps its date.

7. The public line on engines.
- Wagner fails a public invitation of a P&W-Rolls-Royce Joint Venture, on supply grounds.
- The rules give no date for a Joint Venture engine that takes in GTF2 when the venture forms: "6 years later, or earlier if a partner folds in a solo programme that is further along".
- If that engine came after 2037, both P&W and Rolls-Royce would drop out and NGSA would fly CFM alone. No code could repair that.
- The dual-source enabler is met. I will not put it at risk for a third maker the rules cannot date.
- The selection stays open to all three makers, and how they organise is their decision. This departs in part from Board recommendation 3, and I say so in board_response.

8. The NGSA clock.
- EIS 2037 is two years after the technology-ready year.
- A failed gate or an engine slip re-times EIS later (2038 is the honest exposure), never earlier, and never leads to a cancellation.
- No Boeing move re-times it.

9. Board-gate lines.
- There are no Board items this round, because every field is at its default.
- For the record, A350 hold: five pillars pass, Toepfer passes, Wagner passes, ΔPV 0 against the default.

10. Round 1 correction. I expected an fps in 2030 (S2), and Boeing held. This round's decision does not depend on the scenario call, because row A is the best survivor in every column.

11. Next round (2045).
- The A350 Re-engine is re-tested on that round's grid: $1.0B a year, no overlap, no strain. It is closed if Boeing has launched a 787 Re-engine (rule 3).
- No programme will be timed to reopen Delay Tactics. They are never named in public.

airbus.objective_note:
These goals are scored by the GM and never change the payoff. No PV is traded for any of them.

Defend 60/40: not met.
- 2040 is 47.4%; 2045 is 69.0% and 2050 is 74.0%.
- 2040 fails because of our own factory trough: 827 and 852 aircraft in 2039-40, against about 1,057 and 1,078 needed for 60%. The A320 tail winds down faster than NGSA ramps.
- Customer preference for Boeing is not the cause. No order closes the gap, and the Alt plan is already the larger plan.

Protect the A320 family: met (60.0%). The Alt plan keeps it in production through the transition.

Enabler, dual sources: met (CFM + GTF2 in 2040, 2045 and 2050).
- Code 7 is final.
- This holds only while GTF2 keeps its 2036 date. CFM alone is the fallback.

Enabler, three makers: not met.
- Rolls-Royce has no engine that can be ready by 2037. The brief shows a third maker only in the fps columns, and only if P&W and Rolls-Royce launch when selected.
- I keep the selection open to all three makers, but I do not invite a Joint Venture. The rules cannot date its engine, and a date after 2037 would cost the dual-source result we already hold.

priorities: Safety and the five pillars come first, so there is no covert move this round. Boeing has launched no fps, so any Delay Tactics move would be naked and draw the $48.32B fine. Against the default row, one poaching move loses $15.69B in S1 and $15.68B in S6 and S8. It gains at most $0.84B in the fps columns, below the Board's $1B condition even there [AG-0038, A-0331, AG-0053, A-0474, A-0299, AG-0022].

Keep NGSA whole on its 2037 clock, with engine code 7. Continuing beats cancelling in every column, by $19.95B (S4) to $23.84B (S1, S6), and a cancellation would write off about $25.37B ($35.52B x 5/7). NGSA is not a failed case like the A380, and a Boeing move is never a reason to cancel it [AG-0063, A-0225, A-0409, AG-0055, A-0143, A-0364, AG-0039].

One programme at a time, to protect liquidity and the A+/A1 rating. 2035 and 2036 are NGSA's last two cash years, at $5.07B each against the $5.2B line, which leaves $0.13B of headroom. An A350 Re-engine launched now would take both years to $6.67B. Its turn comes once NGSA spend has ended, when it costs $1.0B a year with no strain [AX-0022, A-0402, AG-0062, A-0343, A-0401, AX-0104].

A stable engine supply. Code 7 now gives NGSA CFM plus P&W GTF2 (GTF2 is ready in 2036, one year before EIS), so the dual-source enabler is met in 2040, 2045 and 2050. Three makers in the market is not met: Rolls-Royce has no engine that could be ready by NGSA's 2037 EIS. The Board asks the ExCo to keep code 7 and keep the door open to a third maker. The code is a recommendation and never a veto ground [A-0243, A-0360, AX-0054].

A disciplined ramp, with shareholder returns kept fundable. The A320 Alt plan stays: it beats the base plan in every column. The operating head should account for the capacity trough of 2039-43. The payout stays within 30-50%. No new buyback is committed before NGSA spend ends in 2036 without a Board re-test, and there is no equity raise [A-0303, AG-0067, AG-0068, AG-0058, AG-0059, AG-0054, AG-0034].
board_guidance.risk_appetite: Risk-averse (4 of 5) and long-term (4 of 5), in a round for holding course. The Board accepts NGSA's last two cash years at $5.07B against the $5.2B line and nothing that adds to them. That means no second programme before NGSA spend ends in 2036, no covert move, no cancellation, and no Board item that fails to gain in the CEO's expected column or loses more than $2B in any column from S1 to S9.
board_guidance.expect_to_see:
For each Board item, the Board expects to see the following.

(1) The grid row of the submitted orders. The Board expects 'NGSA: hold (A320 Alt plan) + A350: hold': +10.86 / +5.36 / +6.35 / +2.69 / +5.36 / +10.37 / +4.87 / +4.55 / +0.48. It is positive in every column; the worst is S9 at +0.48, then S4 at +2.69.

(2) The row with each Board item set back to its default. If the ExCo holds every field (ngsa hold, rea350 hold, delay_tactics none, a320_plan alt as the current plan, code 7 unchanged), there are no Board items and the two rows are the same. For any field it changes, show the item value column by column. For example, an A350 Re-engine shows +1.54 / +1.54 / +1.55 / +1.54 / +1.54 / -1.21 / -1.20 / +1.55 / +1.55.

(3) The CEO's expected scenario, named, and the worst plausible column. The bulletin rules out no column:
- Boeing has launched neither an fps nor a 787 Re-engine. It says its balance sheet is 'back where it belongs' and that a new airplane comes when it is ready, which keeps S2-S5 live.
- It intends to keep the 787 'the most efficient in its segment', which keeps S6 and S7 live.
- Embraer says it is in its 'harvest season' with no decision. That makes S8 and S9 less likely, but does not rule them out.
So all nine columns count.

(4) The CFO's peak-cash table:
- 2035 and 2036 at $5.07B each ($0.13B headroom), and no programme spend from 2037.
- The Alt plan's $0.75B, still recorded as post-EIS line cost over 2037-44 (about $0.09B a year).
- Net cash and the rating through 2036.
- Confirmation that the dividend stays within 30-50% and that no new buyback is committed before 2037 without a Board re-test.
- The arithmetic for a 2035 Re-engine ($5.07B + $1.0B + $0.6B strain = $6.67B in 2035-36) and for a 2045 Re-engine ($1.0B a year, no overlap).

(5) Wagner's results:
- The NGSA gates (the run-at-rate wing and the production system) on track for 2037.
- GTF2's one-year readiness margin, and the CFM fallback if it slips.
- Safety, quality, the A320 ramp shield and supply crunch on the Alt plan.
- His reading of the 2039-43 capacity trough. In 2039-40 capacity is 827 and 852 against demand of 1,931 and 1,972, and preference falls to 47.0% and 47.4%.

(6) The engine code and its sources. Code 7 gives CFM + P&W GTF2: 2 sources and 2 makers if the engine makers hold, and 3 makers in the fps columns if Rolls-Royce launches with Boeing. Also confirmation that code 7 is in no forbidden pair. Submit 7 explicitly rather than None.

(7) Any override and its margin. The Board expects none.

(8) A public statement that gives windows rather than dates, leads with the pillars and does not mention Delay Tactics.

(9) A board_response to each round 1 recommendation: the annual cash report to the Audit Committee, the gate reports, and the engine re-test.
would_approve: ngsa: hold. NGSA continues to EIS 2037, with engine code 7 riding on it. This is the default and not a Board item, but the Board backs it: holding beats cancelling by $19.95B (S4) to $23.84B (S1, S6) in every column. The default row gains in all nine columns (+0.48 to +10.86).

a320_plan: alt. This is the current plan and the default this round. If the GM treats it as a Board item, the Board approves it: against base it gains +0.70 / +0.51 / +0.16 / +1.08 / +0.51 / +0.70 / +0.50 / +0.68 / +0.58, so it loses in no column. Its $0.75B falls after EIS.

a320_plan: base, only if Wagner's tests now fail the Alt plan on safety, quality, the A320 ramp shield or a supply crunch. Safety ranks first, so the Board would then accept the base plan's PV cost of at most $1.08B (S4).
ngsa_engine_code 7, kept, as the Board recommends. Codes 5 and 6 would also keep CFM plus a second maker named, though code 5 would fit CFM alone. No code is ever a veto ground.
rea350: hold and delay_tactics: none. These are defaults and are never vetoed.
would_veto: ngsa: cancel, in any row, on the reactive-cancellation ground. Continuing beats cancelling in every column: -23.84 / -21.53 / -21.66 / -19.95 / -21.53 / -23.84 / -21.53 / -22.40 / -20.74. Cancelling with a Re-engine is no better, at -17.84 to -24.48 against the default. It would write off about $25.37B. The Board's test allows a cancel only when continuing loses at least $1B in every plausible column, and never for a Boeing move. Acceptable alternative: hold.

rea350: launch in 2035, on the balance-sheet ground. NGSA develops over 2030-37 and the Re-engine over 2035-40, so 2035 and 2036 carry $5.07B + $1.0B + $0.6B strain = $6.67B against the $5.2B line. Under the plan-level rule the Re-engine is vetoed, never NGSA.
- It passes the downside test: +1.54 in seven columns, and -1.21 (S6) and -1.20 (S7), within $2B.
- It passes the one-clean-sheet test: one launch, with 2 years of overlap.

WHY HOLD THE A350 RE-ENGINE

- In round 1 we told the market we would take on one major development at a time and fund it from our own cash flow.
The $1.54B forgone in S2 is the cost of the cash line, not a doctrine premium: the Re-engine fails a soft veto, so it is not a survivor. I record one cost: the company's 2033-35 window closes this round, and the brief does not price a 2045 Re-engine.

- Boeing now says its own preconditions are met: the balance sheet is back, the 777X is in service and the MAX 7 and MAX 10 are certified.
- "Headroom" points to the 10-year schedule, and its public fps plan is new sites rather than Renton.
- S1, another hold, is the strong alternative, because Boeing gives no date.
- The 787 line keeps S6 and S7 live, but the GEnx upgrade and the Charleston capacity point to an engine upgrade rather than a Re-engine (inference).

OBJECTIVE NOTE

PUBLIC LINE

- One major development at a time, funded from our own cash flow.

- No dates, no internal targets, no mention of Delay Tactics.

WHAT WOULD MOVE ME

- A cash breach from Thomas.

Cross-check: the brief's non-recurring line books $36.3B in 2037, which is $35.52B NGSA + $0.75B Alt at EIS, outside the development years. Even lumped into 2037 alone, $0.75B passes. Code 7 adds $0 in every year.

tests.name: Peak annual cash: row B (A + A350 Re-engine launched 2035, EIS 2040)
tests.threshold: No year above about $5.2B (one year's FCF)
tests.numbers: Re-engine development runs 2035-39 at $5B / 5 = $1.0B a year. Its overlap with NGSA development (2030-36, EIS 2037) is 2 years, 2035-36. Strain is $3B x 2/5 = $1.2B, or $0.6B a year. Year by year: 2035 5.07 + 1.00 + 0.60 = $6.67B; 2036 $6.67B; 2037-39 1.00 + 0.09 = $1.09B; 2040 $0.09B. The peak of $6.67B is 128% of the line: $1.47B over in each of two years, $2.95B in all, drawn from net cash. Nothing on the board brings 2035-36 under the line with a Re-engine. Without strain it would still be $6.07B. Launch aid carries no cash term because it is priced as our own money. The Alt plan has nothing in 2035-36 to defer. Code 7 costs $0, and Delay Tactics only add. The base-plan Re-engine row gives the same result. The only route that passes is a Re-engine whose development starts after 2036, which on this calendar means the 2045 round.

tests.name: Peak-cash line: re-base question (CEO ask 1)
tests.threshold: The $5.2B line is the Board's governing figure this round. I apply the company guardrails and add none
tests.numbers: Breakeven: a 2035 Re-engine passes only if one year's FCF reaches at least $6.67B (about EUR 6.07bn at $1.10). That is 28% above FY2025's EUR 4,753m. The brief's operating profit rises from $3.6B (2026) to $7.1B (2035), but operating profit is not FCF, and the board reports no FCF. The analyst context (2030E FCF EUR 10.7-11.6bn) is real-world only, and neither bank models an A320 successor. I do not recommend re-basing a guardrail mid-programme, on a forecast, to let a second programme into NGSA's last two cash years. A re-base on reported FCF can come with the 2045 brief, where it does not bind. The Board's test decides.

tests.name: Peak annual cash: A350 Re-engine launched 2045 (forward flag, not an order)
tests.threshold: No year above about $5.2B
tests.numbers: Development 2045-49 at $5B / 5 = $1.0B a year. No NGSA overlap and $0 strain; the Alt line cost ends in 2044. Peak $1.0B, 19% of the line. This brief does not price it. Re-test on the 2045 grid; rule 3 closes it if Boeing launches a 787 Re-engine first.

tests.name: Robustness: row A
tests.threshold: Plan dPV positive in the worst plausible Boeing column. The bulletin rules out no column, so all nine count
tests.numbers: S1-S9: +10.86 / +5.36 / +6.35 / +2.69 / +5.36 / +10.37 / +4.87 / +4.55 / +0.48. Positive in every column. Worst S9 +0.48, then S4 +2.69. Expected column S2 +5.36. About +7.12 on the CEO's weights and +5.65 at equal weights. With every field at its default, row A is itself this round's Do Nothing.

tests.name: Robustness and added-item test: row B (Re-engine item)
tests.threshold: Plan positive in the worst plausible column. An added move must gain at least $1B over the same plan without it; one that turns negative in a plausible column and misses $1B fails (drafter's reading). Board: the item gains in the expected column and loses no more than $2B in any column
tests.numbers: Plan S1-S9: +12.40 / +6.90 / +7.90 / +4.23 / +6.90 / +9.16 / +3.67 / +6.10 / +2.03. Worst S9 +2.03, above row A's +0.48. Item against A: +1.54 / +1.54 / +1.55 / +1.54 / +1.54 / -1.21 / -1.20 / +1.55 / +1.55. It clears $1B in S2 and six other columns, and its losses of $1.21B (S6) and $1.20B (S7) are within $2B. About +1.13 on the CEO's weights. The profile's three 2033-35 conditions hold: no 787 Re-engine on record, at least $1B with strain in S2, and overlap of 2 years. The S6 and S7 losses fall exactly where rule 3 would have kept us out. Robustness does not rescue it: it fails on cash.

tests.name: Robustness: row C (A320 base plan) against row A
tests.threshold: A change from the default must gain at least $1B and never turn negative in a plausible column
tests.numbers: C against A: -0.70 / -0.51 / -0.16 / -1.08 / -0.51 / -0.70 / -0.50 / -0.68 / -0.58, negative in every column; raw S9 is -0.10. Cash passes: peak $5.07B with no Alt cost. Row C is the fallback only. If Wagner fails the Alt plan on safety, quality, the ramp shield or supply crunch, the pillars rank first and I withdraw this objection.

tests.name: Overlap and one launch per round: row B
tests.threshold: Rule 6: at most one new launch per round, and NGSA / A350 Re-engine overlap of 2 years or less unless the grid shows at least $1B more
tests.numbers: One new launch (the Re-engine; NGSA is not new). The overlap is 2035-36, 2 years, at the limit, with $1.2B of strain. Rule 6 passes; it is the cash line that binds. Row A has 0 years of overlap and $0 strain.

tests.name: Liquidity and shareholder returns through 2036 (the 2035 annual cash report to the Audit Committee)
tests.threshold: Net cash stays positive through 2036; payout within 30-50%; no new buyback before 2037 without a Board re-test; no equity raise; A+/A1 anchored on positive net cash (inference)
tests.numbers: The board prices only a debt penalty (-0.53 PV in row A's components) and reports no FCF, net cash or rating, so the figures below are bounds (inference). Static FY2025 base: FCF is $5.2B and NGSA takes 97% of it, leaving $0.13B. Net cash starts at $13.4B (EUR 12.2bn) and is held flat to 2030. At the 30% floor the dividend is about $1.74B (scaled from EUR 2,527m at 48%), so net cash falls $1.61B a year: about $5.4B entering 2035 and about $2.1B at end-2036, still positive. At 48% it falls $2.65B a year: about nil entering 2035 and about -$5.2B at end-2036, a fail. So on the static base the payout sits near the floor. On the brief's profit path (operating profit 1.97 times its 2026 level) FCF would be higher and a mid-range payout fundable; the Board sets the payout on reported FCF. With a 2035 Re-engine, the static floor path ends 2036 at about -$1.1B, so net cash turns negative. Row A needs no new buyback before 2037 without a re-test, and no equity raise. The record holds no rating thresholds.

tests.name: Fine exposure: any Delay Tactics move this round
tests.threshold: Rule 4 red line: no move before an fps is on the public record. A naked move draws the $48.32B fine
tests.numbers: No fps is public. One move against A: -15.69 / +0.83 / +0.21 / +0.25 / +0.83 / -15.68 / +0.84 / -15.68 / +0.71. It is naked in S1, S6 and S8 and falls short of $1B even in the fps columns. It is a red line and struck. A bottleneck move beyond a first claim on capacity would also be an integrity flag that I could not defend to the Audit Committee.

tests.name: Second move: delay_tactics both
tests.threshold: Rule 4 red line: never a second move
tests.numbers: Both moves against A: -16.14 / +0.45 / -0.17 / -0.19 / +0.45 / -16.14 / +0.46 / -16.13 / +0.32. That is $0.38-0.46B worse than one move in every column, because the second $1B buys nothing. The Board vetoes both in every round.

tests.name: Delay Tactics cash
tests.threshold: Each $1B move is spread evenly from the order year to fps EIS and added to that year's spend
tests.numbers: Ordered in 2035, one move adds to each of 2035-36: with no fps (S1, S6 and S8; snapshot 2041), $1B / 6 = $0.17B, giving $5.24B; with an fps 7-yr (S4, EIS 2042), $0.14B, giving $5.22B; with an fps 10-yr (EIS 2045), $0.10B, giving $5.17B. That is over the line in four columns. Both moves double the add, to $5.41B in S1.

tests.name: Poaching (rule 5)
tests.threshold: Poaching only while NGSA or an A350 Re-engine is in development
tests.numbers: NGSA is in development through 2036, so rule 5 alone would not bar poaching this round; fine exposure under rule 4 does. In 2045 rule 5 holds only if an A350 Re-engine is then in development. No programme should be timed to reopen this lever.

tests.name: Cancel NGSA (rule 7)
tests.threshold: Never cancel NGSA. Write-off = bill x years elapsed / development years
tests.numbers: Write-off: $35.52B x 5/7 = $25.37B, a reported charge in 2035. It would be excluded from EBIT Adjusted but never hidden. Cancel + A350 hold against A: -23.84 / -21.53 / -21.66 / -19.95 / -21.53 / -23.84 / -21.53 / -22.40 / -20.74. Cancel + Re-engine against A: -17.84 (S4) to -24.48 (S6). No failed case exists, so this is a red line.

tests.name: Capex timing (tie-break within $1B)
tests.threshold: Between options within $1B, prefer the later capex start
tests.numbers: The gap between A and B in S2 is $1.54B, outside the $1B band. If it were inside, the tie-break would favour A, which starts no capex before 2045.

tests.name: Board items
tests.threshold: Every order above EUR 300m is a Board item; within $1B, prefer fewer
tests.numbers: Row A has 0 Board items: ngsa hold, code 7 (unchanged and submitted explicitly), rea350 hold, delay_tactics none, a320_plan alt (the current plan). Row B has 1: the Re-engine, $5B, a Qualified Majority item above EUR 800m. Any take-or-pay, advance or payment above EUR 300m to induce an engine launch would be a separate item; none is proposed.

tests.name: Engine code 7 (cash view)
tests.threshold: No added programme cash in any year. The code is never a cash veto ground
tests.numbers: $0 in every year, so the peak stays $5.07B. I defer to Wagner on the code and expect him to request 7: CFM + GTF2, 2 sources. A public welcome to an engine from a P&W-Rolls-Royce Joint Venture costs nothing, provided there is no payment and no confidential exchange; on those terms I can defend it to the Audit Committee.

tests.name: 2045 A350 Re-engine: the value of waiting (CEO ask 6)
tests.threshold: State only what the brief supports, with no estimate it does not give
tests.numbers: What can be said: cash falls to $1.0B a year with no strain, avoiding the $1.2B. EIS moves from 2040 to 2050, so the 20-year market window and its profit arrive ten years later and are discounted further at the 8% WACC. The A350's lone share gain (1.5 pp a year) and margin lift start later. Waiting also lets the 787 Re-engine question resolve first, which avoids the -1.21 and -1.20 in S6 and S7. What cannot be said: the brief does not price a 2045 launch, so I give no value, no sign and no comparison with the +1.54 forgone. The company's 2033-35 window closes this round. The +1.54 forgone in S2 is the cost of the cash line, not a doctrine premium.

vetoes.plan: Row B: NGSA hold (A320 Alt plan) + A350 Re-engine launched in 2035, EIS 2040 (the base-plan Re-engine row likewise)
vetoes.ground: Failed peak-cash test: $5.07B + $1.0B + $0.6B strain = $6.67B in each of 2035 and 2036, against the $5.2B line. That is $1.47B over in each year and $2.95B in all, drawn from net cash. On the static base, net cash ends 2036 at about -$1.1B even at the 30% payout floor. This is a soft veto, and binding. Grid margin over the best passing option, row A: +1.54 in the expected S2, +1.54/+1.55 in seven columns, and -1.21 (S6) and -1.20 (S7). The S2 margin clears the team rule's $1B bar, but the override is Faury's to make, not mine to pre-clear. Before the Audit Committee I would present any override as what it is: a recorded breach of the liquidity guardrail, made for +1.54 in S2 at the risk of -1.21 and -1.20 in S6 and S7. I would not support it. An override answers only the ExCo rule. The Board's liquidity test is separate, and an ExCo override cannot pass it.

vetoes.plan: Any Delay Tactics row (bottleneck, poaching or both)
vetoes.ground: Rule 4 red line (fine exposure): no fps is on the public record, so any move is naked and draws the $48.32B fine. One move scores -15.69 in S1 and -15.68 in S6 and S8, and at most +0.84 elsewhere, short of $1B. `both` is a second move, also a red line. The Delay Tactics cash test also fails: 2035-36 rise to $5.24B where there is no fps. A bottleneck move beyond a first claim on capacity is an integrity flag (five pillars) that I could not defend to the Audit Committee. No override is possible.

vetoes.plan: Any cancel row (ngsa: cancel, with or without a Re-engine)
vetoes.ground: Rule 7 red line: NGSA is never cancelled, and no failed case exists. The write-off is $35.52B x 5/7 = $25.37B, a reported charge. Against holding, cancelling loses $19.95B (S4) to $23.84B (S1, S6), or $17.84B to $24.48B with a Re-engine. No override is possible.

vetoes.plan: Row C: NGSA hold on the A320 base plan + A350 hold
vetoes.ground: Failed robustness test, a soft veto: against row A it loses in every column (-0.16 to -1.08; -0.51 in S2), and raw S9 is -0.10. Grid margin against the best passing option is -0.51 in S2, so no override margin exists. The veto lapses if Wagner fails the Alt plan on safety, quality, the A320 ramp shield or supply crunch. The pillars rank first, and row C's cash passes (peak $5.07B).

cfo.would_change_mind_if: Any of the following. (1) The Board, on reported FCF, re-bases the peak-cash line to at least $6.67B (about EUR 6.07bn, 28% above FY2025) before orders are sealed. The 2035 Re-engine already passes robustness and overlap, so it would then pass my tests. That is not on this record, and I do not propose it. (2) The Board decides otherwise. (3) A passing plan shows at least $1B over row A in the expected column. (4) Wagner fails the Alt plan on safety, quality, the A320 ramp shield or supply crunch; I would then move to the base plan and withdraw my row C objection. (5) For 2045: a Re-engine at $1.0B a year with no strain passes peak cash, and I would re-test it on that round's grid if Boeing has launched no 787 Re-engine. No grid margin moves me on Delay Tactics or a cancellation, because both are red lines. Only a public fps launch would reopen a single poaching re-test, and only with every Board condition met.
cfo.memo:
CFO test memo, round 2 (2035).

Fundability. NGSA's last two cash years, 2035 and 2036, carry $35.52B / 7 = $5.07B each against a peak-cash line of one year's FCF, about $5.2B (EUR 4,753m at an assumed $1.10). Headroom: $0.13B. From 2037 programme cash is nil. The Alt plan's $0.75B is line cost, about $0.09B a year over 2037-44; the brief books it at NGSA's EIS ($36.3B in 2037), so none falls in 2035-36. Code 7 costs nothing.

A350 Re-engine in 2035. $5.07B + $1.0B + $0.6B strain = $6.67B in 2035 and in 2036, $1.47B over the line. Fail: a soft veto, binding. Its value is real: +1.54 in S2 and six other columns, -1.21 and -1.20 in S6 and S7. The margin clears the team's $1B bar, but the Board's liquidity test is its own; an ExCo override cannot answer it. Launch aid is priced as our own money. I would not re-base the line on a forecast mid-programme: the Re-engine passes only if a year's FCF reaches $6.67B, 28% above FY2025.

Downside. Row A is positive in every column: S9 +0.48, then S4 +2.69.

Strikes. Cancelling writes off $25.37B and loses $19.95-23.84B. Any Delay Tactics move is naked: -15.69 in S1.

Flexibility. On a static FY2025 base the dividend sits near the 30% floor to keep net cash positive through 2036; no new buyback before 2037 without a Board re-test; no equity raise.

Orders: all defaults, code 7 per Wagner. No Board items.

tests.name: Ask 1: production readiness, NGSA gates (run-at-rate wing, production system) for EIS 2037
tests.threshold: NGSA enters service only once the wing has been proven buildable at rate and the production system has matured with the aircraft. EIS no earlier than the 2035 technology-ready year (rule 1, red line). A failed gate or an engine maturity slip moves EIS later, never earlier, and never leads to cancellation.
tests.numbers: The brief shows NGSA in development with EIS 2037. It reports no inject, no failed gate and no safety, quality or supply event. EIS 2037 is two years after the 2035 technology-ready year. The board's NGSA line follows the public plan: 8 aircraft (2037), 27, 93, 296, 562, 822, 998, 1,143 and 1,302 (2045). That puts rate 50 around 2041-42 and about 100 by 2044-45. My record holds no gate data beyond the brief, so this is a pass on 'nothing reported against the gates', not a measured result. This is the gate report for the Board's twice-yearly product-safety review. Honest exposure: a one-year slip would put EIS in 2038, outside 2035-2037. It would widen GTF2's margin to two years and change no code.

tests.name: Ask 2: engine maturity slip, GTF2 margin and CFM fallback
tests.threshold: If the brief reports an engine maturity slip, move NGSA so that EIS stays at or after the new technology-ready year, and never cancel. An unready maker is dropped and CFM is the floor, so rule 8 cannot bind.
tests.numbers: No inject. GTF2 is ready in 2036, one year before EIS 2037. If it slips past 2037, or P&W cancels it (the rules allow this until the engine is ready, so this round), P&W is dropped. NGSA then flies CFM alone: one source, with no change to NGSA's date. In that case CFM's Airbus load, from the brief's deliveries (A320neo tail at 60% CFM, all NGSA on CFM), is 44 sets a month (2039), 53 (2040), 73 (2041), 84 (2042), 92 (2043), 99 (2044) and 95 (2045). On top of that it supplies Boeing's MAX at up to 57 a month, about 155 in all against about 108 today. The code cannot change after this round, because the next round (2045) falls after EIS. Code 7 submitted now is final.

tests.name: Ask 2: supply crunch re-test on the Alt plan with NGSA on CFM + GTF2 (rows A and B)
tests.threshold: If the brief reports a supply crunch, no new concurrency. No plan may ask an engine maker for more than it supplies us today without a rate signal behind it.
tests.numbers: The brief reports no crunch. I computed Airbus engine sets a month from the brief's deliveries: A320neo at CFM 60 / P&W 40; NGSA split equally, or about 43/57 if GTF2's +10 pp applies on NGSA (inference). CFM: 47 (2037), 38-41 (2038-40), 44-51 (2041-44), 41-47 (2045). That is never above the 51 it supplies us today (2034: 1,020 aircraft). P&W: 32 (2037), 26-33 (2038-40), 41-57 (2041-44), 47-54 (2045), against 34 today. All of P&W's growth is on GTF2, a new engine that P&W says will not enter service before its durability is proven. That is the watch item. CFM's total, including Boeing's MAX at up to 57 a month, stays at or below today's level of about 108. The round 1 single-source flag (CFM alone) is closed while GTF2 holds. The Alt tail asks LEAP-1A and GTF for less every year: 940 A320neo in 2036, 740 in 2038, 556 in 2040, 307 in 2042 and 68 in 2044. A Re-engine (row B) adds no narrowbody engine demand.

tests.name: Ask 2: engine supply, NGSA engine code
tests.threshold: Recommend a code that keeps CFM in the set plus at least one second maker (5, 6 or 7), and 7 when it is unclear which maker will be ready by EIS. This is a recommendation, not a veto ground.
tests.numbers: Code 7, submitted explicitly. It gives CFM + P&W GTF2: 2 sources and 2 makers, which meets the dual-source enabler in 2040, 2045 and 2050. Code 6 gives the same sources. Codes 1, 3 and 5 give CFM alone, and codes 2 and 4 GTF2 alone. Code 7 is in no forbidden (fps, NGSA) pair: no listed pair has 7 on the NGSA side, and a forbidden pair moves the later airframe to 7 anyway. It carries no EIS risk, because an unready maker is dropped and CFM is the floor. It is the only code that also names Rolls-Royce. It adds no cash.

tests.name: Ask 2: Joint Venture route, public welcome of a P&W-Rolls-Royce partnership (other move / public line)
tests.threshold: No public line that can cost NGSA its second source at EIS 2037 (supply first). This is a recommendation, not a veto ground.
tests.numbers: A Joint Venture formed in 2035 has its engine ready in 2041 (6 years), or 'earlier' if a partner folds in a solo programme that is further along. GTF2 would fold in when the venture forms, so P&W would reach NGSA only through the Joint Venture engine. The rules give no date for that earlier case. Plain reading (inference): the joint engine takes GTF2's 2036 date. NGSA then keeps 2 sources (CFM + the Joint Venture engine, which counts as one), and Rolls-Royce holds narrowbody share as a third maker in the market. Any reading that puts the joint engine after 2037 drops both P&W and Rolls-Royce. NGSA then flies CFM alone (1 source; CFM load as in the fallback test), and no code can repair it, because this is the last round before EIS. The brief shows the third maker arriving only in the fps columns. So: keep 'NGSA's selection stays open to all three makers'. Do not invite a partnership; how the makers team up is their call.

tests.name: Ask 3: A320 ramp shield, Alt plan (and row B)
tests.threshold: No new programme spend that competes with the open A320 ramp commitment. This passes unless the brief reports a ramp problem.
tests.numbers: The end-2027 commitment (rate 70-75, then 75) is behind us. The A320 holds 85 a month until NGSA EIS. The Alt tail then runs at 82/62/52/42/14 a month over about eight years on existing lines, below today's rate. The brief reports no ramp problem. The 2039-40 trough is the public production plan, not a ramp failure. A 2035 Re-engine spends on the widebody and takes no A320 capacity on the board.

tests.name: Ask 3: safety and quality, Alt plan
tests.threshold: No order whose execution or public explanation contradicts safety and quality (five pillars, binding).
tests.numbers: The brief reports no safety or quality event. Alt keeps a mature product on running lines, below 85 a month, with no new line and no design change. The base plan winds down faster (72/52/42/14 over about five years) and would deepen the 2039-41 trough. It also loses -0.16 to -1.08 against Alt in every column. So there is no safety or quality reason to fall back to it.

tests.name: Ask 4: the 2039-43 capacity trough (Board ask; I hold no threshold on it)
tests.threshold: Reading only. No move may compress testing, cost safety or quality, or claim capacity against a rival. We do not buy share at a PV cost.
tests.numbers: We deliver 827 aircraft (2039) and 852 (2040), about 69-71 a month against 85 today. That is 193 and 178 fewer than in the status quo. After COMAC's roughly 170-175 aircraft, new customers for Boeing and Airbus number 1,761 and 1,797. Preference of 47.0% and 47.4% is exactly what our lines can build. Holding 60% would need about 1,057 and 1,078 aircraft, a gap of 230 and 226 (about 19 a month). The cause: the A320 tail falls from 734 to 556 a year while NGSA, two to three years after EIS, builds 93 and then 296. The board's 1% top-up and the extra lines from 2045 come too late. From 2041 we deliver more than the status quo: +36, +78, +111 and +150 in 2041-44. No order on this board closes the gap; Alt is already the larger plan. Our own unpriced moves protect the ramp: (a) long-range, rate-gated signals now to CFM and P&W for the 2039-44 LEAP-1A/GTF tail and NGSA sets, at the rates above, as with the A320neo ramp; (b) a contingent CFM framework for the CFM-alone case, reserving nothing against other customers; (c) the run-at-rate wing as the producibility gate; (d) hiring and training for the 2039-44 ramp; (e) titanium through Aubert & Duval, DED additive manufacturing and the raw-materials watchlist; (f) Spirit work packages fully integrated.

tests.name: Ask 5: engineering capacity, A350 Re-engine launched 2035 (row B)
tests.threshold: NGSA / A350 development overlap of 2 years or less ($1.2B strain) unless the grid shows at least $1B more. At most one new launch per round (rule 6, red line).
tests.numbers: Re-engine development runs 2035-39 (EIS 2040) and NGSA's runs 2030-36 (EIS 2037). Overlap is 2 years (2035-36) and strain is $3B x 2/5 = $1.2B. It is the only launch, so it passes rule 6 with no $1B test needed. It sits at the limit with no slip margin. A one-year NGSA slip to 2038 makes the overlap 3 years (2035-37) and the strain $1.8B, which fails unless the grid shows $1B more; the grid does not price that case. Item value against A: +1.54 / +1.54 / +1.55 / +1.54 / +1.54 / -1.21 / -1.20 / +1.55 / +1.55. Flags, not fails: (1) its industrialisation years (2038-40) fall in the NGSA ramp and the trough; (2) the A350 flies Rolls-Royce only, the company's default Re-engine engine is UltraFan, and Rolls-Royce has launched no UltraFan widebody. Launched now, that engine would be ready in 2041 (6 years), a year after a 2040 EIS. The board does not tie our Re-engine to it.

tests.name: Ask 5: A350F and Spirit absorption, A350 Re-engine 2035 (row B)
tests.threshold: No A350 Re-engine while the A350F and the Spirit A350 packages are being absorbed. Game proxy: not in round 1; the company window is 2033-35, so round 2 at the earliest.
tests.numbers: 2035 is round 2 and inside the 2033-35 window. The A350F entered its industrial phase in 2025 and the Spirit A350 packages came in during 2025, so ten years of absorption have passed by 2035. The company window closes this round.

tests.name: Ask 5: the same teams for a 2045 Re-engine test (forward)
tests.threshold: Overlap of 2 years or less; evidence that the engineering teams are free (NGSA development finished) moves me toward the Re-engine.
tests.numbers: NGSA development ends in 2036. A 2045 launch develops over 2045-49 for EIS 2050, with 0 years of overlap and $0 strain. NGSA production is near plateau by then: capacity 1,302 in 2045 and 1,429 in 2047. The A350F is long absorbed. On these numbers it passes my tests, unless Boeing has launched a 787 Re-engine (rule 3) or the brief reports a supply crunch.

tests.name: Delay Tactics, any row (rules 4-5, five pillars)
tests.threshold: Only after an fps is on the public record and before its EIS. At most one move ('both' counts as two). Bottleneck only as a first claim on scarce capacity for our own ramp. Poaching only while a programme is in development.
tests.numbers: No fps is on the public record, so any move is naked and draws the $48.32B fine. One move against row A scores -15.69 / +0.83 / +0.21 / +0.25 / +0.83 / -15.68 / +0.84 / -15.68 / +0.71. Both moves score -16.14 to +0.46. Rule 5 would allow poaching (NGSA is in development), but rule 4 bars it. Bottleneck and both also breach the pillars on the Board's reading.

tests.name: Cancel NGSA, any row (company doctrine: never cancel NGSA; rule 7)
tests.threshold: Never cancel NGSA. On a failed gate or an engine maturity slip, move it later instead.
tests.numbers: Cancelling against holding scores -23.84 / -21.53 / -21.66 / -19.95 / -21.53 / -23.84 / -21.53 / -22.40 / -20.74. With a Re-engine it is -17.84 to -24.48. The write-off is about $25.37B ($35.52B x 5/7). Nothing on my tests (gates, engines, supply, quality) calls for anything beyond keeping the schedule.

tests.name: Ask 7: five pillars, orders, other moves and public line
tests.threshold: No order or statement that contradicts safety, quality, integrity, compliance or security.
tests.numbers: Every order is at its default and there is no covert move. The engine invitation offers no payment and no confidential exchange. The rate signals and supply agreements cover our own needs only: our CFM call stays at or below today's 51 sets a month on two sources, so it claims no capacity that Boeing uses. Recruiting is our own and untargeted. Trade advocacy with Boeing stays strictly to public policy. The public line gives windows, not dates, and never mentions Delay Tactics. Condition: no public invitation of a P&W-Rolls-Royce Joint Venture (supply ground, above).

tests.name: Boeing Rate Increase
tests.threshold: No reaction: we keep our own disciplined ramp.
tests.numbers: No Rate Increase is on the record.

vetoes.plan: Any Delay Tactics row (bottleneck, poaching or both, on any plan)
vetoes.ground: Company red line, rule 4: no fps is on the public record, so any move is naked and draws the $48.32B fine. 'Both' counts as two moves, and bottleneck and both also breach the five pillars. One move against row A: -15.69 / +0.83 / +0.21 / +0.25 / +0.83 / -15.68 / +0.84 / -15.68 / +0.71. That is below $1B even in the fps columns. Not overridable.

vetoes.plan: Any cancel row (cancel NGSA, with or without an A350 Re-engine)
vetoes.ground: Company red line: never cancel NGSA (rule 7 and the playbook). No gate, engine, supply or quality case has failed. Against holding it loses -19.95 (S4) to -23.84 (S1, S6), with a write-off of about $25.37B. Not overridable.

vetoes.plan: Row B: NGSA hold (Alt) + A350 Re-engine launched 2035
vetoes.ground: No operating veto. It passes engineering capacity (2 years of overlap, $1.2B of strain, at the limit), A350F and Spirit absorption (inside the 2033-35 window), supply crunch and the ramp shield. Flags for the record: (1) no slip margin, since a one-year NGSA slip makes the overlap 3 years and $1.8B, which would fail my test; (2) no widebody engine on record for a 2040 EIS (UltraFan widebody not launched; ready 2041 if launched now); (3) industrialisation in 2038-40 falls in the NGSA ramp and trough. Item value against A: +1.54 in S2 and in six other columns, -1.21 (S6) and -1.20 (S7). The cash line and the Board's liquidity test are Toepfer's and the Board's. I recommend hold, deferring to them.

ops.would_change_mind_if: (1) GTF2 slips past 2037 or P&W stops it, or a Joint Venture forms with a joint engine dated after 2037. NGSA would then fly CFM alone. I would not move or cancel NGSA, but would ask for a contingent, rate-gated CFM framework sized for up to about 99 Airbus sets a month by 2044, and keep Alt so the GTF tail keeps P&W in our supply to about 2044. (2) A ruling from the GM that a Joint Venture folding in GTF2 is ready on GTF2's 2036 date would let me support a neutral public welcome: CFM + the Joint Venture engine is 2 sources and adds Rolls-Royce as a third maker. (3) A reported supply crunch (LEAP, GTF, titanium, rare earths) or a quality escape: no new concurrency, the Re-engine closed on my test too, and Alt re-tested against base. (4) A failed gate or a slip to 2038: EIS moves later, never earlier, and a 2035 Re-engine would then overlap 3 years ($1.8B) and fail my test unless the grid shows $1B more. (5) On the Re-engine: if Toepfer and the Board pass the cash line, I would not stand in its way at 2 years of overlap. A 787 Re-engine on the record closes it (rule 3). (6) On the code, nothing on this board moves me off 7.
ops.memo:
Operating test, 2035. My tests come from my role; nothing on record is mine (Very low confidence).

NGSA: on track as far as the board shows. No inject, failed gate or quality event; EIS 2037, two years after technology-ready. Exposure: a one-year slip to 2038. A failed gate moves EIS later, never earlier, and never means cancelling.

Engines: code 7, final, since 2045 falls after EIS. CFM plus GTF2: two sources, and GTF2 has one year of margin. With both, CFM never builds more for us than today's 51 sets a month. P&W rises to about 47-57 by 2044, all on a new engine: my watch item. If GTF2 slips or stops, NGSA flies CFM alone, up to 99 of our sets a month by 2044, plus Boeing's 57.

Joint Venture: do not welcome it publicly. GTF2 would fold into it, and the rules give no date for the joint engine. Any date after 2037 costs NGSA its second source, and no code can repair that. Keep "open to all three makers".

Alt plan: pass on safety, quality, ramp shield and supply crunch.

Trough: in 2039-40 we build 827 and 852, about 70 a month, against roughly 1,057 and 1,078 for 60%. The A320 winds down faster than NGSA ramps. No order closes it; early rate signals, hiring and the rate-capable wing protect the ramp.

A350 Re-engine 2035: passes my tests at the limit (2 years, $1.2B), with no slip margin. Cash is Thomas's. I concur with holding.

other_moves.move: NGSA engine selection stays open to all three makers (code 7, final)
other_moves.detail: We restate that NGSA's selection names CFM, Pratt & Whitney and Rolls-Royce. CFM is the floor and P&W GTF2 is the planned second source. Each engine enters service only once its durability is proven. How the engine makers organise themselves is their decision, and we neither invite nor discourage any partnership. We offer no payment, advance or take-or-pay to induce any engine launch (anything above EUR 300m would be a separate Board item, and none is proposed). We exchange no confidential information [A-0243, A-0360, AX-0054].

other_moves.move: Long-range, rate-gated supply signals for the 2037-45 ramp
other_moves.detail: We give CFM and P&W signals early, as for the A320neo ramp, covering the LEAP-1A and GTF tail on the A320 Alt plan and the NGSA engine sets. They are sized to our own needs only: on two sources our CFM call stays at or below today's 51 sets a month (Wagner). We announce them in general terms only, with no volumes and no internal plan targets [A-0159, AX-0005].

other_moves.move: Contingent CFM framework for the single-source case
other_moves.detail: If GTF2 slips past 2037 or P&W stops it, CFM carries NGSA alone, up to about 99 Airbus sets a month by 2044 (Wagner). This is a contingent, rate-gated framework, sized only to our own needs and triggered only by a P&W slip. It reserves nothing against other customers and claims no capacity Boeing uses. NGSA's date does not move for it.

other_moves.move: GTF2 readiness watch at the Board's product-safety review
other_moves.detail: Wagner reports at each twice-yearly review: GTF2's one-year readiness margin (ready 2036 for EIS 2037), P&W's durability testing as P&W makes it public, and the CFM fallback.

other_moves.move: NGSA gate reports to the full Board
other_moves.detail: The run-at-rate wing and production-system gates go to the twice-yearly product-safety review. A failed gate or an engine maturity slip re-times EIS later, never earlier, and never leads to a cancellation. The honest exposure is a one-year slip to 2038 [AX-0015, A-0225, A-0409].

other_moves.move: Secure our own materials and work packages
other_moves.detail: Titanium through Aubert & Duval, additive manufacturing, the raw-materials watchlist, and the Spirit work packages fully integrated. All of it serves our own ramp only [AX-0060, AX-0061, AX-0062, AX-0063].

other_moves.move: Recruiting and training for the 2039-44 ramp and the Airbus of the 2030s
other_moves.detail: Our own hiring, apprenticeships and training, in Europe and across our global footprint. It targets no rival's staff [A-0485, A-0366].

other_moves.move: CFO's 2035 annual cash report to the Audit Committee
other_moves.detail: Covers net cash, the $0.13B headroom in 2035 and 2036, and the rating. On the static FY2025 base the payout recommendation sits near the 30% floor, unless reported FCF has grown as the brief's profit path implies; the Board sets the payout. No new buyback before 2037 without a Board re-test, and no equity raise. Launch aid is priced as our own money. The report is repeated for 2036 [AG-0058, AG-0059, AX-0102, AX-0022].

other_moves.move: A350 Re-engine: re-test in 2045 (ExCo record)
other_moves.detail: No spend is committed. The CFO brings the 2045 grid and cash arithmetic ($1.0B a year over 2045-49, no overlap, no strain), and Wagner re-tests capacity and supply. The re-test is closed if Boeing has launched a 787 Re-engine (rule 3). No programme is timed to reopen any other lever.

other_moves.move: Zero-for-zero trade advocacy in an industry coalition
other_moves.detail: With industry associations on both sides of the Atlantic, Boeing included as an ally on trade. It stays strictly to public trade policy, with no exchange of pricing, capacity, programme or engine-selection information [AX-0088, AX-0046].

decision.public_statement: Our core principles of safety, quality, integrity, compliance and security will remain at the heart of all we do. Our next-generation single-aisle aircraft is in development, and it is the centre of our work to prepare the Airbus of the 2030s. We continue to plan for it to enter service in the second half of this decade, once its technologies, its production system and its engines are mature. Safety and quality come before the calendar. Its engine selection stays open to all three narrowbody engine makers, and we plan for a dual-source engine supply, with each engine entering service only once its durability is proven. How the engine makers organise themselves is their decision. A stable, diversified supply of parts, engines first, is a condition of a disciplined and controlled production ramp-up. The A320neo family, with its two engine options, stays in production through the transition: its lines keep running longer while the new aircraft ramps up, so customers are served without a break. We are giving our suppliers long-range signals for that ramp, and we continue to secure our own materials and work packages. We take on one major development at a time and fund it from our own cash flow, preserving our financial flexibility and a strong balance sheet. With our partners across the industry, on both sides of the Atlantic, we keep working for a tariff-free, zero-for-zero trade regime in civil aerospace. And we keep recruiting and training, in Europe and across our global footprint, the people who will design and build the Airbus of the 2030s.
decision.rationale:
DECISION, ROUND 2 (2035): HOLD COURSE
- Every field stays at its default, and code 7 is submitted explicitly.
- There are no Board items and no override.

MY ORDER OF QUESTIONS
1. The five pillars: no covert move, and no order or statement a regulator could read as misconduct.
2. The ramp: a disciplined and controlled transition, with the A320neo lines kept longer.
3. The 2030s: NGSA stays on its technology clock to EIS 2037.
4. Can I take it to the Board? Yes. There is nothing to take, and nothing the Board said it would veto.

TEAM RULE, STEP BY STEP

1. Deletions. These are company red lines and the pillars, never traded for PV.
- Every Delay Tactics row is deleted.
  - No fps is on the public record, so any move is naked and draws the $48.32B fine (rule 4).
  - Against A, one move scores -15.69 in S1 and -15.68 in S6 and S8, and at most +0.84 elsewhere.
  - Bottleneck and both also fail the pillars, and both counts as two moves.
  - The team's stricter condition (the move must change who enters service first) also keeps it off. I do not set that condition aside.
- Every cancel row is deleted (rule 7). There is no failed case. A cancellation writes off $25.37B ($35.52B x 5/7) and loses $19.95B (S4) to $23.84B (S1, S6).
- The base-plan Re-engine row is deleted because row B dominates it.

2. Tests on the remaining rows.
- Row A (the default) is a survivor.
  - Toepfer passes it on peak cash: $5.07B in 2035 and in 2036, $0.13B of headroom, nothing from 2037. The Alt plan's $0.75B is post-EIS cost, about $0.09B a year.
  - He also passes it on robustness (positive in all nine columns; worst S9 +0.48, then S4 +2.69), on liquidity and on Board items (none).
  - Wagner passes it on the gates (nothing is reported against them), supply crunch and code 7, on the Alt plan for safety, quality, the ramp shield and supply crunch, and on the five pillars.
- Row B (A plus an A350 Re-engine launched in 2035, EIS 2040) is not a survivor.
  - Wagner passes it, at the limit: 2 years of overlap, $1.2B of strain, no slip margin.
  - Toepfer fails it on peak cash. $5.07B + $1.0B + $0.6B = $6.67B in each of 2035 and 2036. That is $1.47B over the line each year, $2.95B in all.
  - On his static base, net cash would end 2036 at about -$1.1B even at the 30% payout floor.
  - This is a binding soft veto.
- Row C (the base plan) is not a survivor.
  - Toepfer fails it on robustness: -0.16 to -1.08 against A, and S9 raw is -0.10.
  - Row C was only the fallback if Wagner failed the Alt plan. He passed it, so the fallback does not apply.

3. Choice. Row A is the only survivor and the company default.
- It is also the highest-scoring survivor in every column.
- S2: +5.36. On my rough weights it is +7.12; at equal weights, +5.65.

4. Override check.
Row B leads row A by +1.54 in S2. That clears the team rule's $1B bar, so the ExCo rule would allow an override recorded as a Board item. I decline it, for four reasons:
- (a) The Board vetoes it on its own liquidity test, and an ExCo override cannot answer a Board test. On its Qualified Majority review the Board also reads the item as trailing hold by $1.21B in S6 and $1.20B in S7.
- (b) My balance-sheet risk appetite is Low. On the static base, the breach would take net cash negative in NGSA's last cash year.
- (c) The Board approves at most one override per game. Spending it on a known veto would be poor governance.
- (d) In 2030 we said in public that we take on one major development at a time and fund it from our own cash flow. The Board recorded that as a capital-markets commitment.
Wagner's flags point the same way:
- There is no slip margin: a one-year NGSA slip would mean 3 years of overlap and $1.8B of strain.
- No widebody engine is on record for a 2040 EIS.
- Industrialisation would fall in the 2038-40 trough.

5. What holding costs, recorded honestly.
- The costs:
  - We forgo +1.54 in S2 and in six other columns.
  - The company's 2033-35 window closes this round.
  - The brief does not price a 2045 Re-engine, so no one can say whether waiting gains or loses (Toepfer).
- What holding buys:
  - No strain and no cash breach.
  - The 787 Re-engine question resolves before we commit, which avoids the -1.21 and -1.20 in S6 and S7.
- The forgone value is the cost of the cash line, not a doctrine premium.

6. Engine code: 7, submitted explicitly, on Wagner's recommendation.
- It gives CFM + P&W GTF2: 2 sources and 2 makers.
- It is in no forbidden pair and adds no cash.
- It is final, because the 2045 round falls after EIS.
- If GTF2 slips past 2037 or P&W stops it, NGSA flies CFM alone and keeps its date.

7. The public line on engines.
- Wagner fails a public invitation of a P&W-Rolls-Royce Joint Venture, on supply grounds.
- The rules give no date for a Joint Venture engine that takes in GTF2 when the venture forms: "6 years later, or earlier if a partner folds in a solo programme that is further along".
- If that engine came after 2037, both P&W and Rolls-Royce would drop out and NGSA would fly CFM alone. No code could repair that.
- The dual-source enabler is met. I will not put it at risk for a third maker the rules cannot date.
- The selection stays open to all three makers, and how they organise is their decision. This departs in part from Board recommendation 3, and I say so in board_response.

8. The NGSA clock.
- EIS 2037 is two years after the technology-ready year.
- A failed gate or an engine slip re-times EIS later (2038 is the honest exposure), never earlier, and never leads to a cancellation.
- No Boeing move re-times it.

9. Board-gate lines.
- There are no Board items this round, because every field is at its default.
- For the record, A350 hold: five pillars pass, Toepfer passes, Wagner passes, ΔPV 0 against the default.

10. Round 1 correction. I expected an fps in 2030 (S2), and Boeing held. This round's decision does not depend on the scenario call, because row A is the best survivor in every column.

11. Next round (2045).
- The A350 Re-engine is re-tested on that round's grid: $1.0B a year, no overlap, no strain. It is closed if Boeing has launched a 787 Re-engine (rule 3).
- No programme will be timed to reopen Delay Tactics. They are never named in public.

Accepted in full.

memo_weighing.ops:
Wagner's tests are role-derived (Very low confidence).

Passed:
- NGSA gates. This is a pass on 'nothing reported against the gates', not a measured result.
- Supply crunch on CFM + GTF2. CFM never goes above today's 51 Airbus sets a month. All of P&W's growth is on GTF2, which is his watch item.

No operating veto on row B. His flags support holding: no slip margin, no widebody engine on record for 2040, and industrialisation in the trough.

Accepted in full, including the Joint Venture point, where I defer to him on engines rather than take the Board's recommended wording.
- His trough reading is in the other moves: no order closes it, and our own unpriced moves protect the ramp.
- I take his contingent CFM framework, sized to our own needs only and reserving nothing against other customers.

decision.expected_scenario:
S2: Boeing launches an fps on the 10-year schedule in 2035 (EIS 2045).
- S1 (rivals hold) is nearly as likely.
- All nine columns are plausible.
- My rough weights (inference): S1 30%, S2 30%, S6 10%, the other six 5% each.
- The worst plausible column for row A is S9 (+0.48), then S4 (+2.69).
decision.best_grid_plan_in_expected_scenario:
Best grid row in S2: NGSA hold (A320 Alt plan) + A350 Re-engine + one Delay Tactics move, at +7.73. It is struck: rule 4 (a naked move draws the $48.32B fine), the five pillars and the Board's veto.

Best row without a red line: NGSA hold (Alt) + A350 Re-engine, at +6.90.
- It fails Toepfer's binding cash soft veto: $6.67B against $5.2B in 2035 and 2036.
- It fails the Board's liquidity test.
- I declined the override.

Chosen: NGSA hold (Alt) + A350 hold, at +5.36. It is the highest-scoring survivor and the company default.
decision.premium_reason:
No doctrine premium is paid: the chosen row is the highest-scoring survivor in S2 and in every other column.
- The 2035 A350 Re-engine row is $1.54B higher in S2. It is not a survivor because it fails a binding soft veto (peak cash) and the Board's liquidity test, so the gap is the cost of the cash line, not a premium.
- The Delay Tactics rows are deleted as red lines.
decision.objective_note:
These goals are scored by the GM and never change the payoff. No PV is traded for any of them.

Defend 60/40: not met.
- 2040 is 47.4%; 2045 is 69.0% and 2050 is 74.0%.
- 2040 fails because of our own factory trough: 827 and 852 aircraft in 2039-40, against about 1,057 and 1,078 needed for 60%. The A320 tail winds down faster than NGSA ramps.
- Customer preference for Boeing is not the cause. No order closes the gap, and the Alt plan is already the larger plan.

Protect the A320 family: met (60.0%). The Alt plan keeps it in production through the transition.

Enabler, dual sources: met (CFM + GTF2 in 2040, 2045 and 2050).
- Code 7 is final.
- This holds only while GTF2 keeps its 2036 date. CFM alone is the fallback.

Enabler, three makers: not met.
- Rolls-Royce has no engine that can be ready by 2037. The brief shows a third maker only in the fps columns, and only if P&W and Rolls-Royce launch when selected.
- I keep the selection open to all three makers, but I do not invite a Joint Venture. The rules cannot date its engine, and a date after 2037 would cost the dual-source result we already hold.
decision.predictions:
Boeing, 2035:
- Hold (S1): about 30%.
- fps 10-yr (S2): about 30%. Its preconditions are now public, and "headroom" points to the 10-year schedule.
- 787 Re-engine alone (S6): about 10%. The GEnx upgrade and Charleston capacity point to upgrades instead.
- Each other column: about 5%.
- In round 1 I expected an fps in 2030; Boeing held.

Embraer: holds in its "harvest season".

Engine makers:
- P&W keeps GTF2 on its 2036 date and proves durability first.
- No Joint Venture forms this round, since P&W has none to announce.
- CFM commits a new engine only with a committed airframer, most likely with a Boeing fps.

Round 2045:
- NGSA is in service from 2037, with code 7 final.
- The A350 Re-engine is re-tested if no 787 Re-engine is on the record.
- Delay Tactics stay off.

Weighted value of the chosen row: about +7.12. At equal weights +5.65; S2 alone +5.36.

board_response.recommendation: R2-1 Hold course on NGSA, continue to EIS 2037 on code 7, and report the gates to the product-safety review.
board_response.response:
Taken up in full.
- ngsa: hold, with code 7 submitted explicitly.
- Wagner's gate report goes to the twice-yearly product-safety review. It is a pass on 'nothing reported against the gates', not a measured result.
- A failed gate or an engine slip re-times EIS later (2038 is the exposure), never earlier, and never leads to a cancellation.
- No Boeing move re-times it.

board_response.recommendation: R2-2 One programme at a time: keep the A350 Re-engine on hold in 2035 and bring it to the 2045 round.
board_response.response:
Taken up in full.
- rea350: hold. Toepfer's binding soft veto is accepted, with no override: $6.67B against $5.2B in 2035 and 2036.
- The 2045 re-test is recorded: the CFO brings the grid and cash ($1.0B a year, no strain), and Wagner tests capacity and supply. It is closed if Boeing has launched a 787 Re-engine (rule 3).
- The cost is recorded: +1.54 forgone in S2, the 2033-35 window closed, and a 2045 value the brief does not price.

board_response.recommendation: R2-3 Engine supply: keep code 7, submit it explicitly, and welcome a P&W-Rolls-Royce partnership engine in public.
board_response.response:
Taken up in part.
- Code 7 is submitted explicitly.
- In public, the selection stays open to all three makers, with no payment and no confidential exchange.
- I do not adopt the specific public welcome of a P&W-Rolls-Royce partnership, on Wagner's supply ground:
  - The rules give no date for a Joint Venture engine that takes in GTF2.
  - Any date after 2037 drops both P&W and Rolls-Royce, so NGSA would fly CFM alone.
  - No code can repair that, because this is the last round before EIS.
- The public line says instead that how the makers organise is their decision. That keeps the door to a third maker open without putting the met dual-source result at risk.
- If the folded engine is confirmed to take GTF2's 2036 date, Wagner would support a neutral welcome.
- Wagner reports GTF2's one-year margin and the CFM fallback.

board_response.recommendation: R2-4 Ramp and capacity: keep the Alt plan and set out the unpriced moves that protect the 2039-43 ramp.
R2-5 Keep Delay Tactics off, noting the 2045 programme-in-development condition.
board_response.response:
Taken up in full.
- delay_tactics: none.
- Noted: in 2045, poaching would need an A350 Re-engine in development. I will not time any programme to reopen this lever, and it is never named in public.

board_response.recommendation: R2-6 Shareholder returns and liquidity stay reserved to the Board, with a cash report each year.
R2-7 Bring the same scenario-led case, with windows in public and trade advocacy kept to public policy.
board_response.response:
Taken up in full.
- Expected scenario: S2, with S1 nearly as likely.
- All nine columns count. The worst is S9 at +0.48, then S4 at +2.69.
- The public line leads with the pillars, gives windows rather than dates, and does not mention Delay Tactics.

board_response.recommendation: R1-1 (round 1) Annual cash report to the Audit Committee through 2036.

Delivered for 2035 and committed for 2036, as in R2-6.

board_response.recommendation: R1-2 (round 1) Re-run the supply-crunch test in 2035 and report the contingency.

Done.

board_response.recommendation: R1-3 (round 1) Gate reports, the re-time-never-accelerate rule and the 2038 slip exposure.

cfm.public_statement:
Safety, quality, delivery and cost, always in that order. That's how we run this business, and it's how we made this call.

Here's what we know. CFM, with our partners at Safran, is on Airbus's next single-aisle, and we appreciate the confidence. We'll support that airplane with the LEAP family, and we'll earn our place on it every day, on time on wing. LEAP-1A durability hardware is in every new -1A engine and is going into the fleet through the shops. On the -1B, we'll tell you the results when the fleet data is in. The GEnx upgrade is ready for our 787 customers.

Here's what we don't know: when the next new narrowbodies will be launched, by whom, and on which engines. That's really not for us to say; it's the airframers' call. We don't have a birthright on that next order. We intend to earn it. A LEAP derivative is on offer to every airframer, and CFM will commit a new engine with a committed airframer.

RISE stays all in as technology, together with Safran. When that architecture enters service is really not for us to say. We'll tell you about dates when the testing tells us.

We get paid in dollars, not in percentages. It's that simple, ain't that hard.
cfm.rationale:
WHAT GAME, HOW WE WIN [CX-0467]
It is the installed-base game [CX-0422]. CFM is fitted on NGSA on the record, so the LEAP family flies it from entry into service. The fps and Embraer's jet are still open. The question I put was whether a defensive Ducted with Partner Embraer earns its $6B bill in the column the record supports. In 2035 it doesn't, by enough. We are not going for share [CX-0493].

DECISION
- Hold on ducted, open_fan, partner_embraer and lobby_emissions. GEnx is hold only: it is already running and ready since 2033.
- Every field is at its default, so nothing goes to the Board.
- Doctrine premium: $0.65B. Game total: $0.65B of $4.0B. RISE allowance: $0.
- RISE stays all in as technology with Safran.
Check file: /tmp/wargame-cfm/dash-2050-emb/work/r2_culp_decide.py (brief numbers only).

THE GRID (S1 / S2 / S3 / S4, $B)
- Hold: -9.47 / -35.02 / -20.25 / -11.87. Best plan in S2.
- Package (Ducted + Partner Embraer): -8.82 / -35.93 / -18.12 / -6.81. Best plan in S1, S3 and S4.
  - Against hold: +0.65 / -0.91 / +2.13 / +5.06.
  - Weighted: +1.45 at my weights, +1.08 at Ghai's, +1.73 at equal weights.
- Ducted alone, against hold: -0.54 / -3.27 / +0.41 / -0.82. It fails Ghai's test.
- Embraer on top of a Ducted: +1.19 / +2.36 / +1.72 / +5.88.
- Open Fan alone, against hold: -29.87 / -10.00 / -30.87 / -28.86.
- Best Open Fan plan, against the package: -19.89 / -14.09 / -21.66 / -19.33.

THE TESTS
- Low case first [CX-0248, CX-0536]. Expected column: S1.
  - On the record: NGSA with CFM and the rival engine fitted.
  - Not on the record: an fps launch (Boeing: 'all three have to be there', no date) or an Embraer launch ('no decision to announce').
  - I won't move the column to make the money work.
- Additive and paid for the risk [CX-0301, CX-0355]. The package is additive in S1, but only by $0.65B on a $6B bill (gross $6.65B, 1.11x).
  - That is inside my $1B ε.
  - It is also inside the Board's $1B margin: the Board would veto the package in an expected S1.
- Tie-break, within ε: safety, quality, delivery and cost, always in that order [CX-0658].
  - Safety and quality: the Ducted would be a new hot-and-harsh engine. Ali says 2041 is the board's year, not a test result; nothing ducted has been turned on and turned off. The LEAP-1B kit outcome is still not in his record.
  - Delivery: the package stacks three projects on the 9 suppliers behind 80% of past shortages, with no supplier-level measurement.
  - Cost: $6B against $0.
  - Hold wins on every count.
- Low case, in numbers (Ghai). S1's +0.65 is gone at any of these:
  - 9.8% off the gross;
  - $0.65B of strain above the $2B floor;
  - a two-year slip of the Ducted (-0.07). A one-year slip leaves about +0.32 (Ghai) or +0.34 (Ali).
  - My frame's quarter haircut 'for the Alt plan' double-counted, because the grid already prices the Alt plan. I take Ghai's correction.
  - The haircut that does apply is for what the board leaves out: a new engine below OE breakeven on its cost curve, supplier shortfalls, and a slip. On Ali's own record, demonstration dates slip [CX-0151, CX-0211].
- No birthright [CX-0564]. S2 is the one column where a rival takes our slot. Nothing on this grid buys it back: the package is -0.91 there and hold is best. The hard-rule-3 trigger is on the record, because a rival engine is fitted next to us on NGSA. A trigger permits a launch; it does not pay for one. I invoke H3 for the record only, and I launch nothing on it.
- Three gates [CX-0433], none fully met:
  - foundation: no test basis for 2041, and the -1B kit is open;
  - partner: Safran yes, but Embraer has no programme;
  - market: NGSA is on the record with no volumes stated.
- H2 [CX-0205]: the Open Fan waits.
  - NGSA enters service in 2037 and an Open Fan launched now is ready in 2045, so the wait penalty hits S1, S3 and S4.
  - The RISE allowance cannot carry it: it would need $19.89B in S1, above the $15B cap.
- H3: no Ducted. H5: RISE is not cancelled.
- H7: no CFM narrowbody order is placed, so Safran's consent is not engaged. RISE and the private airframer talks stay inside joint practice, and price and capacity are joint [CX-0184].
  - Had the package gone ahead, the sentence would have been: the Ducted defends a CFM position on an airframe where a rival engine is fitted, and Partner Embraer serves every airframer [CX-0587]. Both fit joint practice, so consent would be assumed.
- H8: no rival named and no blame. H9: $0.65B of $2.0B this round.
- My 20% line and durability line: not engaged, because no Ducted is launched. If a Ducted ever comes, it is a defensive derivative with less than half the open-fan gain [CX-0183], never the next generation, with durability gated by test [CX-0208]. RISE stays the next engine. Its 'more than 20%' is a design point, not yet flight-proven [CX-0001, CX-0217].

COLLEAGUES' TESTS
- Ghai. His binding vetoes fall on the Open Fan, Lobby without an Open Fan, the Ducted alone, hold with an expected S3 or S4, and any price talk. Hold with an expected S1 passes every one of them.
  - He recommends the package on the money and concurs with hold at $0.65B. I part from him on the tie-break and the Board's margin, not on his numbers.
- Ali. No binding veto. No safety or durability flag. He recommends hold.
- No override is needed.

THE COST OF HOLDING, said plainly
- $0.65B in S1, $2.13B in S3 and $5.06B in S4. That is $1.45B at my weights, $1.08B at Ghai's and $1.73B at equal weights. Holding saves $0.91B only in S2.
- It is probably for good. A 2045 Ducted would be ready in 2051 and would miss about 71% of the NGSA value (Ghai, estimate).
- The rival engine's +10 pp on NGSA goes unanswered. Our NB share falls from 75.9% (2035) to 57.4% (2050) in S1.
- A P&W-RR Joint Venture, not on the record, would take that to about 50.1% (Ghai, inference). The package would have given margin there.
- My deference to airframers can make us late to a rival threat [CX-0452], and that bias is live here. The installed-base lens, 'the price of admission' [CX-0557], pulls the other way. I name both. I decide on the tests, and the tests say hold.

WHERE DOCTRINE, NOT MY RECORD, DROVE THE CHOICE
- Embraer and Lobby on hold: my record is silent, so I follow the doctrine default (profile.md section 6).
- ε = $1B and the low-case haircut are inference.
- On money I defer to Ghai's tests, and on dates to Ali's.

FOR 2045
The Ducted door is effectively closed. I revisit it only if an airframer launches with CFM in its code and the short window still pays. Until then we compete with LEAP derivatives and durability, and RISE stays technology for after 2050.

- NGSA is launched for a 2037 entry into service, with CFM fitted.
- A rival next-generation engine, launched in 2030 and ready in 2036, is fitted next to us.

- This is effectively the last round in which anything we launch counts. A Ducted launched now is ready in 2041. One launched in 2045 would be ready in 2051, and the board counts the narrowbody market only to 2056.

We don't have a birthright on the NGSA split, the fps or Embraer's jet [CX-0564]. So I read S2, where Airbus drops us, as hard as S3 and S4, where we gain.

Mohamed, I want what the testing tells you, not analysis [CX-0009]. I need to feel it and see it [CX-0259].

(1) READY YEARS ON TEST EVIDENCE.

- Set 2041 against each first entry into service:
  - NGSA in 2037: four years late, so the +10 pp counts only from 2041;
  - the S3 fps in 2045;
  - the S4 Embraer jet in 2039, where the partnership counts only from 2042.
- Confirm that no option I am testing rests on an earlier year.

(2) OPEN FAN AND H2.
- A 2035 launch is ready in 2045 at the earliest, with no slack. Confirm that NGSA's 2037 entry comes first, so the wait penalty applies.
- Bring RISE test progress since 2030: ground and flight test, the 'more than 20%' design point, and blade and core durability in dust.
- I will back no RISE date in public beyond what you can test.

(3) SAFETY AND DURABILITY (the foundation gate).

- Any finding goes to a cross-functional team first [CX-0012], and I answer it on evidence before anything launches.

(4) PHYSICS AND MY RED LINES.

(5) SUPPLY LOAD.

(6) DATES IN THE STATEMENT. I plan to give none. Flag any line that would fail your test.

Your own record covers engineering. On supply I am reading my description of your job [CX-0633], so I weigh that part of your memo against company doctrine. Show me the evidence.

BOARD GUIDANCE for your memo (non-binding; its veto follows):
