frame.initial_lean:
LEAN
- Hold on all four narrowbody fields. GEnx keeps running. RISE stays all in as technology with Safran [CX-0214].
- Doctrine premium $0.65B against the package in S1, inside the $2.0B round cap. Game total $0.65B of $4.0B.
- The package stays the live alternative, and I want it tested hard, because this is the last round in which it counts.

EXPECTED COLUMN: S1, on the record.
- NGSA with CFM fitted is a fact. An fps or an Embraer launch is a hope [CX-0248].
- Boeing's words fit S3's shape (more than one engine source, headroom in the schedule), but it gives no date. Embraer has nothing to announce.
- Weights to test: S1 .55, S2 .10, S3 .20, S4 .15.
- I book expected PV low: near the weighted hold figure of about -$14.5B, not S1's -9.47.

WHY HOLD, ON MY TESTS
- Additive and paid for the risk [CX-0301, CX-0355]. The package is additive in S1, but only by $0.65B on a $6B bill, which is inside my $1B ε.
- Low case first [CX-0536]. The +0.65 rests on the NGSA ramp, and Airbus is keeping its A320 lines longer. A quarter off the gross gives -1.01; $1B more strain gives -0.35 (inference). Booked low, it is gone.
- Tie-break: safety, quality, delivery and cost, always in that order [CX-0658].
  - Safety and quality: a new hot-and-harsh engine, with the 1B kit outcome still open.
  - Delivery: the same constrained suppliers carry 2,392 LEAP engines in 2035.
  - Cost: $6B against $0.
  The edge goes to hold unless Ali tells me otherwise on evidence.
- Three gates [CX-0433]:
  - market: half met (NGSA is on the record, with no volumes);
  - partner: half met (Safran yes; Embraer has no programme);
  - foundation: waits on the 1B kit.
- The Board would veto the package in an expected S1, and I won't move the column to get it through.

THE COST OF HOLDING, said plainly
- $2.13B in S3 and $5.06B in S4, probably for good. About $1.45B at my weights and $1.73B at equal weights.
- The rival engine's +10 pp on NGSA goes unanswered.
- My deference to airframers can make us late to a rival threat [CX-0452], and that bias is live here. The installed-base lens, 'the price of admission' [CX-0557], pulls the other way. I name both.

WHAT FLIPS ME TO THE PACKAGE. All of these:
- Ali gives a test basis for 2041, no open flag, the 1B outcome, and measured supplier output that carries the stack.
- Ghai passes price/cost and volumes (I invoke H3 on the rival engine fitted on NGSA), and shows that S1's value survives a low-case ramp.
- The record, not hope, supports S3 or S4 as the expected column, as the Board requires.
Short of that, we hold, and we pay $0.65B to do it.

OPEN FAN: it waits, and we say so.
- NGSA enters service in 2037; the earliest the Open Fan can be ready is 2045.
- The allowance would need $19.89B in S1, above the $15B cap.
- 'Launched and ready by 2050' goes unmet for good, declared at $0 premium.
- RISE is never cancelled for cost [CX-0174, CX-0398].

SAFRAN
- The lean places no CFM narrowbody order, so no consent is needed.
- If the package comes in, consent is assumed [CX-0184]: the Ducted defends a CFM position where a rival engine is fitted, and Partner Embraer serves every airframer [CX-0587].

PUBLIC LINE: tell you what we know, tell you what we don't [CX-0436].
- CFM is on NGSA, with Safran. LEAP durability facts only.
- 'CFM will commit a new engine with a committed airframer.'
- RISE stays technology. It's really not for us to say when it enters service [CX-0205].
- No rival named, no date, no price. It's that simple, ain't that hard.

cfo.memo:
Larry, the money in dollars. In 2030 I said an NGSA launch with CFM in the code would pass the Ducted. It does, at the low end. The running GEnx adds $2B of strain, so the Ducted alone is -$0.54B in S1 and fails. With Partner Embraer it is +$0.65B in S1 on a $6B bill: price/cost positive, best plan in S1, S3 and S4. Volumes first passes: CFM fitted on NGSA is on the record, and so is the rival engine next to us. Embraer's +$1.19B rests on NGSA, not on an Embraer jet. Capex: $1.0B a year, under 2% of revenue; payout and rating whole. Premium $0.

The good news is the downside is bounded: S2 costs $0.91B, and Airbus's code locks at its 2037 entry. Weighted, it is +$1.08B at mine and +$1.45B at yours; once S3 and S4 carry 21%, S2 can't make it negative.

But we're not expecting this magically gets better. S1 is thin: 10% off the gross, or a two-year slip, and it's gone. It covers its bill only around 2054, and the board books no new-engine OE losses.

On the money I'd launch the package, subject to Ali's gate. It is under the Board's $1B margin in S1. If you hold, I concur at a $0.65B doctrine premium, and we say plainly we give up $2.13B in S3 and $5.06B in S4. Book low: about -$14.1B with the package, -$15.2B on hold. Open Fan: $19.89B, above the allowance. Hold it.

tests.name: Turn on, turn off: ready years of every order (binding date test)
tests.threshold: No order's value may depend on a ready year earlier than the board's development time. Ducted: launch + 6. Open Fan: launch + 10 and not before 2045. Partner Embraer: counts at launch + 7. GEnx: launch + 3, and not before the first re-engined 787 or A350 (2042 if none). This is my test standard applied to the board's development times (inference).
tests.numbers: Launch year 2035. Ducted ready 2041 (2035+6). Open Fan ready 2045 (2035+10 = 2045, the floor; no slack). Partner Embraer counts from 2042 (2035+7). GEnx is running: launched 2030, ready 2033, counts from 2042 (no 787 or A350 Re-engine on the record). Lobby is immediate. The grid rows Culp tests (round2.md section 3) rest on those years and nothing earlier: package against hold +0.65 / -0.91 / +2.13 / +5.06 (S1-S4); Ducted alone -0.54 / -3.27 / +0.41 / -0.82; Open Fan alone -29.87 / -10.00 / -30.87 / -28.86; best Open Fan plan against the package -19.89 / -14.09 / -21.66 / -19.33. I checked them against the brief: all correct. Culp's timing test is also correct: a 2045 launch gives a Ducted ready in 2051, an Open Fan in 2055 and Embraer counting from 2052. That is after the 2050 objective year, and the Ducted would have five years before the NB window closes in 2056. Culp asked for the test basis, so here it is plainly: 2041 is the board's year, not a test result. Nothing ducted has been turned on and turned off in my record. The nearest test evidence is hot-section and technology work. LEAP-1A HPT hardware was certified in December 2024 [CX-0225], is in all 1A deliveries and shop visits [CX-0209], and new 1A engines are at CFM56 levels [CX-0996]. RISE has completed over 350 tests with an early focus on durability [CX-0216], dust testing on next-generation HPT blades began in October 2025 [CX-0222], and an Open Fan durability chief has been appointed [CX-0223]. That backs the technology, not a 2041 product date. My pattern: I met near-term fixes backed by tests and missed demonstration dates (the RISE demo slipped from mid-decade to 'this decade'; the 1B kit slipped about a year).

tests.name: Test, not analysis: dates in the public statement and other moves (binding date test)
tests.threshold: Every date said in public must be one a test can back. No Open Fan or RISE entry before 2045, no ready date before launch + development years, no RISE fly-demo or flight-test date.
tests.numbers: Culp plans to give no date. Pass on the lean as framed; I check the final text at step 4. These would fail, and bind: (a) any Ducted ready date before 2041. I advise giving no Ducted date at all, since 2041 is a board year with no test behind it. (b) Any Open Fan or RISE entry date, or any wording that puts RISE before 2045. (c) Any RISE ground or flight-test date: my 'middle of this decade' became 'this decade'. (d) A CFM engine on Embraer's jet before 2042, including at its S4 entry in 2039. (e) Any line implying a new CFM engine is ready at NGSA's 2037 entry. Only the LEAP derivative backs CFM on NGSA from 2037 to 2040. Wording advice, not a date: keep LEAP durability lines to LEAP-1A facts, since the 1B outcome is not in my record. 'We'll tell you about dates when the testing tells us' passes.

tests.name: Ready no later than the airframe: Ducted (advice; report of the gap)
tests.threshold: Give the ready year against each first new-NB entry into service. A Ducted ready after entry still earns +10 pp from its ready year once a new NB is in service. Earlier is better, but a late date does not fail it (inference; dashboard_game.md section 2).
tests.numbers: Ducted ready 2041. NGSA (all columns but S2) enters service 2037: the Ducted is 4 years late, so CFM flies a LEAP derivative on NGSA from 2037 to 2040 and the +10 pp counts only from 2041. S4 Embraer jet enters service 2039: the Ducted is 2 years late, and Partner Embraer counts from 2042, 3 years after the jet enters service, so the jet flies P&W from 2039 to 2041. S2 (NGSA on P&W only): the Ducted has no CFM slot to defend on NGSA (-3.27 alone). Slip exposure (inference, my crude arithmetic, not a test): a one-year slip moves the first +10 pp year to 2042. On the NGSA ramp in rules.md (about 600 aircraft in 2041 rising to about 1,100 by 2045; 8.5% discount; 2.2% price inflation), 2041 is about 5.6% of the Ducted's 2041-2056 stream. tests.name: Physics (wording check; Culp's 20% line)

tests.name: Durability first, and the LEAP report against my promise

tests.numbers: Two projects, $6B bill. Against hold: -0.54 / -3.27 / +0.41 / -0.82 (S1-S4); -0.67 at Culp's weights, -1.05 at equal weights. ops.would_change_mind_if: Test and field data, never analysis. (1) Ducted: a hot-and-harsh core or demonstrator run that turns on and turns off the LEAP harsh-environment failure modes. The LEAP gaps were about 4,800 harsh and 9,882 benign cycles, against the CFM56's 7,000-8,000 and 17,000. That would make 2041 a tested date rather than the board's year, and it would widen the margin I can give the S1 case. (2) LEAP-1B: the certification outcome and field time on wing toward the 8,000 harsh and 17,000 neutral targets. That closes the open item I report each round. (3) Supply: measured output at the 9 suppliers and 15 sites behind 80% of past shortages, carrying Ducted development hardware and 1B shop-visit retrofits alongside 2,467 LEAP engines in 2041. That would let me read the $2B strain as sufficient rather than a floor. (4) RISE: a completed ground and flight test with Airbus measuring 'more than 20%', with open-fan blade and compact-core durability in dust. That confirms the physics. It does not move the calendar: NGSA enters service in 2037, and the Open Fan still waits. (5) The record: an fps or Embraer launch with CFM in its code. The column is Culp's call, but on that record the package's supply load passes with margin (+2.13 in S3, +5.06 in S4) and my dates pass. (6) A durability finding on any of these goes to a cross-functional team, and I would want it closed before any launch.
ops.memo:
As last year, every date rests on the board's years.

Dates. A Ducted launched now is ready 2041, launch plus six. Partner Embraer counts from 2042. The Open Fan, 2045, no slack. No option rests on an earlier year. No binding veto.

Said plainly: 2041 is the board's year, not a test result. Nothing ducted has been turned on and turned off. What we have tested is the hot section: LEAP-1A HPT hardware, certified, at CFM56 levels; RISE dust testing on compact-core blades. That backs the technology, not the date.

Against the airframes: NGSA 2037, four years ahead of the Ducted; the S3 fps 2045, four years behind it; Embraer's S4 jet 2039, our partnership three years after. The Open Fan is eight years behind NGSA. The wait penalty applies. The physics is ours; the calendar is the airframer's.

Physics. A ducted engine has less than half the open-fan gain. A defensive derivative, never the next generation. RISE is designed for more than 20%; the flight test that proves it is not in my record.

Durability. LEAP-1B: I said 2025; it moved to 2026. The outcome is not in my record, and I will not claim it. No safety or durability flag.

Supply. Three projects, $2B strain, read as a floor. In S1 the package clears it by $0.65B; a one-year slip costs about $0.3B (inference). We delivered 2,553 LEAP engines in 2034; the development years run below that. Supplier-level output: not measured.

Orders: hold. Timing: following Culp.

other_moves.detail: RISE stays fully funded as a joint CFM technology programme, with no product launch and no 'program dividend' [CX-0174, CX-0214]. It is never cancelled for cost [CX-0398]. Testing continues with our partners, and RISE technology keeps flowing into LEAP upgrades [CX-0162]. No entry date and no ground-test or flight-test date [CX-0205, CX-0009]. This fits joint practice, and Safran is a full partner in RISE.

other_moves.detail: LEAP-1A durability hardware is in every new -1A engine and goes into the fleet at shop visits [CX-0209, CX-0225]. We report the -1B when the fleet data is in, and we make no claim before then [CX-0210]. Spares never crowd out OE engines [CX-0529]; this is joint practice with Safran. Facts only, no new promise dates [CX-0436].

other_moves.detail: CFM is fitted on NGSA on the record. We work with Airbus on the LEAP derivative for its entry into service and ramp. We make no claim that a new CFM engine is ready at entry into service, offer no launch-era pricing or concession, and quote no volumes Airbus has not stated. Narrowbody price and capacity are a joint decision with Safran [CX-0184, CX-0166]. Platform talks stay private [CX-0586].

other_moves.detail: We refuse no one and lock no one out (H1) [CX-0587, CX-0185]. A LEAP derivative is on offer to both. A new CFM engine follows only with a committed airframer. Talks stay private, terms are standard, and narrowbody pricing is joint with Safran [CX-0184]. No comment on US-Brazil trade.

other_moves.move: Measure supplier output before any stack (lean before capital)
other_moves.detail: Ali measures actual output at the 9 suppliers and 15 sites behind 80% of past shortages [CX-0613]. The load is 2,392 LEAP engines in 2035 rising to 2,467 in 2041, plus the -1B shop-visit retrofits. We fix flow before we add capital [CX-0540, CX-0633]. No capital commitment and no board effect.

other_moves.move: Hot-and-harsh core testing inside the RISE envelope
other_moves.detail: Compact-core HPT durability testing in dust continues inside the existing joint RISE budget, and its results feed LEAP upgrades [CX-0222, CX-0216]. It builds the turn-on, turn-off test basis Ali says we lack for any future derivative [CX-0009]. No Ducted launch, no date, no new bill.

decision.public_statement:
Safety, quality, delivery and cost, always in that order. That's how we run this business, and it's how we made this call.

Here's what we know. CFM, with our partners at Safran, is on Airbus's next single-aisle, and we appreciate the confidence. We'll support that airplane with the LEAP family, and we'll earn our place on it every day, on time on wing. LEAP-1A durability hardware is in every new -1A engine and is going into the fleet through the shops. On the -1B, we'll tell you the results when the fleet data is in. The GEnx upgrade is ready for our 787 customers.

Here's what we don't know: when the next new narrowbodies will be launched, by whom, and on which engines. That's really not for us to say; it's the airframers' call. We don't have a birthright on that next order. We intend to earn it. A LEAP derivative is on offer to every airframer, and CFM will commit a new engine with a committed airframer.

RISE stays all in as technology, together with Safran. When that architecture enters service is really not for us to say. We'll tell you about dates when the testing tells us.

We get paid in dollars, not in percentages. It's that simple, ain't that hard.
decision.rationale:
WHAT GAME, HOW WE WIN [CX-0467]
It is the installed-base game [CX-0422]. CFM is fitted on NGSA on the record, so the LEAP family flies it from entry into service. The fps and Embraer's jet are still open. The question I put was whether a defensive Ducted with Partner Embraer earns its $6B bill in the column the record supports. In 2035 it doesn't, by enough. We are not going for share [CX-0493].

DECISION
- Hold on ducted, open_fan, partner_embraer and lobby_emissions. GEnx is hold only: it is already running and ready since 2033.
- Every field is at its default, so nothing goes to the Board.
- Doctrine premium: $0.65B. Game total: $0.65B of $4.0B. RISE allowance: $0.
- RISE stays all in as technology with Safran.
Check file: /tmp/wargame-cfm/dash-2050-emb/work/r2_culp_decide.py (brief numbers only).

THE GRID (S1 / S2 / S3 / S4, $B)
- Hold: -9.47 / -35.02 / -20.25 / -11.87. Best plan in S2.
- Package (Ducted + Partner Embraer): -8.82 / -35.93 / -18.12 / -6.81. Best plan in S1, S3 and S4.
  - Against hold: +0.65 / -0.91 / +2.13 / +5.06.
  - Weighted: +1.45 at my weights, +1.08 at Ghai's, +1.73 at equal weights.
- Ducted alone, against hold: -0.54 / -3.27 / +0.41 / -0.82. It fails Ghai's test.
- Embraer on top of a Ducted: +1.19 / +2.36 / +1.72 / +5.88.
- Open Fan alone, against hold: -29.87 / -10.00 / -30.87 / -28.86.
- Best Open Fan plan, against the package: -19.89 / -14.09 / -21.66 / -19.33.

THE TESTS
- Low case first [CX-0248, CX-0536]. Expected column: S1.
  - On the record: NGSA with CFM and the rival engine fitted.
  - Not on the record: an fps launch (Boeing: 'all three have to be there', no date) or an Embraer launch ('no decision to announce').
  - I won't move the column to make the money work.
- Additive and paid for the risk [CX-0301, CX-0355]. The package is additive in S1, but only by $0.65B on a $6B bill (gross $6.65B, 1.11x).
  - That is inside my $1B ε.
  - It is also inside the Board's $1B margin: the Board would veto the package in an expected S1.
- Tie-break, within ε: safety, quality, delivery and cost, always in that order [CX-0658].
  - Safety and quality: the Ducted would be a new hot-and-harsh engine. Ali says 2041 is the board's year, not a test result; nothing ducted has been turned on and turned off. The LEAP-1B kit outcome is still not in his record.
  - Delivery: the package stacks three projects on the 9 suppliers behind 80% of past shortages, with no supplier-level measurement.
  - Cost: $6B against $0.
  - Hold wins on every count.
- Low case, in numbers (Ghai). S1's +0.65 is gone at any of these:
  - 9.8% off the gross;
  - $0.65B of strain above the $2B floor;
  - a two-year slip of the Ducted (-0.07). A one-year slip leaves about +0.32 (Ghai) or +0.34 (Ali).
  - My frame's quarter haircut 'for the Alt plan' double-counted, because the grid already prices the Alt plan. I take Ghai's correction.
  - The haircut that does apply is for what the board leaves out: a new engine below OE breakeven on its cost curve, supplier shortfalls, and a slip. On Ali's own record, demonstration dates slip [CX-0151, CX-0211].
- No birthright [CX-0564]. S2 is the one column where a rival takes our slot. Nothing on this grid buys it back: the package is -0.91 there and hold is best. The hard-rule-3 trigger is on the record, because a rival engine is fitted next to us on NGSA. A trigger permits a launch; it does not pay for one. I invoke H3 for the record only, and I launch nothing on it.
- Three gates [CX-0433], none fully met:
  - foundation: no test basis for 2041, and the -1B kit is open;
  - partner: Safran yes, but Embraer has no programme;
  - market: NGSA is on the record with no volumes stated.
- H2 [CX-0205]: the Open Fan waits.
  - NGSA enters service in 2037 and an Open Fan launched now is ready in 2045, so the wait penalty hits S1, S3 and S4.
  - The RISE allowance cannot carry it: it would need $19.89B in S1, above the $15B cap.
- H3: no Ducted. H5: RISE is not cancelled.
- H7: no CFM narrowbody order is placed, so Safran's consent is not engaged. RISE and the private airframer talks stay inside joint practice, and price and capacity are joint [CX-0184].
  - Had the package gone ahead, the sentence would have been: the Ducted defends a CFM position on an airframe where a rival engine is fitted, and Partner Embraer serves every airframer [CX-0587]. Both fit joint practice, so consent would be assumed.
- H8: no rival named and no blame. H9: $0.65B of $2.0B this round.
- My 20% line and durability line: not engaged, because no Ducted is launched. If a Ducted ever comes, it is a defensive derivative with less than half the open-fan gain [CX-0183], never the next generation, with durability gated by test [CX-0208]. RISE stays the next engine. Its 'more than 20%' is a design point, not yet flight-proven [CX-0001, CX-0217].

COLLEAGUES' TESTS
- Ghai. His binding vetoes fall on the Open Fan, Lobby without an Open Fan, the Ducted alone, hold with an expected S3 or S4, and any price talk. Hold with an expected S1 passes every one of them.
  - He recommends the package on the money and concurs with hold at $0.65B. I part from him on the tie-break and the Board's margin, not on his numbers.
- Ali. No binding veto. No safety or durability flag. He recommends hold.
- No override is needed.

THE COST OF HOLDING, said plainly
- $0.65B in S1, $2.13B in S3 and $5.06B in S4. That is $1.45B at my weights, $1.08B at Ghai's and $1.73B at equal weights. Holding saves $0.91B only in S2.
- It is probably for good. A 2045 Ducted would be ready in 2051 and would miss about 71% of the NGSA value (Ghai, estimate).
- The rival engine's +10 pp on NGSA goes unanswered. Our NB share falls from 75.9% (2035) to 57.4% (2050) in S1.
- A P&W-RR Joint Venture, not on the record, would take that to about 50.1% (Ghai, inference). The package would have given margin there.
- My deference to airframers can make us late to a rival threat [CX-0452], and that bias is live here. The installed-base lens, 'the price of admission' [CX-0557], pulls the other way. I name both. I decide on the tests, and the tests say hold.

WHERE DOCTRINE, NOT MY RECORD, DROVE THE CHOICE
- Embraer and Lobby on hold: my record is silent, so I follow the doctrine default (profile.md section 6).
- ε = $1B and the low-case haircut are inference.
- On money I defer to Ghai's tests, and on dates to Ali's.

FOR 2045
The Ducted door is effectively closed. I revisit it only if an airframer launches with CFM in its code and the short window still pays. Until then we compete with LEAP derivatives and durability, and RISE stays technology for after 2050.

pratt_whitney.public_statement: I'll start with what we still owe our customers. For years the GTF fleet was not where it needed to be, and we own that. The next engine will be judged on time on wing, and that is how we will judge it ourselves. So we control what we can control. GTF2, launched in 2030, is in its last year of development and is due to be ready in 2036, six years from launch. It is not proven yet, and it will be proven before it enters service. Airbus has named Pratt & Whitney alongside CFM and Rolls-Royce for its next-generation single-aisle, and we intend to earn that place. GTF2 will not enter service until its durability is proven: endurance testing in severe environments, life-limited parts at full life at entry into service, and time on wing before fuel burn. We will not compress testing to make a date. Any feature that is not proven in time waits for a later block. We will sign Airbus's rate-gated supply agreements on standard terms. We are planning our castings and forgings ahead of the ramp, and the fleet flying today keeps first call on material. For any airframer that selects Pratt & Whitney, GTF2 comes on standard terms. We're not in the early entry phase. The GTF Hot Section kit remains available at shop visit, and we will report its time on wing once the fleet has proven it. We have no Joint Venture to announce: we share risk and investment with partners, not our core technology. We speak for our engines, not for any airframer's dates or rates. We have learned our lesson from the prior iterations of the GTF. These are responsible bets with responsible paybacks.

1. CONSTRAINT FIRST [PX-0035, PX-0073]
- GTF2 is ready in 2036. Against NGSA's 2037 EIS that is +1 year. Against an fps launched in 2035 it is +6 years (2042, 7-year ramp) or +9 years (2045, 10-year ramp). Against an Embraer narrowbody launched in 2035 it is +3 years (2039). Eddy's ground-1 check passes.
- The one-year NGSA margin is thin. It sits below the company's 1.5-2 year slip prior, and my own record on operating dates is optimistic [PX-0017, PX-0098]. So the statement gives no EIS, and the gate is durability, not the calendar.
- 2036-37 is certification and production margin, not test time. Nothing is compressed.
- The durability gate falls due in 2036. Eddy has no 2035 test data and no post-2025 removal data, and he reports the gate neither met nor failed. I accept that rather than ask for reassurance.
- I take his standing ground-1 condition as binding on every future order and statement. CMCs are the watch item; a feature not proven waits for a later block.

2. START FROM EDDY'S PROPOSAL: hold/hold.

3. STRIKE WHAT FAILS A BINDING VETO
- Rows B and D (`jv_with_rr: commit`): struck. Mitchill's ground-4 veto binds: on the grid the commit never gains against hold (0 / 0 / 0 / -6.13 / 0), so any case for it rests on unrecorded upside, either a Rolls-Royce commitment or an S2-plus-S4 hedge. Eddy's gear flag is a company red line [P-1233], and I confirm it: a 2035 formation folds GTF2's gear and core into a shared programme.
- Rows C and D (`gtf2_solo: cancel`): struck. Mitchill's objection is return, which is advice, not one of his four grounds. But a cancel breaks my own rule against harvesting a programme a live airframe has asked for [P-1342]: NGSA is on code 7 and GTF2 is ready before its EIS. It trails hold in every column (-25.03 / -3.89 / -25.18 / -25.03 / -23.77), and the Board has said it would veto it.
- No Eddy veto binds on any row.

4. OPTIMISE INSIDE THE CONSTRAINT
- Row A is weakly best in every column: +6.10 / -15.04 / +6.25 / +6.10 / +8.31.
- I adopt Mitchill's weights over mine, because my 2030 incrementalism under-called the NGSA launch [PX-0093]: S1 0.47, S2 0.10, S3 0.22, S4 0.08, S5 0.13.
- Expected PV on his weights: A +4.31, B +3.82, C -18.48, D -18.30. On my illustrative weights: +4.70, +4.09, -18.51, -18.29.
- Worst column: S2, -15.04. That is Airbus's move to code 5, and no order of ours closes it.
- Row A's expected PV turns negative only if S2 reaches about 0.30. My scratch check is in /tmp/wargame-pratt_whitney/dash-2050-emb/work/r2_ev.txt.

5. TESTS
- Safety and durability: pass (section 1).
- Visible demand: met. NGSA code 7 is on the record [PX-0109]. `launch` and `launch_if_selected` are not on the menu.
- Miss a cycle [PX-0071, RTX-wide, applied here by inference]: answered. GTF2 is live for NGSA, any 2035 fps and an Embraer line. S2 is the miss-a-cycle column, but a cancel makes it worse (-3.89), not better.
- Responsible bet [PX-0010]: the doctrine order, the best-PV order and the objective order are the same. Premium $0B.
- Dividend safe [PX-0081, P-0686, P-0669]: Mitchill confirms no new R&D. The remaining ~$0.33B is 5.6% of the ~$6B envelope and competes with buybacks, not the dividend. The pre-ASR debt path is untouched, and the one-time stretch stays unused.
- Value, not share [PX-0055, PX-0100]: every other move is on standard terms. Mitchill's ground-3 check passes.
- Ground 2 on `hold`: GTF2 is a selected engine (code 7), so hold carries no unselected engine. Even read as a hedge, hold beats cancel in every column.

6. CANCEL, AND LOCKING IN
- This is the last legal cancel round (rules.md: until ready). Holding locks GTF2 in for good, and I am comfortable with that.
- A cancel writes off $2B x 5/6 = $1.67B to save $0.33B. It would lose credibility in every column.
- Even in S2, a ready GTF2 off NGSA still carries about $4.22B of engine value (the board's +10 pp for a ready GTF2 on new types).

7. JOINT VENTURE
- My record here is Low, so this follows doctrine, Mitchill's cash test and Eddy's technical test.
- The trigger is met on paper: code 7 includes Rolls-Royce, and Rolls-Royce "stands ready". The commit still fails:
  - weighted value -0.49;
  - S4 is -6.13, 3.1 times its $2B bill, and all of it is share given to Rolls-Royce on NGSA at the equal split;
  - it brings no cost relief, because GTF2's spend already fills P&W's $2B share;
  - it adds nothing in S2;
  - it puts the gear into a shared programme.
- Standing-commitment risk: Rolls-Royce commits only once we are on the record, so a commit now would likely form the Joint Venture in 2045. Mitchill puts the cost at very roughly $3-4.4B. That is named, not booked.
- I name my architecture-loyalty bias [PX-0014]. The grid says no on its own terms.
- The GTF risk-sharing partnership model is critical [PX-0038]; we keep partners under strain. We share risk and investment, never technology.

8. TIE-BREAKS
- The fleet beats a new engine [PX-0080]: the castings and forgings plan gives the fleet first call.
- "Miss a cycle" beats "cross that bridge" only on visible demand: the demand is visible, and GTF2 is already live.
- A rival's discount never moves the answer: none is on the record, and none would.

9. GOVERNANCE
- Not a Board item. The full case is recorded at the Board's request [PG-0016].
- No red line is traded. The shared-source relief on code 7 is declared at $0B: it is franchise defence for a programme already committed (about 40% of the shared A320neo) [PX-0058, P-1292].

frame.question:
Control what you can control [PX-0020]. Round 2, decision year 2035.

The 2030 conditional order did its job. Airbus launched NGSA on code 7, the trigger fired, and GTF2 is live: launched 2030, ready 2036. If nothing changes, NGSA flies CFM + P&W.

This round's question is narrow. Do we carry GTF2 whole to its 2036 ready year and keep the Joint Venture off? Or does anything on the grid justify one of the two moves still open:
- cancelling a programme a live airframe has asked for, or
- committing to a Joint Venture now that NGSA's code 7 includes Rolls-Royce and Rolls-Royce says it "stands ready"?

Two facts make this round final for GTF2. Because GTF2 is ready in 2036, this is the last round in which a cancel can be ordered. And `launch_if_selected` is off the menu, because the engine is already live.

The one big loss on the grid is S2: Airbus moves NGSA to code 5, a swing of -21.14 against S1. That is Airbus's call. No order of ours closes it. We answer it with product, durability and supply, never with price.

So the job is to hold the safety and durability constraint, take the best PV inside it, and not hand the gear to a partner along the way.
frame.situation:
PUBLIC RECORD, 2035
- Airbus: NGSA launched 2030, EIS 2037. Engine selection code 7 (CFM, P&W, RR). Fitted if nothing changes: CFM + P&W, because RR is not ready by EIS. Airbus has adopted the Alt plan, which keeps the A320 lines running longer through the NGSA ramp. It has announced rate-gated supply agreements: the A320neo GTF tail to about 2045, and framework agreements with all three makers for NGSA. It says it wants a stable, diversified engine supply.
- P&W: GTF2 (Solo) launched 2030, ready 2036. Our conditional offer has been used.
- CFM/GE: GEnx upgrade ready since 2033. LEAP durability going into new engines and the fleet. RISE kept as technology, with no dates. No ducted launch on the record.
- Boeing: no fps launch, no date. Its next narrowbody will be planned around a stable engine supply, more than one engine source, and durability first.
- Rolls-Royce: "stands ready to commit" to a Joint Venture with P&W, on terms that credit its technology. This is not a `jv_with_pw: commit`: it commits only once our commitment is on the record. No UltraFan NB launch.
- Embraer: still "in harvest season". Building cash, no decision, talking to all engine makers. Its narrowbody, if launched, flies P&W engines.

OUR POSITION (brief, hold/hold)
ΔPV +6.10 $B: engine value +8.10, R&D -2.00. Yield 105.5%.

The year-by-year row shows a transition trough before the payoff:
- Engine value falls below the status quo in 2039 (5.5 vs 6.5) and 2040 (6.3 vs 6.7).
- It then builds from 2041 (8.7 vs 6.9) to 2050 (14.4 vs 9.7).
- NB engines rise from 752 (2036) to 1,054 (2041), 1,361 (2044) and 1,449 (2049). The fleet nearly doubles. Forging capacity takes 2 to 2.5 years to add [P-0079].

OBJECTIVE STATUS
- Restore credibility: MET on NGSA under hold in S1, S3, S4 and S5. Lost in S2.
- Capitalise (ΔPV ≥ 0): MET at +6.10. Lost in S2 (-15.04). Under a JV commit it is also lost in S4 (-0.03).

GRID, ITEM VALUES AGAINST HOLD/HOLD (S1-S5)
- `jv_with_rr: commit`: 0 / 0 / 0 / -6.13 / 0.
- `gtf2_solo: cancel`: -25.03 / -3.89 / -25.18 / -25.03 / -23.77.
- Hold/hold is the brief's best plan in all five columns.

BOARD (risk appetite 3.5, unchanged)
- Expects hold/hold. It is not a Board item.
- Would veto a cancel with either JV value, a commit with GTF2 hold, any item carrying an unresolved veto, a red-line flag or an override, and any case resting on unrecorded upside, such as an S2-plus-S4 Joint Venture "hedge".
- Asks that the round notes still record the full case.

MY BIAS, NAMED
In 2030 my likeliest column was "rivals hold" (0.32), and Airbus launched NGSA that round. My incrementalism showed [PX-0093]. This round I want Neil's weights on the airframers' moves ahead of mine.
levers_in_play: `gtf2_solo`: `hold` (carry GTF2 to its 2036 ready year; spend left about $0.33B) | `cancel` (write off $2B x 5/6 = $1.67B in 2035, saving $0.33B; the last round a cancel is possible). `launch` and `launch_if_selected` are not on the menu: GTF2 has been live since 2030.

`jv_with_rr`: `hold` | `commit` (public at once and standing. It forms in the first round both are committed. A live GTF2 folds in and its spend counts toward P&W's $2B share. Ready 6 years after formation, or 2036 with GTF2 folded in. P&W and Rolls-Royce then hold equal NB shares).

Other moves (no grid effect): the 2035 disclosure. Answer Airbus's rate-gated supply agreements on standard terms. GTF2 available to any fps or new narrowbody that selects P&W, on standard terms. Answer Rolls-Royce's invitation. Hot Section kit continues at shop visit on standard terms. Internal: castings and forgings plan, durability gate report, annual GTF2 NPV review with the Board.
Board items this round: none if both fields hold. `cancel` and `commit` would each be Board items, and the Board has said it would veto both.

Row C: `gtf2_solo: cancel`, `jv_with_rr: hold`. S1-S5 = -18.93 / -18.93 / -18.93 / -18.93 / -15.46. Item value -25.03 / -3.89 / -25.18 / -25.03 / -23.77. Trails hold in every column, even S2. Loses credibility everywhere. Dominated. Illustrative EV -18.51.

Row D: `gtf2_solo: cancel`, `jv_with_rr: commit`. S1-S5 = -18.93 / -18.93 / -18.93 / -16.68 / -15.46. The commit's +2.25 in S4 exists only because the cancel destroys GTF2's value first. Dominated by Row A in every column. Illustrative EV -18.29.

Illustrative weights, mine, to be replaced by Neil's: S1 0.50, S2 0.08, S3 0.20, S4 0.10, S5 0.12. Code 5 would leave Airbus on CFM alone at a 2037 EIS, against its own 'diversified supply' line. Rolls-Royce says it commits only after we do. Boeing wants multiple sources and headroom (fits a 10-year fps). Embraer is still in harvest. The ranking A > B > D > C holds under any weights, because A is weakly best in every column.
red_lines: Safety and durability first [PX-0035, PX-0073]. No P&W engine on an airframe before it is ready and proven. GTF2 is ready in 2036 against NGSA's 2037 EIS. No compressed testing to hold the date. All life-limited parts at full life at entry into service. Time on wing before fuel burn. An unproven feature waits for a later block. Eddy's readiness and durability check binds on me.

No harvesting a selected programme. No `cancel` while a live airframe not yet in service carries a P&W code and GTF2 can be ready by its EIS. A cancel would have to beat `hold` in every plausible column, and it beats it in none (Board would-veto) [P-1342, P-1191].

Committed airframer [P-0746]. GTF2 rides on NGSA code 7, which is on the record. The shared-source relief on code 7 (and on a code 6 or 7 fps) is declared at $0B. On NGSA it is franchise defence: we held about 40% of the shared A320neo [PX-0058, P-1292]. It is relief for a programme already committed. It never justifies an unconditional launch for the fps alone.

Joint Venture: we spread risk and investment, never the gear or core technology [P-1233]. The trigger is met on paper (code 7 includes Rolls-Royce). A commit still needs all four: a non-negative weighted item value; no plausible column worse than -$2B against hold; the JV engine ready by EIS; and the gear kept out. Board would-veto: commit with GTF2 hold fails three of these. A commitment is public at once and stands.
No widebody engine: we are narrowbody focused [PX-0027]. There is no move here anyway.

Capital order [PX-0081, P-0686, P-0669]: dividend first, then debt back to pre-ASR levels, then buybacks. No plan that needs a dividend cut or reverses the debt path. Mitchill confirms. The Board's one-time envelope stretch stays unused.

Value, not share [PX-0055, PX-0100]. Airbus supply agreements, any Boeing or Embraer approach, and the Hot Section kit all go on standard terms. No launch-style discount, concession, free upgrade or volume promise beyond the capacity plan. A rival's discount never moves the answer.

Disclosure discipline [PX-0062]. Nothing on Airbus's or Boeing's dates or rates. No EIS earlier than launch + 6. No durability claim not yet proven. No time-on-wing figure for the Hot Section kit until the fleet proves it. No selection, Rolls-Royce commitment or Joint Venture that is not on the record. No booked upside [PX-0311].

No case built on upside the grid does not show (Mitchill ground 4; Board would-veto). That includes a combined S2-plus-S4 Joint Venture 'hedge' or a Boeing selection of P&W. I name such options; I do not book them.

Governance: empty `overrides`. A binding veto from Mitchill (four grounds) or Eddy (two grounds) means I revise once, within it. Premium cap: doctrine plus objective premium never exceeds $1B. The Board passes a Board item that trails hold only on a declared premium of $0.5B or less that serves the objective. Row A needs none.

(2) ITEM VALUES AGAINST HOLD/HOLD
Confirm these, and their weighted values on your weights:
- cancel: -25.03 / -3.89 / -25.18 / -25.03 / -23.77
- commit: 0 / 0 / 0 / -6.13 / 0
- cancel + commit: -25.03 / -3.89 / -25.18 / -22.78 / -23.77

(3) CANCEL ARITHMETIC

(4) JOINT VENTURE

- Confirm the dividend and the pre-ASR debt path are untouched and the one-time stretch stays unused.
- The 2026 analyst models stop at 2030E, so state the 2035 position on management's own figures for the Finance Committee.

(6) PAYOFF SHAPE
The hold row sits below the status quo in 2039-40 and pays from 2041. Tell me how much of the +6.10 rests on 2041-2050, so the Board's annual GTF2 NPV review has a baseline [P-1191]. Do not use it to move an NGSA date; that is Airbus's.

frame.initial_lean:
MY LEAN
Row A: `gtf2_solo: hold`, `jv_with_rr: hold`. Premium $0B. Not a Board item, but the case goes into the notes in full, because the Board asked for it. It gets all the data, with all the thinking [PG-0016].

WHY HOLD GTF2
- It is the brief's best plan in every column.
- It carries the engine a live airframe asked for to its 2036 ready year.
- It meets both objectives wherever they can be met (S1, S3, S4, S5).
- A cancel trails hold by 3.89 to 25.18 in every column. It writes off $1.67B to save $0.33B, and it is exactly the harvesting I reject while an airframer is still flying our code [P-1342].
- Since this is the last cancel round, holding locks GTF2 in for good. I am comfortable with that.

WHY NO JOINT VENTURE
- The trigger is met on paper, but the grid fails it: 0 in four columns, -6.13 in S4, three times its own bill.
- It folds the gear into a shared programme, and it does nothing for S2.
- Rolls-Royce has said it commits once we do, so a standing commitment now is likely to form the JV later at the equal split.
- The GTF risk-sharing partnership is critical [PX-0038], but we spread risk and investment, never technology [P-1233].
- My record is thin here (Low). This follows doctrine and Neil's and Shane's tests.

TESTS
- Visible demand: met. NGSA code 7 is on the record.
- Miss a cycle: answered. GTF2 is live for NGSA, any 2035 fps, and an Embraer line.
- Responsible bet: the doctrine order, the best-PV order and the objective order are the same, so the premium is $0B.
- Dividend: no new R&D.
- Value, not share: standard terms throughout.

OTHER MOVES, PUBLIC (no grid effect)
1. Answer Airbus's rate-gated supply agreements: we will sign on standard terms, rate-gated, with no volumes promised beyond our capacity plan and no discount.
2. Tell Boeing, and any airframer, that GTF2 is available on standard terms for any new narrowbody that selects P&W, with durability first. We claim no selection.
3. Answer Rolls-Royce: no Joint Venture to announce; we spread risk and investment, not technology.
4. The Hot Section kit continues at shop visit on standard terms, with no time-on-wing figure until the fleet proves it.

OTHER MOVES, INTERNAL
1. Shane's castings and forgings plan for the four loads, with this year's decisions named.
2. The durability gate report to the Governance and Public Policy Committee before entry into service.
3. An annual whole-programme NPV review of GTF2 with the Board [P-1191].
4. If S2 happens, no chasing: we win it back on durability and supply, not price.

PROPOSED DISCLOSURE, IN MY VOICE
"I'll start with what we still owe our customers. The GTF fleet had to earn back their trust, and the next engine has to be better on the thing that matters most to them: time on wing. So we control what we can control. GTF2, launched in 2030, is in development and is ready six years from launch. Airbus has named Pratt & Whitney, alongside CFM and Rolls-Royce, for its next-generation single-aisle, and we intend to earn that place. GTF2 will not enter service until its durability is proven: endurance testing in severe environments, life-limited parts at full life, time on wing before fuel burn. We will not compress testing to make a date. For any airframer that selects Pratt & Whitney, GTF2 comes on standard terms. We're not in the early entry phase. For the fleet flying today, the GTF Hot Section kit is available at shop visit, and we will report its time on wing once the fleet has proven it. We have no Joint Venture to announce: we spread risk and investment, not technology. We speak for our engines, not for any airframer's dates or rates. These are responsible bets with responsible paybacks."

WHERE I AM BIASED
- I am optimistic on operating dates [PX-0017, PX-0098]. A one-year gap between ready and EIS is thin, which is why the statement states no EIS and the gate is durability, not the calendar.
- My incrementalism under-called the 2030 launch. Neil's weights replace mine.

tests.name: Cancel arithmetic and cancel test: gtf2_solo cancel (Rows C, D)
tests.threshold: Write-off = R&D x years elapsed / 6. Cancel only at the first round in which no live airframe can still select GTF2 in time, and only if the cancel row beats hold in the columns I weight (inference).

- Write-off: $2B x 5/6 = $1.67B, booked in 2035. It saves $0.33B.

Why the cancel trails hold by 3.89 even in S2:
- With a ready GTF2 off NGSA, engine value is -15.04 + 2.00 = -13.04.
- Cancelled, it is -18.93 + 1.67 = -17.26.
- So a ready GTF2 carries about $4.22B of engine value without NGSA. That is the board's +10 pp shift on the new types for a ready GTF2, taken 5 pp each from CFM and RR (dashboard_game.md §2).
- Against $0.33B saved, the net is -3.89.

In the other columns, the cancel gives up $24.1-25.5B of engine value. In S2, the cancel would tie hold only if GTF2's remaining cost rose by about $3.9B, to about $4.2B. The cancel fails.

- GTF2 is offered on standard terms to any fps or new narrowbody that selects P&W.

cfo.would_change_mind_if:
On the cancel: a brief where the cancel row beats hold in every plausible column. That means NGSA cancelled or moved publicly off every P&W code, and also a jump in GTF2's remaining cost of about $3.9B, to about $4.2B, since a ready GTF2 still carries about $4.22B of engine value off NGSA in S2. It would also take Eddy reporting that GTF2 cannot be proven ready by any live EIS; I would defer to him on that. This is the last cancel round, so this is the only round in which this can happen.

On the Joint Venture: a grid on which the commit's weighted value against hold is at least 0 and no plausible column is below -$2B, with Rolls-Royce's commitment on the record, the Joint Venture engine ready by the EIS it serves, and terms that keep the gear and core out. An airframe on code 1 or 4 that only a Joint Venture could serve would be the test case.

On the weights: hard evidence that Airbus is moving NGSA to code 5 would raise S2 and cut my booked number. It would not change the orders, since hold is the best row in every column. Row A's expected PV turns negative only if S2 reaches about 0.30.

On capital: new spend that breaks the roughly $6B envelope, which would bring ground 1 into play.
cfo.memo:
Low end first. Hold/hold is worth +6.10 if nothing moves and -15.04 if Airbus takes NGSA to code 5. That swing is Airbus's call; no order of ours closes it. On my weights (S1 0.47, S2 0.10, S3 0.22, S4 0.08, S5 0.13), hold/hold is +4.31 expected, against +3.82 with a Joint Venture commit and -18.48 cancelled. It is the best row in every column, so the weights don't change the answer. They change the low end I worry about. I weight the airframers' moves at 0.45, against Chris's 0.40.

A cancel writes off $1.67B to save $0.33B. It trails hold by 3.89 even in S2, because a ready GTF2 still carries about $4.2B of engine value off NGSA. GTF2 is a selected engine (code 7 is on the record), so hold carries no unselected engine. This is the last cancel round, and I'm comfortable locking GTF2 in.

The commit adds nothing in four columns and costs 6.13 in S4. All of it is share. GTF2's spend already counts toward our $2B, so there is no new cash, no write-off and no relief on the bill. Any case for it rests on upside nobody has recorded: ground 4, binding.

Cash: no new R&D, about $0.33B left, 5.6% of the envelope. The dividend and the debt path don't move.

The payoff comes late: 2041-50 carries $6.08B of the engine value. I read the 2039-40 dip as timing. I want a few more reps before I call the rest.

ops.proposal:
PROPOSED ENGINE ORDERS (round 2, decision year 2035): gtf2_solo: hold; jv_with_rr: hold. Neither is a Board item.

WHY gtf2_solo: hold. It carries GTF2 (launched 2030, ready 2036) whole to its ready year for the airframe that asked for it: NGSA, code 7, EIS 2037. GTF2 is ready by every live or possible EIS. On the brief's grid, 'GTF2: hold' is the best row in all five columns: +6.10 / -15.04 / +6.25 / +6.10 / +8.31. Cancelling is not one of my grounds, and my record has nothing on cancels, so on that I defer to Calio and Mitchill. My report: GTF2 can still be ready by the EIS of a live airframe whose code includes P&W (NGSA, 2036 against 2037). The cancel item value is -25.03 / -3.89 / -25.18 / -25.03 / -23.77. Cancel test flagged to Mitchill and Calio. This is the last round a cancel is legal, and holding locks GTF2 in. I'm comfortable with that.

WHY jv_with_rr: hold. The trigger is met on paper: NGSA's code 7 includes Rolls-Royce. But Rolls-Royce's 'stands ready' is not a commitment on the record. My technical conditions are readiness and the gear. Readiness passes: 2036 with GTF2 folded in. The gear fails: a fold-in puts GTF2's gear and core into a shared programme [P-1233]. Grid item value 0 / 0 / 0 / -6.13 / 0. The call is Calio's. I propose hold.

ANSWERS TO CALIO
(1) As above.

(2) READINESS. GTF2: launch 2030, ready 2036.
- NGSA EIS 2037: +1 year.
- fps launched 2035: 7-year ramp EIS 2042 (+6); 10-year ramp or via Embraer EIS 2045 (+9).
- Embraer narrowbody launched 2035: EIS 2039 (+3).
  - On the board it flies P&W engines whatever GTF2's status: S5 adds +2.21 on the hold row and +3.47 on the cancel row.
  - My operating view (inference): launch it on today's GTF family at the Advantage standard, not GTF2. In 2039 GTF2 has two years in service and is far short of the roughly 1M fleet hours that surface a new engine's issues [P-0847].
  - For the shops, that means more of the same pacing parts as the A320neo tail and the installed fleet, at the same time as the NGSA ramp.
  - GTF2 is available on standard terms if Embraer selects it, durability first. Embraer's selection is its own call.
- Joint Venture formed now (needs Rolls-Royce in 2035, S4) with GTF2 folded in: ready 2036.
- Joint Venture formed in 2045 after our commitment is on the record: ready at formation in 2045, on my reading that a ready GTF2 is 'further along', or 2051 if it does not fold in. The rules don't say how an engine that is already ready folds in. No live airframe needs either date.

(3) DURABILITY GATE. The bad news first: the board does not model durability. Neither my evidence nor the brief holds a 2035 GTF2 test result or any GTF Advantage or Hot Section fleet removal data after 2025. So I can't bring those figures from this seat's record, and I won't fill the gap with reassurance [PX-0112].

What stands proven (the baseline GTF2 inherits):
- GTF Advantage certified in 2025: more than double the original endurance testing, about 3x the base programme, up to 2x time on wing, full-life LLPs [P-0779][P-1095][P-0785].
- Hot Section kit: 90-95% of those gains, in shop visits since 2026 [PX-0088][PX-0106].

Still to prove, by the 2036 ready year and before NGSA EIS:
(a) Severe-environment endurance (hot and sandy, where the GTF fell short [PX-0122]), at no less than the Advantage multiple (inference).
(b) All life-limited parts at full life at EIS [PX-0128].
(c) The composite fan, CMC hot-section parts and the next-generation fan-drive gear, each instrumented and tested on its own [P-1214][P-0790].
(d) No compressed testing. 2036-37 is certification and production margin, not test time.

No feature is reported off track, and I can't name one. My watch item is the CMCs: they are the newest material, in the section where we fell short. If they aren't proven at the multiple by 2036, GTF2 enters service with the Advantage-derived hot section and the CMCs wait for a later block (inference). The fleet data goes to the Governance and Public Policy Committee with the endurance results before EIS.

(4) CASTINGS, FORGINGS AND SHOPS: one plan for four loads.
Numbers from the brief's hold row:
- NB engines: 752 (2036) to 1,054 (2041, +40%), 1,361 (2044, +81%) and 1,449 (2049, +93%).
- 2040 to 2041 alone is +271 (+35%).
- 2044 is +67% on the 2034 high of 816; 2052 peaks at 1,597 (+96%).
- Trough: 623 in 2038 (-137, -18% on 2037).
- Embraer (S5) adds up to 192 engines a year gross at 8 a month by 2045 (my arithmetic), partly offset because it takes customers from Boeing and Airbus.

Due this year:
(i) Approve the castings and forgings plan for the 2041 step and the 2044 level. At 2 to 2.5 years of lead [P-0079], 2041 capacity must be ordered by 2038-39 and the 2044 level by 2041-42. Both dates fall before the 2045 round, so the plan and its gates are set now. Capital goes in tranches against Airbus's rate signals, through Mitchill.
(ii) Sign Airbus's rate-gated agreements on standard terms, with volumes inside this plan.
(iii) Confirm GTF2 production-part qualification for the 2036-37 engines. Test hardware keeps priority over early production: we ramp to the parts, not the calendar.
(iv) Embraer: pre-qualify supplier capacity, with no capital until a launch is on the record.
(v) Use the 2038-40 trough for fleet lift, GTF2 spares and shop tooling, not to shed suppliers.

Cadence: daily allocation between Airbus engines and the shops, weekly to the ExCo [PX-0123][PX-0131], balanced with Airbus [PX-0099][PX-0110]. The fleet keeps first call. The split between the four loads is my inference; the board does not model parts.

(5) ENGINEERING LOAD. One new development: GTF2, in its final year ($0.33B of $2B left), certification in 2036, EIS support in 2037. The Hot Section kit is sustaining work. Embraer on today's GTF family is an installation, not a development. GTF2 on Embraer for 2039 would be a second installation before fleet hours, and I'd want NGSA's first-year data first (inference). The peak window is 2036-39.

(6) JOINT VENTURE, TECHNICAL. It brings Rolls-Royce's UltraFan technology and a partner. It brings nothing GTF2 needs: GTF2 is ready for 2037 on its own, and Rolls-Royce alone is not. A fold-in puts the gear and core into the shared programme. Terms I'd need, if Calio ever reopens it (inference):
- P&W owns, designs and builds the fan-drive gear and the core modules, and keeps their design data.
- P&W holds the type certificate and integration.
- Rolls-Royce shares risk and investment on the modules it owns.
- IP is licensed for the Joint Venture product only.
Even on those terms the grid gives -6.13 in S4.

(7) VETO CHECKS.
- Row A: ground 1 pass, ground 2 pass.
- Row B: both grounds pass. Its architecture test fails (company red line, not my ground).
- Rows C and D: a cancel puts no engine on an airframe early, so neither ground applies. No veto from me; I defer.
- The durability gate and parts views are my record [PX-0128][PX-0123]. The Joint Venture, cancel, engineering-load and Embraer engine views are the seat's doctrine and my inference.

Calio's draft disclosure passes my test: 'ready six years from launch' (2036), no EIS date, and durability as a commitment.

ops.memo:
The bad number first: one year. GTF2 is ready in 2036; NGSA enters service in 2037. That's the whole margin, and my own Advantage certification slipped a year. The second: the hold row takes us from 752 narrowbody engines in 2036 to 1,361 in 2044, and forgings take 2 to 2.5 years to add.

My proposal: `gtf2_solo: hold`, `jv_with_rr: hold`. GTF2 is the engine a live airframe asked for, and it's ready by every EIS: NGSA 2037, an fps 2042 or 2045, an Embraer narrowbody 2039. A cancel isn't my ground. I report that GTF2 can still serve NGSA, and the call is Calio's and Mitchill's.

The Joint Venture brings nothing GTF2 needs for 2037. With GTF2 folded in, it's our gear and core in a shared programme.

Durability: I won't tell you there's no surprise coming. The board carries no test data, and I have none for 2035. The gate is the Advantage standard: severe-environment endurance, full-life parts at entry into service, and the new fan, CMCs and gear instrumented. Anything not proven by 2036 waits for a later block. We don't compress testing to hold 2037.

Capacity: this year we set the castings and forgings plan for the 2041 step, gated on Airbus's rate signals, and use the 2038-40 trough for fleet lift. The fleet keeps first call.

Both my checks pass. Where my record is thin: one investor day, June 2023. The Joint Venture and cancel views are the seat's doctrine.

decision.public_statement: I'll start with what we still owe our customers. For years the GTF fleet was not where it needed to be, and we own that. The next engine will be judged on time on wing, and that is how we will judge it ourselves. So we control what we can control. GTF2, launched in 2030, is in its last year of development and is due to be ready in 2036, six years from launch. It is not proven yet, and it will be proven before it enters service. Airbus has named Pratt & Whitney alongside CFM and Rolls-Royce for its next-generation single-aisle, and we intend to earn that place. GTF2 will not enter service until its durability is proven: endurance testing in severe environments, life-limited parts at full life at entry into service, and time on wing before fuel burn. We will not compress testing to make a date. Any feature that is not proven in time waits for a later block. We will sign Airbus's rate-gated supply agreements on standard terms. We are planning our castings and forgings ahead of the ramp, and the fleet flying today keeps first call on material. For any airframer that selects Pratt & Whitney, GTF2 comes on standard terms. We're not in the early entry phase. The GTF Hot Section kit remains available at shop visit, and we will report its time on wing once the fleet has proven it. We have no Joint Venture to announce: we share risk and investment with partners, not our core technology. We speak for our engines, not for any airframer's dates or rates. We have learned our lesson from the prior iterations of the GTF. These are responsible bets with responsible paybacks.
decision.rationale:
DECISION: `gtf2_solo: hold`, `jv_with_rr: hold` (Row A). Neither order is a Board item. Premium $0B. `overrides` empty.

1. CONSTRAINT FIRST [PX-0035, PX-0073]
- GTF2 is ready in 2036. Against NGSA's 2037 EIS that is +1 year. Against an fps launched in 2035 it is +6 years (2042, 7-year ramp) or +9 years (2045, 10-year ramp). Against an Embraer narrowbody launched in 2035 it is +3 years (2039). Eddy's ground-1 check passes.
- The one-year NGSA margin is thin. It sits below the company's 1.5-2 year slip prior, and my own record on operating dates is optimistic [PX-0017, PX-0098]. So the statement gives no EIS, and the gate is durability, not the calendar.
- 2036-37 is certification and production margin, not test time. Nothing is compressed.
- The durability gate falls due in 2036. Eddy has no 2035 test data and no post-2025 removal data, and he reports the gate neither met nor failed. I accept that rather than ask for reassurance.
- I take his standing ground-1 condition as binding on every future order and statement. CMCs are the watch item; a feature not proven waits for a later block.

2. START FROM EDDY'S PROPOSAL: hold/hold.

3. STRIKE WHAT FAILS A BINDING VETO
- Rows B and D (`jv_with_rr: commit`): struck. Mitchill's ground-4 veto binds: on the grid the commit never gains against hold (0 / 0 / 0 / -6.13 / 0), so any case for it rests on unrecorded upside, either a Rolls-Royce commitment or an S2-plus-S4 hedge. Eddy's gear flag is a company red line [P-1233], and I confirm it: a 2035 formation folds GTF2's gear and core into a shared programme.
- Rows C and D (`gtf2_solo: cancel`): struck. Mitchill's objection is return, which is advice, not one of his four grounds. But a cancel breaks my own rule against harvesting a programme a live airframe has asked for [P-1342]: NGSA is on code 7 and GTF2 is ready before its EIS. It trails hold in every column (-25.03 / -3.89 / -25.18 / -25.03 / -23.77), and the Board has said it would veto it.
- No Eddy veto binds on any row.

4. OPTIMISE INSIDE THE CONSTRAINT
- Row A is weakly best in every column: +6.10 / -15.04 / +6.25 / +6.10 / +8.31.
- I adopt Mitchill's weights over mine, because my 2030 incrementalism under-called the NGSA launch [PX-0093]: S1 0.47, S2 0.10, S3 0.22, S4 0.08, S5 0.13.
- Expected PV on his weights: A +4.31, B +3.82, C -18.48, D -18.30. On my illustrative weights: +4.70, +4.09, -18.51, -18.29.
- Worst column: S2, -15.04. That is Airbus's move to code 5, and no order of ours closes it.
- Row A's expected PV turns negative only if S2 reaches about 0.30. My scratch check is in /tmp/wargame-pratt_whitney/dash-2050-emb/work/r2_ev.txt.

5. TESTS
- Safety and durability: pass (section 1).
- Visible demand: met. NGSA code 7 is on the record [PX-0109]. `launch` and `launch_if_selected` are not on the menu.
- Miss a cycle [PX-0071, RTX-wide, applied here by inference]: answered. GTF2 is live for NGSA, any 2035 fps and an Embraer line. S2 is the miss-a-cycle column, but a cancel makes it worse (-3.89), not better.
- Responsible bet [PX-0010]: the doctrine order, the best-PV order and the objective order are the same. Premium $0B.
- Dividend safe [PX-0081, P-0686, P-0669]: Mitchill confirms no new R&D. The remaining ~$0.33B is 5.6% of the ~$6B envelope and competes with buybacks, not the dividend. The pre-ASR debt path is untouched, and the one-time stretch stays unused.
- Value, not share [PX-0055, PX-0100]: every other move is on standard terms. Mitchill's ground-3 check passes.
- Ground 2 on `hold`: GTF2 is a selected engine (code 7), so hold carries no unselected engine. Even read as a hedge, hold beats cancel in every column.

6. CANCEL, AND LOCKING IN
- This is the last legal cancel round (rules.md: until ready). Holding locks GTF2 in for good, and I am comfortable with that.
- A cancel writes off $2B x 5/6 = $1.67B to save $0.33B. It would lose credibility in every column.
- Even in S2, a ready GTF2 off NGSA still carries about $4.22B of engine value (the board's +10 pp for a ready GTF2 on new types).

7. JOINT VENTURE
- My record here is Low, so this follows doctrine, Mitchill's cash test and Eddy's technical test.
- The trigger is met on paper: code 7 includes Rolls-Royce, and Rolls-Royce "stands ready". The commit still fails:
  - weighted value -0.49;
  - S4 is -6.13, 3.1 times its $2B bill, and all of it is share given to Rolls-Royce on NGSA at the equal split;
  - it brings no cost relief, because GTF2's spend already fills P&W's $2B share;
  - it adds nothing in S2;
  - it puts the gear into a shared programme.
- Standing-commitment risk: Rolls-Royce commits only once we are on the record, so a commit now would likely form the Joint Venture in 2045. Mitchill puts the cost at very roughly $3-4.4B. That is named, not booked.
- I name my architecture-loyalty bias [PX-0014]. The grid says no on its own terms.
- The GTF risk-sharing partnership model is critical [PX-0038]; we keep partners under strain. We share risk and investment, never technology.

8. TIE-BREAKS
- The fleet beats a new engine [PX-0080]: the castings and forgings plan gives the fleet first call.
- "Miss a cycle" beats "cross that bridge" only on visible demand: the demand is visible, and GTF2 is already live.
- A rival's discount never moves the answer: none is on the record, and none would.

9. GOVERNANCE
- Not a Board item. The full case is recorded at the Board's request [PG-0016].
- No red line is traded. The shared-source relief on code 7 is declared at $0B: it is franchise defence for a programme already committed (about 40% of the shared A320neo) [PX-0058, P-1292].

memo_weighing.cfo:
Weighted heavily. I trust Neil's cash numbers over my own operating dates.
- Weights: I adopted his column weights (S1 0.47, S2 0.10, S3 0.22, S4 0.08, S5 0.13) in place of mine. They put more on airframer moves (0.45 against my 0.40), which corrects my 2030 under-call of the NGSA launch.
- Arithmetic: I confirmed his item values, his cancel arithmetic ($1.67B write-off, $0.33B saved, last cancel round), his S2 explanation (a ready GTF2 is worth about $4.22B off NGSA) and his decomposition of the -6.13 (all share; no fold-in write-off; no new spend).
- Vetoes: his ground-4 veto on `commit` is binding, and I struck Rows B and D without contest. His cancel objection is on return, outside his four grounds, so I took it as advice. My own no-harvesting rule and the Board's veto strike the cancel anyway.
- Baseline: I took his payoff shape (+6.08 of the +6.10 rests on 2041-50) as the baseline for the annual NPV review.
- 2035 figure: he would not invent a 2035 Finance Committee number and gave the 2030E broker anchors and management's frame instead. I accepted that, with a dated follow-up.
- Advice: keep the wording at 'named alongside'. Applied in the statement.
memo_weighing.ops:
His proposal (hold/hold) was my starting point, and his two veto checks bind on me. Both pass on Row A, and he binds no other row.
- Readiness: I take his readiness table as given, and defer to him on readiness, parts and capacity.
- Durability: his candour that he has no 2035 test or post-2025 removal data, and his refusal to call the gate met, is what I want from that seat. He gets the gate report, not a date.
- Standing condition: accepted as binding. No compressed testing, full-life LLPs, CMCs to a later block if not proven.
- Capacity: his plan (the 2041 step ordered by 2038-39, the 2044 level by 2041-42, tranches on Airbus's rate signals, the trough used for fleet lift) is adopted as an internal move.
- Joint Venture: I confirm his gear flag on the commit as a company red line.
- Where his views rest on doctrine: his seat's record is one event, an investor day in June 2023 (Low). So his views on the Joint Venture, the cancel, the Embraer engine standard and the engineering load are the seat's doctrine and his inference, as he says. I weighed them as such: they agree with the grid and Mitchill, but they did not decide the call alone. His durability and parts views rest on his record [PX-0128, PX-0123], and I gave them full weight.

rolls_royce.public_statement: So. Rolls-Royce commits to a Joint Venture with Pratt & Whitney for the next narrowbody. Our preference has always been partnership, and there is no change of strategy. The commitment stands, for an airframe that has chosen both of us, on terms that credit the technology we bring. No solo narrowbody programme. The engine enters service only when it is ready and its durability is proven. Maturity sets the date, and we compress nothing. Support through partner shops will be in place before entry into service. Widebody is our core, and we will protect it. We are not after market share. We won't do anything not profitable. rolls_royce.rationale:
DECISION: `jv_with_pw: commit`, with `ultrafan_nb_solo: hold`, `ultrafan_wb: hold` and `t1000_upgrade: hold`. This is my framing proposal, unchanged. The only Board item is the commit.

1. TEAM RULE, STEP BY STEP
- Start: my proposal, 'UltraFan NB: hold + commit to JV'.
- Binding vetoes. McCabe co-signs the commit. Her binding vetoes cover the unconditional Solo, UltraFan WB, the upgrade beside a narrowbody item, and the upgrade alone without a premium; none is submitted. Watson invokes no Civil veto. His three binding grounds are each met below (section 5).
- Expected scenario: S1, rivals hold (0.45).
- Best grid plan inside the red lines on expected PV: 'UltraFan NB if selected + commit to JV', +1.09. My plan is +0.95, $0.14B below it. I keep it as the plan favoured by doctrine and the mission, and declare the premium, inside the $3B cap.
- Red-line strike: no red-line flag is raised against the submitted plan. The flags both memos raise apply to rejected plans (widebody beside narrowbody, and the 'if selected' pairs), and those are struck.
- Tie-break: mine. It was not needed, because all three recommend the same orders.

2. GRID ROWS FOR THE BOARD (S1-S7, $B ΔPV against the status quo)
- Submitted, 'UltraFan NB: hold + commit to JV': -0.56, -0.56, -0.56, +14.67, -0.65, -0.65, -0.56. Expected +0.95. Worst column -0.65 (S5-S6).
- Commit at hold, 'UltraFan NB: hold': -0.56, -0.56, -0.56, -0.56, -0.65, -0.65, -0.56. Expected -0.57.
- Item (commit against hold): 0, 0, 0, +15.23, 0, 0, 0. That is +1.52 weighted and never below 0 under any weights. Worst column 0, against a -$4B bill.
- Weights (mine, the same as McCabe's and the Board's illustrative set): S1 0.45, S2 0.10, S3 0.10, S4 0.10, S5 0.10, S6 0.05, S7 0.10. Each non-hold column has at most a weak signal on the record (P about 0.10).
- Off-grid reasonable worst case (McCabe): P&W commits and Airbus recodes NGSA to code 6. The Joint Venture forms and fits nothing, so we lose at most the bill, -4.00, with a joint weight of about 0.01. No item can lose more than its own bill.

3. THE TEAM RULE 'jv_pw only if P&W announced', READ OPENLY
- Read literally, the rule is not met. P&W's words are 'We have no Joint Venture to announce'. In 2030 I said we would commit once P&W was on the record, and McCabe's 2030 condition was the same. She says so plainly, and so do I.
- The rule has two purposes. We never hold a Joint Venture commitment that no airframe can use [RX-0051], and we never partner without alignment [R-0318].
- Both purposes are met in substance:
  - The Joint Venture forms, and our $4B is spent, only in a round in which P&W commits. In six columns nothing moves.
  - The alignment is in the airframe's own code. NGSA is live, not in service, and code 7 names P&W and us.
- Orders are sealed and simultaneous. 2035 is the only round in which a Joint Venture can reach NGSA, so waiting for P&W on the record would mean choosing to miss NGSA.
- The dashboard maps our rule to 'commit when P&W has committed, or commit first if your doctrine allows'. The Board's partner test (a live airframe's code includes P&W) is met. I read this as a doctrine-allowed first commit. That reading is inference and doctrine, not my record.
- Binary framing [RX-0050]: P&W comes to the table, or the commitment is withdrawn in 2045.

4. READY BY EIS AND THE 2030 LINE (Watson's ruling)
- If the Joint Venture forms in 2035 (S4), P&W's GTF2 folds in. GTF2 was launched in 2030 on P&W's public six-year, durability-first programme with no compressed testing. The rules let a further-along programme bring the ready year forward, so the engine is ready in 2036, one year ahead of NGSA's 2037 EIS.
- Nothing is compressed: the fold carries GTF2's own test clock. We count on no entry into service before 2036.
- Our 2030 public line, 'no earlier than six years from the Joint Venture's formation' (2041 for a 2035 formation), was written for a Joint Venture without a fold. Watson rules that service from a 2036 ready year is not an early date under his test.
- To keep our word clean, I record openly that the fold sets the ready year and that the 2030 formation + 6 line is superseded. The 2035 statement does not repeat it and gives no date at all: 'Maturity sets the date, and we compress nothing.'
- My own dates have slipped before [RX-0077, RX-0129], so I rely on his date, not mine. I am sure enough to commit [RX-0124], because the readiness is P&W's public, durability-first programme and not a new clock of ours.

5. WATSON'S BINDING GROUNDS, EACH MET
(a) No EIS or ready date earlier than 2036, and no NGSA date, in the statement or any public other move. There are none.
(b) Nothing counts on entry into service before 2036. Nothing does.
(c) A support plan in place before NGSA's EIS, recorded here. It has six parts:
- P&W's narrowbody network (the GTF shops on the A320neo fleet) as the base;
- partner shops on the Singapore Joint Venture model, named at formation;
- spares, repair technology and field service inside our $4B share;
- an EIS support team with Airbus before entry into service;
- castings and forgings with high-performing suppliers, off the Trent lines;
- our V2500 operator relationships.
That gives two years from formation to EIS. The plan works because P&W's network already exists. The milestones stay private.
His condition (4) is also met: UltraFan content goes in only where it does not reopen the test programme, and changes to the core definition go in as a later insertion after EIS.

6. McCABE'S CO-SIGNATURE AND HER CONDITIONS
- She co-signs: +1.52 expected, worst column 0, a crude IRR of about 58% and NPV at 18% of about +4.4 to +4.6.
- Her four withdrawal cases are all avoided:
  - Watson confirms 2036 without compression.
  - No concession or aggressive terms are attached.
  - No widebody item is beside the commit.
  - The 2045 review is recorded: withdraw unless a live airframe not yet in service can use the engine by its EIS.
- Capex at 1.36 $/£:
  - On six-year phasing, $0.67B, about £0.49bn a year (£2.94bn in total). That is 53% of MS 2030E company-funded R&D (£927m) and 6.4% of MS 2030E FCF.
  - If the board books it towards the 2036 ready year: £1.47bn a year over two years (19% of MS FCF), or £2.94bn in one year (39%). The cash is there. A flat envelope would be strained in those years; she flags it as advice.
  - It is funded from FCF. Net cash of £12.7-16.3bn in 2030E. No equity, no borrowing, and the 2026-28 buybacks closed and untouched.
- The GTF2 write-off at the fold is P&W's. No Solo of ours is live, so nothing folds and nothing is written off.

7. WHAT HOLD GIVES UP, PRICED
- `launch_if_selected` held: +1.40 in S3 only, +0.14 weighted.
  - If it fired, it would put $8.0B of our own narrowbody money against Control's $4B bound, with no way back.
  - It would cost about £0.84bn a year (91% of 2030E R&D) and take the one-programme slot.
  - It contradicts our public 'partnership, not a solo programme'.
  - Declared premium $0.14B. It is a narrowbody premium, so the $1B UltraFan WB sub-cap does not apply.
  - It also gives up narrowbody entry in S3 (29.0% in 2050). That is the price of the mission's terms.
- The unconditional Solo is rejected: -3.46 weighted, worst -4.20. Beside the commit it is -3.06. Ready in 2042, it is after NGSA's EIS, and no fps is on the record. Airframers first [RX-0058].
- Trent 1000 upgrade alone: -1.01 (worst -1.03). It would need a $1.01B premium against hold and $2.67B against the best plan. It gives up the +15.23 in S4. Widebody share is 55.2%, above 50%, so it is not needed. Deferred.
- UltraFan WB: -3.69, worst -4.00. No Re-engine is on the record. Rejected.
- Widebody beside narrowbody: the upgrade costs -6.03 in S4 and UltraFan WB -9.00, both worse than their own bills, with $5B of strain. Struck.

8. CONTROL'S MISSION, EVERY COLUMN (own narrowbody money / strain / widebody share 2050 / narrowbody share 2050)
- S1, S2, S3, S5, S6, S7: $0.0B / $0B / 55.2% / 0.0%.
- S4: $4.0B / $0B / 55.2% / 32.3%.
- Met in every column.

9. CONSEQUENCES CARRIED FORWARD
- If the Joint Venture forms (S4), any later UltraFan WB or Trent 1000 upgrade carries $5B of strain for the rest of the game and breaks the mission's 'never both'. A Re-engine answer would then need that price weighed openly.
- If it does not form, the 2045 order is `withdraw`, unless a live airframe not yet in service can use the engine by its EIS. With the commitment withdrawn and no narrowbody on record, the upgrade is re-tested then.
- UltraFan WB is re-tested only against an A350 Re-engine, or a 787 Re-engine that names UltraFan, on the record.

Where this rests on doctrine rather than my record: the first-commit reading (dashboard_game.md §5 and the Board's partner test), and the fold-sets-the-date reading (public rules and Watson). My record has no Joint Venture terms [erginbilgic.md §6].

- Worst column: the commit's is 0; the off-grid reasonable worst case is -4.00, the bill.
- Capex: about £0.49bn a year on six-year phasing (53% of MS 2030E company-funded R&D), or £1.47bn a year if booked over two years. It is redeployed from base UltraFan maturation and funded from FCF.
- No equity, no borrowing, and the 2026-28 buybacks untouched.
- No concession, payment or aggressive term is attached. Pricing discipline goes through the Investment Committee.

priorities: 1. Product safety and maturity come first. A Joint Venture engine serves NGSA only if it is ready by NGSA's 2037 EIS. If the Joint Venture forms this round, P&W's GTF2 (launched 2030, ready 2036 on the public record) folds in, so the engine is ready in 2036, one year of margin. If it forms in any later round, it misses NGSA. No compressed maturity, no entry date disclosed, and support through partner shops in place before EIS. 'product safety, which is and always must be our most important priority' [RG-0027, RG-0025, R-0970, R-1476, RX-0296, RX-0283, RX-0284].

2. Protect the widebody cash cow (Control's mission). Our own narrowbody money stays within $4B. The Joint Venture share fits: $4.0B, spent only in S4. An $8B UltraFan NB Solo does not fit, whether conditional or unconditional. No narrowbody item beside a widebody programme, because the $5B strain is charged whatever the dates. Widebody dominance holds without any programme: 55.2% in 2045 and 2050 in every column of the hold row [RG-0068, R-1574, RX-0214].

3. Partner first and airframe first, and this is the round to act. NGSA is live, not yet in service, and carries code 7 (RR, P&W and CFM). A live airframe's code therefore includes P&W, so our partner-alignment test is met without waiting for P&W's commitment to appear on the record. 2035 is the only round in which a Joint Venture can reach NGSA's 2037 EIS; a Solo launched now is not ready until 2042. The commit costs nothing unless P&W commits in the same round, and it is worth +15.23 if P&W does [R-1010, R-0916, R-0318, RX-0118, R-0994, R-1005].

4. Profit over share, and one big programme at a time. Every narrowbody item needs a weighted value of at least 0 with no premium. No item may lose more than its own bill in any plausible column. No widebody programme beside any narrowbody item, inside a broadly flat R&D envelope [R-1011, R-1582, R-1561, RG-0033, R-0929, R-1127, RG-0019].

5. The balance sheet and the capital order stand: balance sheet first, then the dividend, then investment, with the 2026-28 buybacks untouched. A Joint Venture at about $0.67B (about £0.49bn) a year fits inside the envelope [RX-0242, RG-0041, RG-0059, R-0900].
board_guidance.risk_appetite: Averse, 4 of 5. We accept staged and shared narrowbody risk only. The Joint Venture commit (worst column 0, +15.23 if P&W commits) is the form our doctrine prefers, and it keeps our own narrowbody money within $4B. We will not accept an unconditional UltraFan NB Solo, a widebody programme committed without a Re-engine on the record, or any item that can lose more than its own bill.
