recommendations.text: Commit to the Joint Venture with Pratt & Whitney this round, with every other field at hold. NGSA's code 7 already names both P&W and us. The commitment stands and costs nothing unless P&W commits too: 0 in six columns, +15.23 in S4, with own narrowbody money of $4.0B and $0 strain. Orders are sealed, and 2035 is the only round in which a Joint Venture can reach NGSA's 2037 EIS. Waiting for P&W's commitment to appear on the record would therefore mean missing NGSA. The dashboard maps our rule to 'commit when P&W has committed, or commit first if your doctrine allows', and this case is the risk-sharing form our doctrine prefers. If the ExCo holds, it should price what it gives up in `rationale`.

Safety first, before anything else. The public statement should give no entry date at all, not even a 'formation plus six' line, and nothing on NGSA's or any airframer's dates. It should say that the engine enters service only when it is ready and its durability is proven, with support in place before entry into service. Watson should state the 2036 ready year from the folded GTF2 and the one-year margin to 2037, confirm that nothing is compressed, and name the support plan: P&W's network, partner shops on the Singapore model, spares inside the bill, and castings and forgings off the Trent lines.

Hold UltraFan NB Solo in both forms. The unconditional launch cannot meet NGSA's EIS and loses about $4B in six columns. `launch_if_selected` is worth only +1.40, and only in S3 (about +0.14 weighted), and it would put $8.0B against Control's $4B bound for the fps alone. The narrowbody entry, inside the bound, is the Joint Venture. If the conditional form is held, declare the +0.14 forgone in `rationale`.

No widebody programme this round. Widebody share is 55.2% in 2045 and 2050 in every column, above the 50% line, and no Re-engine is on the record. Beside the Joint Venture, the Trent 1000 upgrade costs -6.03 in S4 and UltraFan WB -9.00, and either would breach 'never both'. Keep the one-programme slot for the narrowbody entry. In 2045, re-test the upgrade only if the Joint Venture has not formed and the commitment is withdrawn. Re-test UltraFan WB only against a Re-engine on the record (in S5 a 787 Re-engine cuts Airbus's widebody airframe share to 30.2%).

Review the standing commitment every round. If the Joint Venture has not formed by 2045 and no live airframe not yet in service can use its engine in time, withdraw it. That stops a late P&W commitment from committing $4B to an orphan programme, and stops it from locking the widebody slot under the mission. Cancel what no airframe can use.

Show every item's worst column and its capex a year against a broadly flat R&D envelope. The Joint Venture is about £0.49bn a year, about 53% of MS 2030E company-funded R&D (£927m). The Solo would be about £0.84bn. The capital order stays as it is: balance sheet, then the dividend, then investment, with the 2026-28 buybacks untouched. 'Terms that credit the technology we bring' asks for value, not a concession: no aggressive terms without joint CEO-CFO sign-off.

frame.situation:
Public record (round 2 bulletin):
- NGSA (Airbus): launched 2030, EIS 2037, code 7 (RR, P&W, CFM). If nothing changes it gets CFM and P&W; RR is dropped because we have no engine ready by its EIS. Airbus runs the Alt A320 plan, with A320 lines kept longer through the ramp-up.
- P&W GTF2 Solo: launched 2030, ready 2036. P&W's words: "We have no Joint Venture to announce", standard terms, and no compressed testing to make a date.
- CFM/GE GEnx upgrade: ready since 2033. CFM gives no date on a new engine and "will commit a new engine with a committed airframer".
- Boeing: no fps and no date. When it does launch, it wants more than one engine source. It is adding 787 capacity at Charleston.
- Embraer: no decision, no segment, no date. Any Embraer airframe flies P&W or CFM engines, never ours.
- No 787 or A350 Re-engine is on the record.
- Our own record: we launched nothing in 2030. Our 2030 public statement said we stand ready to commit to a Joint Venture with P&W, that our route is "a partnership, not a solo programme", and that EIS comes "no earlier than six years from the Joint Venture's formation".

Timing if we move this round (public rules):
- A Joint Venture formed in 2035 takes in the folded GTF2, which is further along, so it is ready in 2036: one year of margin to NGSA's 2037 EIS. Formed in 2045 or later, it misses NGSA.
- A Solo launched in 2035 is ready in 2042. That misses NGSA. It could meet an fps 7-year launched now (EIS 2042, zero margin) or an fps 10-year (EIS 2045, three years of margin). `launch_if_selected` fires only for an fps launched this round on a code that includes RR.
- 2035 is the last round in which any narrowbody engine of ours can be fitted in time to count for 2045.

Our position:
- Hold row: -0.56 (S1-S4, S7) and -0.65 (S5-S6). The loss is the GEnx upgrade from 2042.
- Objectives:
  - Enter the narrowbody: not met (0% in 2045 and 2050).
  - Widebody dominance: met, 58.0% to 2041 and 55.2% from 2042 in every column of the hold row.
  - Control's mission: met, with $0 of narrowbody money and $0 strain.

The Board's guidance:
- Its lean: `jv_with_pw: commit`, everything else hold. It reads its partner test as met, because NGSA's code 7 includes P&W.
- It would approve `launch_if_selected` but does not recommend it. It would approve the Trent 1000 upgrade only alone, with the shortfall declared.
- It would veto:
  - an unconditional Solo;
  - UltraFan WB;
  - any widebody item beside a narrowbody item;
  - a commit without McCabe's co-signature, or one that fails Watson's ready year or support test.
- It wants a public statement with no dates at all.

- This round's public statement gives no entry date at all, not even a 'formation + 6' line, and nothing on any airframer's dates.
- Never disclose an EIS earlier than launch plus development years.

If either test fails, hold. The team rule 'jv_pw only if P&W announced' is read openly against the dashboard mapping ('commit when P&W has committed, or commit first if your doctrine allows') and the Board's partner test. I set this out in the decision.

Watson's Civil veto binds [RX-0296, RX-0283, RX-0284]: compressed maturity, a disclosed early EIS, or no support in place before EIS. Overrides stay empty.
Premium cap: at most $3B a round against the best expected plan, and at most $1B on an UltraFan WB. Every premium is declared.

   - No Solo is live, so nothing of ours folds and there is no cancel write-off this round.

6. Premiums:
   - Choosing B ('hold + commit to JV') over C ('if selected + commit to JV') costs $0.14B. Confirm it.
   - If we hold everything, we give up $1.52B.
   - What would the Trent 1000 upgrade alone need as a premium: against hold, and against the best plan?
   - Your view: is $0.14B the right price for keeping the $4B bound and our 'partnership, not a solo programme' line?

7. Terms. 'Terms that credit the technology we bring' asks for value; it is not a concession. Confirm that no aggressive terms are in play.
frame.asks_ops:
Rob, maturity and delivery. My own dates have slipped before [RX-0077, RX-0129], so I lean on yours.

1. Ready by EIS.
   - A Joint Venture formed in 2035, with GTF2 (launched 2030) folded in, is ready in 2036 against NGSA's 2037 EIS: one year of margin. Is that a full-maturity programme or compressed? P&W says it runs six years of development, durability first, and will not compress testing.
   - What does our UltraFan technology add to that engine, and can it go in without taking time out of the test programme?
   - Are you sure we can deliver to 2037? "Until I am sure we will deliver, I'm not committing" [RX-0124].

2. The early-date test.
   - Our 2030 statement said entry into service "no earlier than six years from the Joint Venture's formation". That would be 2041 for a 2035 formation.
   - Does serving NGSA in 2037 on the folded engine breach your Civil veto, or our own word? My reading: the engine's development clock started with GTF2 in 2030, so 2036 is launch plus six. The rules allow a fold to bring the date forward.
   - The new statement will carry no date at all. Is that enough? Rule on it before I decide.

3. The Solo, for the record.
   - Launched in 2035 it is ready in 2042. That misses NGSA, gives zero margin against an fps 7-year launched now (EIS 2042), and three years against an fps 10-year (EIS 2045).
   - Confirm that `launch_if_selected` can fire only when the engine would be ready by EIS.

4. Strain and the one-programme slot.
   - Confirm $0 strain with the Joint Venture alone.
   - Once it forms, any UltraFan WB or Trent 1000 upgrade carries $5B for the rest of the game.
   - What do we give up on widebody if a Re-engine comes later?

5. Capacity.
   - In S4 our narrowbody share is 32.3% in 2050. On 2050 demand of 1,933 aircraft, two engines each, that is roughly 1,250 engines a year (inference), against 197 Trent a year.
   - How do we split build and overhaul with P&W, and what keeps Trent time on wing and the Trent XWB and Trent 7000 ramps first?

6. Support plan before EIS. Name it:
   - P&W's narrowbody network;
   - partner shops on the Singapore model [RX-0287];
   - spares and field service inside the bill;
   - an EIS support team with Airbus;
   - castings and forgings with high-performing suppliers, off the Trent lines.

7. Widebody share against the 50% line.
   - Confirm, in every column of the hold row and the Joint Venture row: 58.0% to 2041, 55.2% in 2045 and 2050.
   - Upgrade 60.0%. UltraFan WB 64.8% only in S5 and S6.
   - Confirm nothing widebody is needed this round.
   - Name the 2045 re-test condition for the upgrade: the Joint Venture has not formed, and the commitment is withdrawn.

8. Check the draft public statement in my lean against your veto.
frame.initial_lean:
My proposal: `jv_with_pw: commit`, with `ultrafan_nb_solo: hold`, `ultrafan_wb: hold` and `t1000_upgrade: hold`.

Why:
- Airframers first, and the airframer has gone first. NGSA is live, not in service, and its code 7 names both P&W and us [RX-0058, R-1005].
- Partner alignment is in the airframe's own code. That is the test whose failure took us out of IAE [R-0318].
- "We don't need partnership for capability, but our preference is that" [RX-0118]. There is no change of strategy [RX-0098]: in 2030 we said publicly we stand ready to commit, and "when we commit something, we honor it" [RX-0124].
- The commitment is 0 in six columns and +15.23 in S4. Worst column 0 against a $4B bill, +1.52 weighted. Own narrowbody money is $4.0B at most, inside Control's bound. Strain $0.

On the team rule:
- The literal rule is 'jv_pw only if P&W announced'. In 2030 I said I would commit once P&W was on the record.
- The rule exists so that we never hold a Joint Venture commitment no airframe can use [RX-0051], and never partner without alignment.
- Here a live airframe can use it, and only this round. Orders are sealed, so waiting for P&W on the record means choosing to miss NGSA.
- The dashboard allows a first commit where doctrine does, and the Board reads its partner test as met. I read this as a doctrine-allowed first commit (inference).
- Binary framing [RX-0050]: P&W comes to the table this round, or the commitment is withdrawn in 2045 if no live airframe can use it.

Conditions: McCabe's co-signature, and Watson's confirmation of the 2036 ready year with nothing compressed, plus the support plan. If either fails, the order goes to hold. That is Do Nothing, giving up +1.52.

Solo:
- Held in both forms. `launch_if_selected` is worth +0.14, and only in S3, where it is $8B against a $4B bound.
- It would also break our public 'partnership, not a solo programme'. Declared premium: $0.14B, inside the $3B cap. It is a narrowbody premium, so the $1B UltraFan WB sub-cap does not apply.

Widebody:

- The upgrade beside the Joint Venture loses -6.03 in S4, and UltraFan WB -9.00. Both are struck.

Draft statement (no dates):
"So. Rolls-Royce commits to a Joint Venture with Pratt & Whitney for the next narrowbody, on terms that credit the technology we bring. Our preference has always been partnership. It is for an airframe that has chosen both of us. The engine enters service only when it is ready and its durability is proven, with support through partner shops in place before entry into service. No solo narrowbody programme. Widebody is our core, and we will protect it. We won't do anything not profitable."

Safety, then the balance sheet; the commit passes both.

Against hold the row is 0, 0, 0, +15.23, 0, 0, 0. It spends nothing unless P&W commits this round, so the worst column is 0 against a $4B bill: +1.52 on the illustrative weights, positive on any weights. Off the grid, if P&W commits and Airbus recodes NGSA to code 6, we lose the $4B bill at most.

What has moved is an announced customer: Airbus has put us and P&W on NGSA. The commitment carries its own partner test, because no money moves without P&W. I co-sign on that basis. The 2036 ready year is Rob's to confirm; if it fails, S4 is no longer +15.23 and my signature goes with it.

Cash: about £0.49bn a year over six years, 53% of 2030E company-funded R&D, so redeployed, not added. Booked over two years, £1.5bn a year, 19% of 2030E free cash flow. No equity, no borrowing, buybacks untouched.

I would co-sign `launch_if_selected` (+1.40, S3 only), but $0.14B is a fair price for the $4B bound. I will not sign an unconditional Solo (-3.46), UltraFan WB (-3.69), or a widebody item beside the commit (-6.03, -9.00).

My record on launch economics is thin; these are board numbers. In 2045, withdraw unless a live airframe can use it. That's how you should hold it.

That gives a ready year of 2036 against NGSA's 2037 EIS: one year of margin, more than the zero margin I passed in 2030. Nothing is compressed. The fold carries GTF2's own test clock (2030 + 6) and takes nothing out of it. Condition (inference): our UltraFan content goes into the Joint Venture engine only where it does not reopen the GTF2 test programme. Anything that would change the core definition goes in as a later insertion after EIS, so 2036 stays a real date. A Joint Venture formed in 2045 or later misses NGSA, which is in service from 2037. In S1-S3 and S5-S7 nothing forms and nothing is fitted. UltraFan NB launched in 2035 is ready in 2042. Against NGSA (EIS 2037) it is five years late, so the unconditional Solo fails (advice). Against an fps 7-year launched in 2035 (EIS 2042) it has zero margin, but no column shows that case. Against an fps 10-year launched in 2035 (EIS 2045, S3) it has three years of margin. `launch_if_selected` fires only if the engine would be ready by the EIS, so it passes by construction. Embraer flies P&W or CFM, never us: not applicable.

tests.name: No early date
tests.threshold: No disclosed EIS or ready date earlier than these, and nothing on any airframer's dates: for the Joint Venture, formation + 6 (2041 for a 2035 formation) or the bulletin's folded-GTF2 ready year (2036); for UltraFan NB, launch + 7 (2042); for UltraFan WB, launch + 6 (2041).
tests.numbers: The CEO's draft statement carries no date at all and says nothing on NGSA's 2037 EIS. 'Enters service only when it is ready and its durability is proven, with support through partner shops in place before entry into service' passes. Our 2030 statement said 'no earlier than six years from the Joint Venture's formation', which is 2041 for a 2035 formation. That line was written for a Joint Venture without a fold. The rules let a folded Solo that is further along bring the ready year forward, and the bulletin shows GTF2 ready in 2036. Serving NGSA in 2037 from a 2036 ready year is therefore not an early date under my test. Advice: do not repeat the formation + 6 line, because it would contradict service in 2037. Record openly in the rationale that the fold sets 2036, and keep the support milestones in the private rationale, not the statement. I will recheck the final text and the public other moves at step 4.

tests.name: Support before EIS
tests.threshold: RR has no narrowbody MRO scale, so a support plan through partner shops must exist before any narrowbody EIS (inference).
tests.numbers: This passes only if the plan below goes into the rationale with the commit. NGSA's EIS is 2037 and formation would be 2035, so there are two years to stand support up. That is tight for us alone; it works because P&W's network already exists (inference). The plan: (1) P&W's narrowbody network, the GTF shops already supporting the A320neo fleet, as the Joint Venture's base (inference). (2) Partner shops on the Singapore Joint Venture model, named at formation in 2035. (3) A spares pool, repair technology and field service, funded inside our $4B share. (4) An EIS support team with Airbus, in place before entry into service. (5) Narrowbody castings and forgings placed with high-performing suppliers, off the Trent lines. (6) Our V2500 relationships with A320 operators, whose aftermarket runs 'into the 2030s'. The round-1 groundwork study (a private other move) means the plan is ready to name. These milestones stay private: none goes in the statement, because they would imply a date.

tests.name: Engineering load
tests.threshold: $5B of strain whenever a narrowbody project (UltraFan NB or the Joint Venture) and a widebody project (UltraFan WB or the Trent 1000 upgrade) are both on record, whatever their dates. Red lines: no UltraFan WB beside an UltraFan NB Solo unless both are selected; no upgrade while an UltraFan is in development (inference).
tests.numbers: Recommended plan ('UltraFan NB: hold + commit to JV'): $0 strain in all seven columns. A standing commitment that has not formed is not a programme on record: 'commit to JV + T1000 upgrade' shows $0 strain outside S4. In S4 the folded engine is one year from ready, so our 2035-36 load is integration, certification support and the support and supply set-up, not a fresh seven-year development (inference). Rejected plans: (1) 'commit to JV + T1000 upgrade': $5B in S4 and -6.03 against 'hold + commit to JV', worse than its own $2B bill. The upgrade runs 2035-38 and the Joint Venture engine is in development to 2036. (2) 'commit to JV + UltraFan WB': $5B in S4, -9.00. (3) 'if selected + T1000 upgrade': $5B in S3, -6.03, with the upgrade (2035-38) overlapping UltraFan NB (2035-42) for 3 years. That breaks the red line. (4) 'if selected + UltraFan WB': $5B in S3, and UltraFan WB (2035-41) sits beside an UltraFan NB Solo with no Re-engine selecting it. That breaks the red line. Once the Joint Venture forms, any later widebody programme carries $5B for the rest of the game. The engine is ready in 2036, so it can no longer be cancelled to remove the strain. A commitment still standing in 2045 could form late and charge the same $5B, so review it then.

tests.name: Capacity and suppliers
tests.threshold: State RR's engines a year from the brief's year table. The board has no engine capacity limit, so the result is not applicable unless the brief reports one. A narrowbody ramp is flagged as needing partner MRO and high-performing supplier capacity, as advice (inference).
tests.numbers: Hold year table: 197 widebody engines a year to 2041 and 188 from 2042, with 0 narrowbody. The brief has no year table for the Joint Venture plan. In S4 our narrowbody share is 32.3% in 2050. On 2050 demand of 1,933 aircraft at two engines each, that is about 1,250 engines a year credited to us (inference). That is about 6.6 times the Trent rate, with P&W holding an equal share. The build and overhaul split with P&W should be set in the Joint Venture agreement at formation. I have no evidence on it, so this is inference: my default is that P&W's network leads overhaul, and we bring the technology and partner-shop capacity on the Singapore model. My own midterm ramp was widebody: OE 300-350 a year, total shop visits 1,100-1,200. I use my figure, not the 1,400-1,500 Helen gave. Advice: Trent time on wing and the Trent XWB and Trent 7000 ramps keep first call on engineers, shops and castings.

tests.name: Widebody dominance
tests.threshold: RR widebody engine share of at least 50% in 2040, 2045 and 2050 on the brief's projection. Time on wing is the lever (inference).
tests.numbers: Hold row and 'hold + commit to JV' row: 58.0% in 2040, then 55.2% from 2042 (after the GEnx upgrade, ready since 2033), so 55.2% in 2045 and 2050 in every column, S1-S7. That is 5.2 pp above the line, and the Joint Venture does not move widebody share. The upgrade would give 60.0% in 2050. UltraFan WB gives 64.8% only in S5 and S6. Nothing widebody is needed this round. The 2045 re-test condition for the upgrade: the Joint Venture has not formed and the commitment is withdrawn, so no narrowbody programme is on record. Re-test UltraFan WB only against a Re-engine on the record. In S5 Airbus's widebody airframe share falls to 30.2%, but the board's engine shares do not move with that split.

tests.name: Technology pull-through
tests.threshold: An idle or cancelled UltraFan still feeds the Trent fleet. Noted qualitatively; grid values are never adjusted (inference).
tests.numbers: UltraFan maturation continues inside base R&D and feeds Trent time on wing. In S4 the Joint Venture could add a two-way flow: geared-core durability learning from GTF2 back into UltraFan and Trent (inference). No grid adjustment.

vetoes.plan: 'UltraFan NB: hold + commit to JV' (the CEO's lean)
vetoes.ground: Not invoked. I hold the Civil veto for step 4, on its grounds only. Under the team rule it binds if: (a) the final statement or a public other move gives any EIS or ready date earlier than 2036 (the bulletin's folded-GTF2 ready year), or any NGSA date; (b) the statement, an other move or the rationale counts on the engine entering service before 2036; or (c) the rationale carries no partner-shop support plan in place before NGSA's 2037 EIS. The ground rests on attributed transcript turns [RX-0296, RX-0284, RX-0283].

vetoes.plan: Our 2030 public line ('no earlier than six years from the Joint Venture's formation') against service on NGSA in 2037
vetoes.ground: Note, not a veto ground. The fold rule and the bulletin set a ready year of 2036 (GTF2 2030 + 6), so 2037 is not an early date. To keep our word clean, do not repeat the line, and record the supersession openly in the rationale.

vetoes.plan: Unconditional 'UltraFan NB Solo' (2035, ready 2042)
vetoes.ground: Ready by EIS fail against NGSA's 2037 EIS, and no fps is on the record. This is advice, not a Civil veto. It is also a Board veto and fails the CFO's grounds. Its support would rest on partner shops alone, with no P&W network.

vetoes.plan: 'UltraFan NB if selected' (alone or beside the commit)
vetoes.ground: No Civil ground. It passes Ready by EIS by construction: three years of margin against S3's fps 10-year (EIS 2045), zero against an fps 7-year (EIS 2042). My advice is hold. It would put a second narrowbody architecture, all-RR, on engineers with no MRO scale. The $8B against Control's $4B bound is the CEO's and CFO's call.

vetoes.plan: Any widebody item beside a narrowbody item (commit + upgrade, commit + UltraFan WB, if selected + either)
vetoes.ground: Red-line breach and strain, not a Civil veto. Each carries $5B of strain: -6.03 (upgrade) and -9.00 (UltraFan WB) in S4, and -6.03 in S3. The 'if selected' pairs break 'no upgrade while an UltraFan is in development' and 'no UltraFan WB beside an UltraFan NB Solo unless both are selected'. The CEO strikes them.

vetoes.plan: 'UltraFan NB: hold + T1000 upgrade' (alone)
vetoes.ground: Advice. The upgrade is my time-on-wing tool, but on this grid it is -1.01 weighted (worst -1.03), and it gives up the only round in which the Joint Venture can reach NGSA. Defer it; re-test in 2045 if the Joint Venture has not formed and the commitment is withdrawn.

ops.would_change_mind_if: I would move `jv_with_pw` to hold, or invoke the Civil veto, in five cases. (1) The rationale carries no partner-shop support plan before NGSA's 2037 EIS: the veto binds. (2) The final statement or a public other move discloses any EIS or ready date before 2036, or any NGSA date: the veto binds. (3) The statement or rationale counts on entry into service before 2036: the veto binds. (4) 'Terms that credit the technology we bring' turns into UltraFan content that reopens the GTF2 test programme. 2036 would then no longer be a mature ready year, and a 2037 service date would be compressed maturity in practice, so the order should hold unless that content moves to a later insertion (inference). (5) Public evidence shows GTF2 slipping past 2036 or its testing being cut. Helen withholding her signature also sends the order to hold, and I would concur with Do Nothing, which passes every test of mine. I would back `launch_if_selected` only if Tufan and Helen decide Control's $4B bound does not govern; readiness passes by construction. I would back the Trent 1000 upgrade only once no narrowbody programme is on record, or a Re-engine is.
ops.memo:
Tufan, Helen: one Rolls-Royce, one programme.

Maturity. A Joint Venture formed this round takes in GTF2, launched 2030 and ready 2036 on P&W's six-year, durability-first programme. Against NGSA's 2037 EIS that is one year of margin, more than the zero I passed in 2030. Nothing is compressed: the fold carries GTF2's test clock, it does not shorten it. One condition: our UltraFan content goes in only where it does not reopen that test programme; the rest is a later insertion.

Dates. Your draft carries none: enough. Our 2030 line, "no earlier than six years from formation", was written without a fold. Don't repeat it; record in the rationale that the fold sets 2036, and say nothing on Airbus's dates.

Support. Two years from formation to EIS. P&W's narrowbody network; partner shops on the Singapore model, named at formation; spares and field service inside our $4B; an EIS support team with Airbus before 2037; castings and forgings with high-performing suppliers, off the Trent lines. Put it in the rationale, or I veto at step 4.

Load. Strain $0. Once formed, any widebody programme carries $5B for good: the upgrade beside it is -6.03 in S4, UltraFan WB -9.00.

Capacity. S4 means about 1,250 narrowbody engines a year by 2050 against 197 Trent. Trent time on wing keeps first call.

Widebody: 58.0% in 2040, 55.2% in 2045 and 2050, every column.

Solo: hold in both forms. I recommend commit, the rest hold. No veto. We're pacing that programme properly.

other_moves.move: Standing Joint Venture commitment with Pratt & Whitney, on standard terms
other_moves.detail: The `jv_with_pw: commit` is public at once and stands until withdrawn. It is for an airframe that has chosen both makers. The terms credit the technology Rolls-Royce brings, which asks for value; it is not a concession. There is no payment to P&W or to any airframer, no launch-style pricing and no free upgrades. No dates.

other_moves.move: Continue UltraFan technology maturation inside the existing R&D envelope
other_moves.detail: Demonstrator and geared-architecture work carries on inside base R&D and feeds Trent time on wing. No new programme, no new bill, no dates.

other_moves.move: Name the narrowbody support plan at formation (Watson)
other_moves.detail:
If the Joint Venture forms this round, the plan is named at formation and in place before entry into service. It has six parts:
(1) P&W's narrowbody network, the GTF shops already supporting the A320neo fleet, as the Joint Venture's base.
(2) Partner shops on the Singapore Joint Venture model, named at formation.
(3) A spares pool, repair technology and field service, funded inside our $4B share.
(4) An EIS support team with Airbus, in place before entry into service.
(5) Narrowbody castings and forgings placed with high-performing suppliers, off the Trent lines.
(6) Our V2500 relationships with A320 operators.
The milestones stay private, because they would imply a date.

other_moves.move: UltraFan content in the Joint Venture engine: nothing that reopens the test programme
other_moves.detail: Our technology goes into the Joint Venture engine only where it does not reopen the folded engine's test programme. Anything that changes the core definition goes in as a later insertion after entry into service. The engine's ready year stays a mature date, and nothing is compressed (Watson's condition).

other_moves.move: 2045 review of the standing commitment
other_moves.detail: If the Joint Venture has not formed by 2045, the 2045 order is `jv_with_pw: withdraw`, unless a live airframe not yet in service can use the engine by its EIS. A hold would leave the commitment standing. This stops a late P&W commitment from putting $4B into an orphan programme and from locking the widebody slot (McCabe's condition, the Board's recommendation 5).

other_moves.move: Pricing discipline on every engine campaign
other_moves.detail: No concessions to buy a narrowbody selection. Every new contract goes through the Investment Committee, with win-win terms and value paid for [RX-0081, RX-0055, RX-0097]. Any aggressive term needs joint CEO-CFO sign-off, and none is proposed.

other_moves.move: Capital order unchanged
other_moves.detail: The Joint Venture share is funded from free cash flow and redeployed inside a broadly flat R&D envelope, with the UltraFan maturation work in base R&D as the natural source. No equity, no new borrowing, no levering up for buybacks. The order stays: balance sheet first, then the dividend, then investment.

decision.public_statement: So. Rolls-Royce commits to a Joint Venture with Pratt & Whitney for the next narrowbody. Our preference has always been partnership, and there is no change of strategy. The commitment stands, for an airframe that has chosen both of us, on terms that credit the technology we bring. No solo narrowbody programme. The engine enters service only when it is ready and its durability is proven. Maturity sets the date, and we compress nothing. Support through partner shops will be in place before entry into service. Widebody is our core, and we will protect it. We are not after market share. We won't do anything not profitable. I will say that categorically.
decision.rationale:
DECISION: `jv_with_pw: commit`, with `ultrafan_nb_solo: hold`, `ultrafan_wb: hold` and `t1000_upgrade: hold`. This is my framing proposal, unchanged. The only Board item is the commit.

1. TEAM RULE, STEP BY STEP
- Start: my proposal, 'UltraFan NB: hold + commit to JV'.
- Binding vetoes. McCabe co-signs the commit. Her binding vetoes cover the unconditional Solo, UltraFan WB, the upgrade beside a narrowbody item, and the upgrade alone without a premium; none is submitted. Watson invokes no Civil veto. His three binding grounds are each met below (section 5).
- Expected scenario: S1, rivals hold (0.45).
- Best grid plan inside the red lines on expected PV: 'UltraFan NB if selected + commit to JV', +1.09. My plan is +0.95, $0.14B below it. I keep it as the plan favoured by doctrine and the mission, and declare the premium, inside the $3B cap.
- Red-line strike: no red-line flag is raised against the submitted plan. The flags both memos raise apply to rejected plans (widebody beside narrowbody, and the 'if selected' pairs), and those are struck.
- Tie-break: mine. It was not needed, because all three recommend the same orders.

2. GRID ROWS FOR THE BOARD (S1-S7, $B ΔPV against the status quo)
- Submitted, 'UltraFan NB: hold + commit to JV': -0.56, -0.56, -0.56, +14.67, -0.65, -0.65, -0.56. Expected +0.95. Worst column -0.65 (S5-S6).
- Commit at hold, 'UltraFan NB: hold': -0.56, -0.56, -0.56, -0.56, -0.65, -0.65, -0.56. Expected -0.57.
- Item (commit against hold): 0, 0, 0, +15.23, 0, 0, 0. That is +1.52 weighted and never below 0 under any weights. Worst column 0, against a -$4B bill.
- Weights (mine, the same as McCabe's and the Board's illustrative set): S1 0.45, S2 0.10, S3 0.10, S4 0.10, S5 0.10, S6 0.05, S7 0.10. Each non-hold column has at most a weak signal on the record (P about 0.10).
- Off-grid reasonable worst case (McCabe): P&W commits and Airbus recodes NGSA to code 6. The Joint Venture forms and fits nothing, so we lose at most the bill, -4.00, with a joint weight of about 0.01. No item can lose more than its own bill.

3. THE TEAM RULE 'jv_pw only if P&W announced', READ OPENLY
- Read literally, the rule is not met. P&W's words are 'We have no Joint Venture to announce'. In 2030 I said we would commit once P&W was on the record, and McCabe's 2030 condition was the same. She says so plainly, and so do I.
- The rule has two purposes. We never hold a Joint Venture commitment that no airframe can use [RX-0051], and we never partner without alignment [R-0318].
- Both purposes are met in substance:
  - The Joint Venture forms, and our $4B is spent, only in a round in which P&W commits. In six columns nothing moves.
  - The alignment is in the airframe's own code. NGSA is live, not in service, and code 7 names P&W and us.
- Orders are sealed and simultaneous. 2035 is the only round in which a Joint Venture can reach NGSA, so waiting for P&W on the record would mean choosing to miss NGSA.
- The dashboard maps our rule to 'commit when P&W has committed, or commit first if your doctrine allows'. The Board's partner test (a live airframe's code includes P&W) is met. I read this as a doctrine-allowed first commit. That reading is inference and doctrine, not my record.
- Binary framing [RX-0050]: P&W comes to the table, or the commitment is withdrawn in 2045.

4. READY BY EIS AND THE 2030 LINE (Watson's ruling)
- If the Joint Venture forms in 2035 (S4), P&W's GTF2 folds in. GTF2 was launched in 2030 on P&W's public six-year, durability-first programme with no compressed testing. The rules let a further-along programme bring the ready year forward, so the engine is ready in 2036, one year ahead of NGSA's 2037 EIS.
- Nothing is compressed: the fold carries GTF2's own test clock. We count on no entry into service before 2036.
- Our 2030 public line, 'no earlier than six years from the Joint Venture's formation' (2041 for a 2035 formation), was written for a Joint Venture without a fold. Watson rules that service from a 2036 ready year is not an early date under his test.
- To keep our word clean, I record openly that the fold sets the ready year and that the 2030 formation + 6 line is superseded. The 2035 statement does not repeat it and gives no date at all: 'Maturity sets the date, and we compress nothing.'
- My own dates have slipped before [RX-0077, RX-0129], so I rely on his date, not mine. I am sure enough to commit [RX-0124], because the readiness is P&W's public, durability-first programme and not a new clock of ours.

5. WATSON'S BINDING GROUNDS, EACH MET
(a) No EIS or ready date earlier than 2036, and no NGSA date, in the statement or any public other move. There are none.
(b) Nothing counts on entry into service before 2036. Nothing does.
(c) A support plan in place before NGSA's EIS, recorded here. It has six parts:
- P&W's narrowbody network (the GTF shops on the A320neo fleet) as the base;
- partner shops on the Singapore Joint Venture model, named at formation;
- spares, repair technology and field service inside our $4B share;
- an EIS support team with Airbus before entry into service;
- castings and forgings with high-performing suppliers, off the Trent lines;
- our V2500 operator relationships.
That gives two years from formation to EIS. The plan works because P&W's network already exists. The milestones stay private.
His condition (4) is also met: UltraFan content goes in only where it does not reopen the test programme, and changes to the core definition go in as a later insertion after EIS.

6. McCABE'S CO-SIGNATURE AND HER CONDITIONS
- She co-signs: +1.52 expected, worst column 0, a crude IRR of about 58% and NPV at 18% of about +4.4 to +4.6.
- Her four withdrawal cases are all avoided:
  - Watson confirms 2036 without compression.
  - No concession or aggressive terms are attached.
  - No widebody item is beside the commit.
  - The 2045 review is recorded: withdraw unless a live airframe not yet in service can use the engine by its EIS.
- Capex at 1.36 $/£:
  - On six-year phasing, $0.67B, about £0.49bn a year (£2.94bn in total). That is 53% of MS 2030E company-funded R&D (£927m) and 6.4% of MS 2030E FCF.
  - If the board books it towards the 2036 ready year: £1.47bn a year over two years (19% of MS FCF), or £2.94bn in one year (39%). The cash is there. A flat envelope would be strained in those years; she flags it as advice.
  - It is funded from FCF. Net cash of £12.7-16.3bn in 2030E. No equity, no borrowing, and the 2026-28 buybacks closed and untouched.
- The GTF2 write-off at the fold is P&W's. No Solo of ours is live, so nothing folds and nothing is written off.

7. WHAT HOLD GIVES UP, PRICED
- `launch_if_selected` held: +1.40 in S3 only, +0.14 weighted.
  - If it fired, it would put $8.0B of our own narrowbody money against Control's $4B bound, with no way back.
  - It would cost about £0.84bn a year (91% of 2030E R&D) and take the one-programme slot.
  - It contradicts our public 'partnership, not a solo programme'.
  - Declared premium $0.14B. It is a narrowbody premium, so the $1B UltraFan WB sub-cap does not apply.
  - It also gives up narrowbody entry in S3 (29.0% in 2050). That is the price of the mission's terms.
- The unconditional Solo is rejected: -3.46 weighted, worst -4.20. Beside the commit it is -3.06. Ready in 2042, it is after NGSA's EIS, and no fps is on the record. Airframers first [RX-0058].
- Trent 1000 upgrade alone: -1.01 (worst -1.03). It would need a $1.01B premium against hold and $2.67B against the best plan. It gives up the +15.23 in S4. Widebody share is 55.2%, above 50%, so it is not needed. Deferred.
- UltraFan WB: -3.69, worst -4.00. No Re-engine is on the record. Rejected.
- Widebody beside narrowbody: the upgrade costs -6.03 in S4 and UltraFan WB -9.00, both worse than their own bills, with $5B of strain. Struck.

8. CONTROL'S MISSION, EVERY COLUMN (own narrowbody money / strain / widebody share 2050 / narrowbody share 2050)
- S1, S2, S3, S5, S6, S7: $0.0B / $0B / 55.2% / 0.0%.
- S4: $4.0B / $0B / 55.2% / 32.3%.
- Met in every column.

9. CONSEQUENCES CARRIED FORWARD
- If the Joint Venture forms (S4), any later UltraFan WB or Trent 1000 upgrade carries $5B of strain for the rest of the game and breaks the mission's 'never both'. A Re-engine answer would then need that price weighed openly.
- If it does not form, the 2045 order is `withdraw`, unless a live airframe not yet in service can use the engine by its EIS. With the commitment withdrawn and no narrowbody on record, the upgrade is re-tested then.
- UltraFan WB is re-tested only against an A350 Re-engine, or a 787 Re-engine that names UltraFan, on the record.

Where this rests on doctrine rather than my record: the first-commit reading (dashboard_game.md §5 and the Board's partner test), and the fold-sets-the-date reading (public rules and Watson). My record has no Joint Venture terms [erginbilgic.md §6].

memo_weighing.cfo:
Weighed fully. Her numbers carry the cash case.
- I accept her co-signature on the commit and her open reading: her 2030 condition (P&W on the record) is not met as written, but it is met in substance, because no money moves without P&W in the same round. NGSA's code 7 is an announced customer naming both makers.
- I adopt her capex figures: £0.49bn a year on six-year phasing, £1.47bn a year or £2.94bn in one year if compressed in booking. I also adopt her balance-sheet passes and her off-grid worst case: the bill, -4.00, at a joint weight of about 0.01.
- I accept her price of $0.14B for holding `launch_if_selected` as fair for keeping the $4B bound.
- All four of her withdrawal cases are avoided. Her 2045 review condition is recorded as a private other move and becomes the 2045 default: withdraw.
- Her binding vetoes are respected: no unconditional Solo, no UltraFan WB, no upgrade beside the commit or alone.
- Her advice on a flat envelope under compressed booking is noted. The money is redeployed from base UltraFan maturation, not added.
memo_weighing.ops:
Weighed fully on maturity, dates and support. His word decides the ready year, because my own dates have slipped [RX-0077, RX-0129].
- I accept his ruling: the fold carries GTF2's 2030 + 6 test clock, so the 2036 ready year is mature, nothing is compressed, and serving NGSA from it is not an early date.
- I took his advice not to repeat the 2030 formation + 6 line, and recorded its supersession openly.
- His three binding grounds are each met: no date in public, nothing counting on service before 2036, and the six-part support plan in the rationale.
- His condition that UltraFan content goes in only where it does not reopen the test programme is adopted as a private other move.
- I take his strain warning (once formed, any widebody programme carries $5B for good) and his capacity advice (about 1,250 narrowbody engines a year in S4 by 2050; Trent time on wing and the Trent XWB and Trent 7000 ramps keep first call).
- His widebody check (58.0% in 2040, 55.2% in 2045 and 2050, every column) confirms that nothing widebody is needed.
- He flags red-line breaches only on rejected plans, and they are struck.

decision.expected_scenario: S1: rivals hold (weight 0.45). P&W keeps its GTF2 Solo and does not commit to the Joint Venture this round. Airbus keeps NGSA on code 7, and CFM and P&W are fitted. Boeing launches no fps, there is no Re-engine, and Embraer does not launch. Our standing commitment then costs nothing and is reviewed in 2045.
decision.best_grid_plan_in_expected_scenario: In S1, four rows tie as the best plan at -0.56: 'UltraFan NB: hold', the submitted 'UltraFan NB: hold + commit to JV', and both 'UltraFan NB if selected' rows. Across all seven columns, the best plan on expected PV is 'UltraFan NB if selected + commit to JV', at +1.09 on the weights S1 0.45, S2 0.10, S3 0.10, S4 0.10, S5 0.10, S6 0.05, S7 0.10. embraer.public_statement:
Safety first and quality always: that is the foundation of our culture. We believe we are still in our harvest season, right? We keep delivering our plan with the products we have: the E2 family, our executive jets, defence and services. And we keep a healthy balance sheet to support a potential next move.

On a new airplane I will give the same answer I always give. We are investing in new technologies so that we are prepared to make that decision when the time comes. A launch needs a strong product with a strong value proposition and a robust, I mean, funding strategy, because we don't want to put in risk the financial health of the company. We have done the work, and the numbers today do not prove the return. So today we have no decision to announce, and we will not discuss a segment or a date. We continue to talk to our partners, including in Korea, and to all the engine makers. Any large investment will be made with partners, with the funding defined at the time of approval. I will not say conservative, but I would say, realistic.

On the decisions of other manufacturers: those are their decisions. We have our own strategy, and I can only speak for Embraer.

On trade, Embraer is about engineering. We focus on data and things that are under our control. More than 40% of our aircraft is US content, so tariffs mean fewer US parts bought and fewer US jobs. We continue to work with both governments for zero tariffs in aerospace, and we are cautiously optimistic.

We compete hard in every campaign, but we don't sell our aircraft below cost. As we proudly say in Embraer, We Live for the Challenge.
embraer.rationale:
Decision: Hold (`enb: hold`), the default. It is not a Board item, and no override is needed. This is a Hold on the grid, not on the tie-break.

1. The grid (brief §3, Launch the new narrowbody with Korea against Do Nothing, debt penalty included):
- S1 (Rivals hold): -0.58 $B (94.7%, -5.3 yp);
- S2 (Boeing launches fps 10-yr): -0.82 $B (-7.5 yp);
- S3 (Boeing launches fps 7-yr): -0.86 $B (-7.8 yp);
- S4 (Airbus cancels NGSA): -0.58 $B (-5.3 yp).
Do Nothing is +0.00 $B (100.0%) in every column and is the brief's best plan in all four. My expected column is S1: the bulletin shows NGSA on its path and no fps, and I do not speculate on Boeing's or Airbus's sealed orders. The risk column is S3, the worst plausible, since the brief labels no risk case. Three rebuilds (mine, Santana's, Meijer's) agree, and so does the Board's: $0.99B of operating profit in PV, less $1.42B for our $5.50B share booked at 2039, less a $0.15B PV debt-penalty rise, gives -0.58. The grid already nets the penalty, so it is not subtracted again.

2. My four questions.
- (1) Strong product, strong value proposition? Weak. The jet enters service in 2039, two years after NGSA (2037). It is slightly better than the A320neo and 737 MAX but worse than a new-generation airplane, and wins 6.3% of new customers, 3.6% once fps follows. $6.0M a jet is slight, not compelling.
- (2) Robust funding without risk to financial health? No. Team Korea's 30% is in the brief, so H1 passes. But our 55% takes net debt from $0.7B to $6.2B (56% of EV, about 7.5x against the inherited 2x), and investment grade does not survive that in Santana's reading. Leg 2 (S1 at or above zero) fails by $0.58B; leg 3 (S3 within -5 yp) fails at -7.8 yp. That breaches H2, my own line [EX-0140].
- (3) Technology available? Yes on the brief: P&W is fitted, GTF2 is ready in 2036, and the brief reports no engine or supply problem. But the window is narrow in S1-S3.
- (4) Will the investment prove its return? No. Even in S4, with the window open, the 96-a-year line caps operating profit at $0.576B a year, and that does not carry a $5.50B bill. Meijer said it plainly: it's the bill.

3. Team rule, in order.
- The CFO's funding veto binds, with no override: legs 2 and 3 fail.
- Meijer's soft veto stands: NGSA is in service before our 2039 entry into service in S1-S3. An override would need a plan more than +5 yp ($0.55B) above Hold in S1; the launch is 5.3 yp below, $1.13B short. No override is recorded.
- The hard rules: H3 is not engaged (fps in 2042 or 2045, both more than 2 years after 2039), and H6 is not live.
- The 2035 tie-break (launch if ΔPV is at or above zero) does not apply: the gap is 2.6 to 3.9 times the 2-yp band, and ΔPV is negative.
- It is also a one-way door: no round falls between 2035 and the 2039 entry into service, so no cancel could answer a slip.

4. What I did not let decide.
