cfo.memo:
Felipe here. Funding test on the brief's numbers. Expected column S1, as Gomes Neto named it; risk column S3, worst plausible, since none is labelled. Tests and thresholds are inherited from Garcia, unchanged; the 5-point limit is the team rule.

Leg 1, partners: pass. Team Korea 30% ($3.0B), suppliers 10%, Brazilian research 5%, all in the brief. Our 55%, $5.50B, is booked at entry into service in 2039.

Leg 2, cost of capital: fail. Launch against Do Nothing in S1 is -0.58 $B, -5.3 yield points, debt penalty netted once ($0.59B rise, $0.15B in present value). S4 reads the same: the line binds, not demand. My rebuild reconciles: $0.99B operating profit, less $1.42B bill, less $0.15B.

Leg 3, bad case: fail. S3 is -0.86 $B, -7.8 points, against a 5-point limit. S2 is -7.5.

So I veto the 2035 launch, and the team rule makes it binding.

Advice, inherited from Garcia: net debt goes to $6.2B, 56% of enterprise value, about 7.5x against "below 2x". In my reading investment grade does not survive that. The cash call is $1.375B a year in 2035-38, 3.4x our capex run rate. No cancel round before 2039: a one-way door.

The gap closes only near a 36% own share, about $1.9B more partner money. Tariffs do not help in S1, right? No credit until a brief shows it.

The 2040 objective costs 5.3 points, above the 5-point cap, and never cures a failed leg. Premium zero. Do Nothing. A conservative approach.

tests.name: Market window against fps and NGSA (veto leg a)
tests.threshold: From the bulletin, find any launched fps or NGSA and its EIS. Window = the first new-generation EIS minus ours. Pass if none is launched or the window covers our ~6-year ramp. Flag (advice) if it is shorter than the ramp. Fail (soft veto, leg a) if a new-generation type is due at or before our EIS. Basis: my E2 record applied by inference, plus company record (no head-to-head entry while Boeing and Airbus hold that segment).
tests.numbers: Bulletin: NGSA launched 2030, EIS 2037; no fps launched. Our EIS is 2039 (2035 + 4). Window = 2037 - 2039 = -2 years, so we enter two years behind a new-generation type in S1, S2 and S3. S4 (Airbus cancels NGSA this round, a sealed order): no type in service, window open-ended. An fps launched this round enters service in 2042 (S3, 3 years after ours) or 2045 (S2, 6 years after). Value that depends on the rivals: S4 -0.58 = S1 -0.58, so NGSA in service costs $0.00B on the grid, because the line binds at 6.3% (next test). The second type costs $0.24B (S2, 2.2 yp) and $0.28B (S3, 2.5 yp). The NGSA date is a bulletin fact, not a sealed order, so leg (a) fails on the record. (Record by inference; company record.)

tests.name: Share path through the ramp, by column: who sets deliveries (CEO ask 2)
tests.threshold: Read our share at EIS and at full rate in the brief; say whether the line or customer demand sets deliveries (inference, using the rules' demand curve with COMAC off the top).
tests.numbers: Share of new customers after the US cut. S1: 10.8% in 2035-36, then 6.3% from 2037 to 2058. S2: 6.3% to 2044, 3.6% from 2045. S3: 6.3% to 2041, 3.6% from 2042. S4: 10.8% throughout. Line: 16, 32, 48, 64, 80, 96 (2039-2044), then 96 to 2058 (20 market years). Wanted aircraft (share x the rules' demand, less COMAC; before COMAC in brackets): 6.3% wants 96-120 a year in 2039-2050 (106-132), against a 96 line. So the line binds in S1 and S4, which is why they read the same. The brief's S1 rows show deliveries equal to the line in every year to 2060, with overflow filling the 2054-58 tail (69-91 wanted). 3.6% wants 52-69 a year (61-75), so the share binds from 2043 in S3 and from 2045 in S2. My share-bound shortfall is $0.30B (S3) and $0.25B (S2) in PV, against the grid's $0.28B and $0.24B; overflow refills a few slots. CEO's reading confirmed. S1 rebuild: operating profit PV $0.986B, less bill PV $1.416B (5.50 / 1.11^13), less the debt-penalty rise of $0.590B (net debt $0.7B to $6.2B, 56% of EV; PV $0.152B) = -0.582 $B (-5.3 yp). It matches the grid. Work: work/r2_meijer_test_calc.py, work/r2_meijer_check.py.

tests.name: Product edge over the A320neo and 737 MAX
tests.threshold: State the edge in the brief's numbers and whether it is compelling (company record: no head-to-head entry without a compelling advantage). Inference: my E2 case does not carry over to a 150-180 seater. Advice only; not a veto leg.
tests.numbers: Rules: 'slightly better for airlines than the 737 MAX and A320neo and worse than a new-generation airplane'. On this bulletin the narrowbody enters service in 2039, already worse than NGSA (in service 2037). It wins 6.3% of new customers, not 10.8%, and 3.6% once fps is also in service. $50M at 12% is $6.0M a jet, $0.576B a year at 96. That is slight, not compelling. My E2 case (trip cost, complementing the big jets) does not carry over to an airplane that fights them head-on, and the first E-Jet 'struggled to get to the right cost level' against them. I name my E2 anchoring here. Advice, not a veto ground.

tests.name: Customers and campaigns
tests.threshold: Back a launch only where Embraer's share is positive at EIS and at full rate in the expected case and Hold's E2 business is not reduced (inference from record).
tests.numbers: Expected column S1, share of market deliveries: 0.9% (2039, 16 jets), 1.8% (2040), 4.8% at full rate (2044, 96 jets), 5.0-5.7% in 2045-2055. Positive. Brief: E-Jets and business jets are the same in every plan, so Hold's E2 business is not reduced. Buyers (inference): E-Jet operators moving up, multi-OEM buyers, lessors and low-cost carriers. Even at 6.3% they want 96-120 a year against a 96 line. I note my campaign optimism; only the brief's share is in these numbers.

tests.name: Price discipline
tests.threshold: Report the price effect from the brief and whether it reaches Embraer's own margin, as a number (inference).
tests.numbers: Rules: from 2038 (one year before our EIS), the prices Boeing and Airbus get on new single-aisle jets fall by up to 2.0%, in a straight line over 7 years (to 2045). The cut is 2.6% on Boeing in years with no new Boeing narrowbody in service: every year in S1 and S4, to 2042 in S3, to 2045 in S2. It falls on their margins, not ours: the brief fixes our $50M at 12%. Advice (inference against company record): 12% is 4.6 times the 2.6% Commercial Aviation earned in 2025. Each 1 pp of our margin is worth $0.082B in PV. Zero in S1 needs about 19.1% at $50M, and the override bar needs about 25.8%. The brief shows 12%, so no credit; pricing to win against NGSA would push it down, not up.

tests.name: Supply chain and ramp (veto leg b)
tests.threshold: Take the brief's ramp as given, never a faster one. Fail (soft veto) if the brief reports a supply-chain problem that would hold the line; flag a lesser risk (advice). Mostly company record.
tests.numbers: The brief reports no supply-chain problem. Ramp as given: 16, 32, 48, 64, 80, 96 (2039-2044). Advice flags, not veto grounds. (1) Company record: the E-Jet line climbs toward 120 commercial jets a year by 2030, 'if the investments justify the return', with bottlenecks that move between suppliers. Adding 96 makes 216 a year by 2044, 1.8 times the 2030 target. (2) In the same years Airbus runs the A320 Alt-plan tail (82, 62, 52, 42, then 14 a month over about eight years from 2037) beside the NGSA ramp (rate 50 about 2041, 100 about 2045), and adds up to 20 a month from 2045. Korean industry builds structures for Boeing and Airbus today (rules), so a second line competes for the same supply base (inference). Our hit has been 'a lot less than on the competitors' because core work stays in-house (record).

tests.name: Engines and system supply (veto leg b, CEO ask 3)
tests.threshold: Pass if the brief shows an engine on offer by EIS with no live delivery or durability problem; fail (soft veto) if no engine is on offer or a live engine problem would hold the line. Record plus company record.
tests.numbers: Rules: the narrowbody flies P&W engines (the E2's maker). CFM's Embraer partnership is not live (no such order on the bulletin). P&W's GTF2 was launched in 2030 and is ready in 2036, three years before our 2039 EIS. P&W says nothing enters service before durability is proven. The brief reports no engine problem, so nothing holds the line or the four-year development. Advice (bulletin plus inference): P&W's output is tied to Airbus under rate-gated agreements (the GTF tail on the A320 Alt plan through about 2045, plus NGSA framework agreements). At full rate our line needs 192 P&W engines a year before spares. P&W admits its GTF fleet fell short 'for years', and the Hot Section kit's time on wing is not yet proven. Engines were 'part of the supply chain challenges' in our guidance (record). Korea has no airliner engine (research, unverified). The board prices no engine shortfall.

tests.name: Clean-sheet schedule and certification (CEO ask 5)
tests.threshold: Advice only: set the board's 4-year development against our own record. A slip is a veto ground only if the brief reports it (inference).
tests.numbers: The brief reports no development or certification problem, so there is no veto ground. Company record: the E2, a re-wing and re-engine of an existing family, took about 4 years 10 months from launch (June 2013) to first delivery (April 2018), with a clean entry into service. The board gives a clean-sheet 150-180 seater, a step Embraer has never taken, four years (2035-2039), then a 6-year line ramp. One-way door: no round falls between 2035 and 2039, so a cancel could never answer a slip (the board prices none). Embraer integrates and certifies; the partner cannot fill that gap (research, unverified).

tests.name: Partner fit (Team Korea)
tests.threshold: Report the partner's share of the bill from the brief; flag a plan that relies on the partner for integration or certification (inference).
tests.numbers: Brief: Team Korea 30% ($3.0B), risk-sharing suppliers 10% ($1.0B), Brazilian state research money 5% ($0.5B). Embraer carries 55% ($5.50B), booked at EIS 2039. Embraer leads the airframe (inference from the 2011 lead-airframer stance); the brief does not rely on the partner for integration or certification. The funding verdict is Santana's.

tests.name: Customer politics and the high-volume market (CEO ask 6)
tests.threshold: Advice only: report the tariff effect from the brief and discount US campaigns by a number (company record plus inference).
tests.numbers: Brief: the US climate cuts our share of new customers by 10% (7% to 6.3%, 4% to 3.6%). In S1 and S4 the line binds: 7.0% would want 118-146 a year, 6.3% wants 96-120, against 96. The cut costs about $0.01B in PV, in the 2054-58 tail, which overflow fills. In S2 and S3, 4.0% against 3.6% is about 6-8 jets a year: $0.04B (S2) and $0.05B (S3). So yes, the jet sells its line into the big markets in S1 and S4, the US included. The US discount is 10% of share, worth $0.00-0.05B on this grid. Not priced: BNDES credit, the golden share, any US response to a Brazil-Korea airliner. Over 40% US content cuts both ways (company record).

tests.name: Override of my soft veto (team rule, CEO ask 7)
tests.threshold: An override needs a plan more than 5 yp (+$0.55B) better than Hold in the expected column, recorded by the CEO as a Board item.
tests.numbers: Expected column S1: Launch -0.58 $B (94.7%, -5.3 yp) against Hold +0.00. The bar is +0.55 $B, so the launch is $1.13B (10.3 yp) short. No valid override exists on this grid. On the brief's terms it would take our own share near 17% or a margin near 26% (CEO's and my rebuilds); the brief shows neither, so no credit.

tests.name: Hard-rule check (H3 shut window, H6 fps via Embraer, H1 partner)
tests.threshold: Flag an order the rules or profile hard rules forbid (not my veto).
tests.numbers: H3: at EIS 2039 only NGSA is in service (2037). fps is due 2042 (S3, 3 years after) or 2045 (S2), not within 2 years, so H3 is not engaged in any column. H6: Boeing's fps via Embraer is not live. If Boeing orders it this round, its order stands and our launch is refused. H1: Team Korea's 30% is in the brief. H2 and the funding legs are Santana's; I state only the grid: -0.58 (S1, S4), -0.82 (S2), -0.86 (S3).

tests.name: Forward flag: a 2045 launch, EIS 2049 (CEO ask 8)
tests.threshold: The same window rule applied forward: narrow (soft veto) if one type is in service at 2049; shut (H3) if both are in service or due within 2 years. Not this round's order.
tests.numbers: NGSA would have been in service for 12 years by 2049, so leg (a) fails for every later launch unless Airbus cancels NGSA this round (S4). If Boeing launches fps now (7-yr, EIS 2042; 10-yr, EIS 2045), both types are in service at 2049: the window is shut (H3), no launch. If fps is launched only in 2045 (sealed then), it enters service in 2052 (7-yr, 3 years after ours) or 2055: narrow, not shut. A 2049 entry into service sells into falling demand: 1,701 a year in 2055 and 1,106 in 2060 (rules). fps via Embraer bars us for good.

vetoes.plan: Launch the new narrowbody with Korea in 2035 (EIS 2039)
vetoes.ground: Narrow window, leg (a). The bulletin shows NGSA launched in 2030 and due in service in 2037, two years before our 2039 EIS. In S1, S2 and S3 the narrowbody would enter service behind a new-generation type, with its share of new customers already cut from 10.8% to 6.3% before its first delivery, and to 3.6% once fps follows (2042 in S3, 2045 in S2). Leg (b) passes: P&W is fitted, GTF2 is ready in 2036, and the brief reports no engine or supply-chain problem. Under the team rule this is a soft veto. It binds unless Gomes Neto records an override, as a Board item, for a plan more than 5 yp (+$0.55B) better than Hold in the expected column. In S1 the launch is -0.58 $B (-5.3 yp), $1.13B short of that bar, so no valid override exists. For the Board, plainly: on the grid the window is not what sinks the launch. S4 (window open) reads the same -0.58 as S1, because the 96-a-year line, not demand, sets deliveries. The problem is the bill.

vetoes.plan: Readiness advice on any launch (not binding)
vetoes.ground: Advice only, not a veto ground, since the brief reports none of these as a problem. (1) Supply base: 216 commercial jets a year by 2044 (1.8 times the 2030 E-Jet target), on suppliers that also feed Airbus's A320 Alt tail and NGSA ramp. (2) Engines: 192 P&W engines a year at full rate, behind Airbus's rate-gated agreements, with GTF durability still being proven in service. (3) Schedule: a clean sheet certified in four years against the E2's roughly five, with no cancel round before 2039. (4) US tariffs: worth $0.00-0.05B on this grid.

vetoes.plan: Forward flag: launch in 2045 (EIS 2049), not this round's order
vetoes.ground: NGSA in service since 2037 puts any later launch under leg (a) of my soft veto. If Boeing launches fps this round (EIS 2042 or 2045), both types are in service at 2049: shut window, hard rule H3, no launch at all. I will recount on the 2045 bulletin.

ops.would_change_mind_if: On the window, leg (a): only if NGSA would not be in service by 2039, which is Airbus cancelling it (S4). That is a sealed order I cannot see this round. Even then S4 reads -0.58, the same as S1, because the line binds, so lifting my veto would not make the launch pay. Toward a launch: a brief showing ΔPV at or above zero in S1 with the debt penalty included. On these terms that means our own share near 36% (partners near 64%), or a margin near 19% at $50M. Clearing my veto by override takes more than +0.55 $B in S1 (own share near 17%, margin near 26%). No credit until a brief shows any of it. Toward a harder line: a brief reporting a P&W delivery or durability problem, or a supplier constraint that would hold the line (leg b). Or fps launched this round, which shuts a 2045 launch under H3.
ops.memo:
That's a triple layer question. Three parts.

First, the window. NGSA is launched and due in service in 2037. Our entry into service is 2039. In S1, S2 and S3 we come in two years behind a new-generation airplane, and our share of new customers drops from 10.8% to 6.3% before we deliver a jet. That is leg (a) of my soft veto, and it stands. An override needs a plan 5 yield points better than Hold. This one is 5.3 below, $1.13B short of the bar. Only S4 opens the window, and that is a sealed order.

Second, the line. P&W is fitted, GTF2 is ready in 2036, and the brief reports no engine or supply problem, so leg (b) passes. Three flags, advice only: 216 commercial jets a year by 2044 on suppliers that also feed Airbus's two single-aisle lines; 192 P&W engines a year behind Airbus's supply agreements; and a clean sheet in four years, when the E2 took nearly five.

Third, the customers. Even at 6.3% they want 96 to 120 jets a year against a 96 line. So in S1 and S4 the line sets deliveries, and NGSA costs us nothing on the grid. fps costs $0.24-0.28B, the US cut at most $0.05B. If no one sits on the seat, it's pure cost. Here the seats are full and we still lose $0.58B. It's the bill, right?

Hold. Window and customers rest on my E2 record, by inference; supply and schedule on company record.

other_moves.move: Deliver the plan and keep building cash to support a potential next move
other_moves.detail: We keep delivering the E2 family, the business jets, defence and services to plan in the harvest season. Productivity comes before new capacity. Commercial output rises toward about 120 jets a year only where the return justifies it, keeping supply-chain headroom [EX-0053, EX-0080, EX-0077, EX-0078, EX-0087]. The cash and the low net debt ($0.7B) are kept to support a potential next move. The board does not price this.

other_moves.move: Keep technology readiness funded for the next product cycle
other_moves.detail: Studies continue for a new cycle of products, naming no segment and no date. We keep talking to all the engine makers and select none, because engine selection comes before any business case [EX-0112, EX-0141, EX-0133, EX-0044]. Meijer's readiness advice is logged for any later case: supplier headroom for a second line beside the E2 ramp, P&W's durability-before-entry-into-service stance, and a four-year clean-sheet certification against the E2's roughly five years.

other_moves.move: Continue the Team Korea / KAI talks on a funding solution
other_moves.detail: I follow the talks personally every two weeks [EX-0028]. The aim is a funding solution defined before any business-case approval [EX-0046, EX-0034]. On this brief's terms a launch reaches zero in S1 only with our own share near 36% (partners near 64%, about $1.9B more than the $4.5B the brief shows). It stays within -5 yp in S3 only near 45%, and clears the Board's -2 yp near 34%. No credit until a brief shows the money. No segment, no date, no commitment. Embraer keeps control and no military technology moves, so the state's consent is not needed (golden share; Board recommendation 7).

other_moves.move: Carry the 2035 numbers into the 2045 package
Trade: argue on data, not politics
other_moves.detail: We keep working with both governments for zero-for-zero in aerospace. Our case is more than 40% US content and US jobs: tariffs mean fewer US parts bought and a limited ability to invest in the future [EX-0098, EX-0100, EX-0101, EX-0124]. The 10% share cut is already in the brief. It is not a reason for this decision, and on this grid it is worth $0.00-0.05B.

decision.public_statement:
Safety first and quality always: that is the foundation of our culture. We believe we are still in our harvest season, right? We keep delivering our plan with the products we have: the E2 family, our executive jets, defence and services. And we keep a healthy balance sheet to support a potential next move.

On a new airplane I will give the same answer I always give. We are investing in new technologies so that we are prepared to make that decision when the time comes. A launch needs a strong product with a strong value proposition and a robust, I mean, funding strategy, because we don't want to put in risk the financial health of the company. We have done the work, and the numbers today do not prove the return. So today we have no decision to announce, and we will not discuss a segment or a date. We continue to talk to our partners, including in Korea, and to all the engine makers. Any large investment will be made with partners, with the funding defined at the time of approval. I will not say conservative, but I would say, realistic.

On the decisions of other manufacturers: those are their decisions. We have our own strategy, and I can only speak for Embraer.

On trade, Embraer is about engineering. We focus on data and things that are under our control. More than 40% of our aircraft is US content, so tariffs mean fewer US parts bought and fewer US jobs. We continue to work with both governments for zero tariffs in aerospace, and we are cautiously optimistic.

We compete hard in every campaign, but we don't sell our aircraft below cost. As we proudly say in Embraer, We Live for the Challenge.
decision.rationale:
Decision: Hold (`enb: hold`), the default. It is not a Board item, and no override is needed. This is a Hold on the grid, not on the tie-break.

1. The grid (brief §3, Launch the new narrowbody with Korea against Do Nothing, debt penalty included):
- S1 (Rivals hold): -0.58 $B (94.7%, -5.3 yp);
- S2 (Boeing launches fps 10-yr): -0.82 $B (-7.5 yp);
- S3 (Boeing launches fps 7-yr): -0.86 $B (-7.8 yp);
- S4 (Airbus cancels NGSA): -0.58 $B (-5.3 yp).
Do Nothing is +0.00 $B (100.0%) in every column and is the brief's best plan in all four. My expected column is S1: the bulletin shows NGSA on its path and no fps, and I do not speculate on Boeing's or Airbus's sealed orders. The risk column is S3, the worst plausible, since the brief labels no risk case. Three rebuilds (mine, Santana's, Meijer's) agree, and so does the Board's: $0.99B of operating profit in PV, less $1.42B for our $5.50B share booked at 2039, less a $0.15B PV debt-penalty rise, gives -0.58. The grid already nets the penalty, so it is not subtracted again.

2. My four questions.
- (1) Strong product, strong value proposition? Weak. The jet enters service in 2039, two years after NGSA (2037). It is slightly better than the A320neo and 737 MAX but worse than a new-generation airplane, and wins 6.3% of new customers, 3.6% once fps follows. $6.0M a jet is slight, not compelling.
- (2) Robust funding without risk to financial health? No. Team Korea's 30% is in the brief, so H1 passes. But our 55% takes net debt from $0.7B to $6.2B (56% of EV, about 7.5x against the inherited 2x), and investment grade does not survive that in Santana's reading. Leg 2 (S1 at or above zero) fails by $0.58B; leg 3 (S3 within -5 yp) fails at -7.8 yp. That breaches H2, my own line [EX-0140].
- (3) Technology available? Yes on the brief: P&W is fitted, GTF2 is ready in 2036, and the brief reports no engine or supply problem. But the window is narrow in S1-S3.
- (4) Will the investment prove its return? No. Even in S4, with the window open, the 96-a-year line caps operating profit at $0.576B a year, and that does not carry a $5.50B bill. Meijer said it plainly: it's the bill.

3. Team rule, in order.
- The CFO's funding veto binds, with no override: legs 2 and 3 fail.
- Meijer's soft veto stands: NGSA is in service before our 2039 entry into service in S1-S3. An override would need a plan more than +5 yp ($0.55B) above Hold in S1; the launch is 5.3 yp below, $1.13B short. No override is recorded.
- The hard rules: H3 is not engaged (fps in 2042 or 2045, both more than 2 years after 2039), and H6 is not live.
- The 2035 tie-break (launch if ΔPV is at or above zero) does not apply: the gap is 2.6 to 3.9 times the 2-yp band, and ΔPV is negative.
- It is also a one-way door: no round falls between 2035 and the 2039 entry into service, so no cancel could answer a slip.

4. What I did not let decide. I did not launch for the 2040 objective, on 'last chance' grounds, to pre-empt Boeing's fps via Embraer (by rule Boeing's order would stand anyway), or because of what Airbus or Boeing did [EX-0093, EX-0069]. The US share cut is in the grid and is worth $0.00-0.05B; it did not drive the decision.

5. 'Not yet' bias. Not displayed: every test is resolved, and the answer on these terms is no, reported plainly. Partner dependence is shown only in keeping the talks going, with no credit for money the brief does not show.

6. Doctrine against record. My record drove this: funding defined at approval, return first, financial health [EX-0046, EX-0079, EX-0140]. The team rule and the hard rules confirmed it. No fallback to company doctrine was needed.

memo_weighing.cfo: Accepted in full. Santana's binding veto stands on leg 2 (S1 -0.58 $B, -5.3 yp, against a threshold of at or above zero) and leg 3 (S3 -0.86 $B, -7.8 yp, against the -5 yp limit). Leg 1 passes (Team Korea 30%, partners 45%, $4.5B). His rebuild ($0.986B operating profit, $1.416B bill, $0.152B penalty, -0.582) reconciles to mine and the brief, and the penalty is counted once. His advice lines (56% of EV, about 7.5x against 2x, investment grade lost, a $1.375B yearly call at 3.4x the capex run rate and 69% of the ~$2B cash floor) all point the same way, and I take them as advice. Gap-closing shares are logged for 2045 with no credit: 36.3% for zero in S1, 45.2% for -5 yp in S3, 34.2% for the Board's -2 yp, 16.6% for the override bar. I note his forward estimate of about -0.21 $B for a 2045 launch on a pure discount, which I treat as a rough flag only; the 2045 grid decides. Premium $0.00B confirmed. No override exists, and I sought none.
memo_weighing.ops: Accepted. Meijer's soft veto stands on leg (a): NGSA in service in 2037, two years before our 2039 entry into service in S1-S3. The window is open only in S4 and shut in no column (H3 not engaged). Leg (b) passes: P&W fitted, GTF2 ready in 2036, and no engine or supply problem in the brief. No override recorded: the team rule needs a plan more than +5 yp above Hold in S1, and the launch is 5.3 yp below. I take his central finding: the line, not demand, sets deliveries in S1 and S4 (6.3% wants 96-120 a year against a 96 line), so NGSA costs $0.00 on this grid, and the problem is the bill, not the window. fps costs $0.24-0.28B (S2, S3) and the US cut at most $0.05B. His readiness advice is logged for any later case: 216 commercial jets a year by 2044 on a shared supply base, 192 P&W engines a year behind Airbus's agreements, and a four-year clean sheet against the E2's nearly five. So is his margin finding: zero in S1 needs about 19% at $50M against the brief's 12%. Forward flag for 2045 noted: NGSA in service since 2037 puts any later launch under his leg (a), and an fps launched this round would shut a 2049 entry into service under H3.

decision.expected_scenario: S1 (Rivals hold). The bulletin shows NGSA launched in 2030, in development, with entry into service in 2037, and no fps launched. I do not speculate on Boeing's or Airbus's sealed orders. S1, tied with S4, is also the column most favourable to a launch, so the decision holds in every column. Risk column: S3 (Boeing launches fps 7-yr), the worst plausible, since the brief labels no risk case.
decision.best_grid_plan_in_expected_scenario: Do Nothing (no new narrowbody): +0.00 $B (100.0%) in S1. It is also the best plan in S2, S3 and S4. The Launch row reads -0.58 (S1), -0.82 (S2), -0.86 (S3) and -0.58 (S4) $B.
decision.premium_reason: No value is given up: Hold is the best grid plan in every column (+0.00 $B). Meeting the 2040 objective with a 2035 launch would cost $0.58B (5.3 yp) in S1, $0.82B (7.5 yp) in S2 and $0.86B (7.8 yp) in S3. All of these are beyond the $0.55B (5 yp) cap of H5, and they come against a binding CFO funding veto and a standing soft veto from Meijer, which no premium can cure. Premium logged at $0.00B (0 yp).
decision.objective_note:
The brief's objective has two parts.

'Profitable, the balance sheet safe: ΔPV at or above zero, debt penalty included' stays met (+0.00 $B).

'New narrowbody in service by 2040' is not met, and after this Hold it can no longer be met. 2035 was the last round in which a launch (entering service in 2039) could reach it. Meeting it would have cost at least 5.3 yp ($0.58B) in S1, above the 5-yp cap, against a binding CFO veto and a standing soft veto from Meijer.

We give that part up rather than pay for it. The objective changes no payoff, and it never cures a failed test. A place in the large single-aisle market stays open only if a later brief shows the launch paying on its own grid.
decision.predictions:
Private. Hold stands without Board review: ΔPV +0.00 $B, yield 100.0%, in every column. I do not forecast Boeing's or Airbus's orders. I keep S1 as the planning column, and the decision holds in S1 to S4.

For 2045, a launch would enter service in 2049, with NGSA in service for twelve years and demand falling after the mid-2050s. I expect the Launch row to stay below zero at a 55% share. Santana's rough ten-year-discount flag is about -0.2 $B, and the 2045 grid decides. So Do Nothing is likely right again, unless a brief shows partners carrying near two-thirds of the bill.

If this round's bulletin shows fps launched (7-yr, entry into service 2042; 10-yr, 2045), both types are in service at 2049. The window is then shut under H3, and there is no launch at all.

If Boeing orders fps via Embraer, our narrowbody is barred for good and we hold by rule.

The 2045 brief should show net debt still low, since no programme debt was added.

board_response.recommendation: Hold in 2035, and put the grid in the rationale. Log the premium at $0.00B.
board_response.response: Taken up in full. The order is Hold. The rationale carries the Launch row against Do Nothing in all four columns, debt penalty included: S1 -0.58 $B (-5.3 yp), S2 -0.82 (-7.5), S3 -0.86 (-7.8), S4 -0.58 (-5.3). This is a Hold on the grid, not on the tie-break: the launch fails my own condition of a funding strategy that does not put the company's financial health at risk. Premium logged at $0.00B.

board_response.recommendation: Record in the objective note that 2035 is the last round for the 2040 objective, that it is no longer reachable after this Hold, and that meeting it would have cost at least 5.3 yp ($0.58B), above the cap.
board_response.response: Taken up. The objective note records all of this. 2035 was the last round in which a launch (entering service in 2039) could meet the 2040 objective, and after this Hold it cannot be met. Meeting it would have cost at least $0.58B (5.3 yp), above the 5-yp cap, against Santana's binding veto and Meijer's standing soft veto. We give it up rather than pay for it. 'ΔPV at or above zero' stays met.

board_response.recommendation: Santana should carry the 2035 numbers into the 2045 package, with no credit for money a brief does not show.
board_response.response:
Taken up as an internal other move.
- Santana carries $0.99B of operating profit in PV, against $1.42B of bill and $0.15B of debt penalty.
- He carries net debt of $0.7B to $6.2B (56% of EV) against the 2x comfort and the ~$2B cash floor.
- He carries the gap-closing shares: our share near 36% for zero in S1 (about $1.9B more partner money than the $4.5B shown), 45% for -5 yp in S3, and 34% for the Board's -2 yp.
No credit until a brief shows the money.

board_response.recommendation: Keep technology readiness funded and the Team Korea talks going. For 2045, Santana and Meijer bring the Launch row (in service 2049), the window from the 2045 bulletin and the H3 check, and say plainly if the window is shut.
board_response.response: Taken up. Technology readiness stays funded (a public move, no segment, no date). I follow the Team Korea / KAI talks personally every two weeks (private). For 2045 I have asked Santana for the Launch row with a 2049 entry into service. I have asked Meijer for the window count from the 2045 bulletin with the H3 check, stated plainly. He has already flagged that an fps launched this round would shut it.

board_response.recommendation: Meijer should record the 2039 window count, note that in S1 and S4 the line sets deliveries so the problem is the bill, and keep supplier headroom and P&W's durability stance as readiness advice, not veto grounds.
board_response.response: Done in Meijer's memo, and I adopt it. The window is narrow in S1-S3 (NGSA in service from 2037), open only in S4, and shut in no column. The line sets deliveries in S1 and S4, so the problem is the bill, not the window. Supplier headroom for a second line (216 commercial jets a year by 2044) and P&W's durability-before-entry-into-service stance are logged as readiness advice. The brief reports no engine or supply problem, so neither is a veto ground.

board_response.recommendation: Keep the public statement on economics, not politics. Name no segment and no entry-into-service date. Make no comment on Airbus's NGSA or Boeing's choices. On US tariffs, argue US content, US jobs and zero-for-zero.
board_response.response: Taken up. The public statement names no segment and no date, and does not comment on other manufacturers' decisions ('those are their decisions').
